docs.title: Keel
docs.text:
Stop rebuilding the pipeline for every agent.

Keel is a context layer for the AI agents inside a product: a vertical SaaS, a consumer app, an internal tool. Domain events from your product go in. A bitemporal context graph per tenant comes out, whatever your unit is (an end-customer, a household, a team). Every agent you build reads and writes it through the same five tools, over MCP, HTTP or a typed SDK.

You describe your vertical once, in a cartridge: ontology, event catalog, semantic rules, memory policies. Keel's core knows nothing about your domain. Your second agent connects in a day instead of weeks, because there is no second pipeline to write.

Status

0.35.0, alpha. Runs embedded in Python, as a container (ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel), or hosted during the pilots. See the roadmap.

Pilot it with us

Run Keel on your product's events with your agents, with our help: your first pilot in a day. Open a pilot request, book 30 minutes at calendar.app.google/3oKUSqXTQPYmjya56, or write to angel@angelkurten.com.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Every new agent in a product repeats the same work: extract the customer's data, normalize it, decide what "critical" means, keep its own memory, expose its own tools to the model. Four agents, four copies of the customer's context, four definitions of "critical", four memories that never talk.

Existing memory layers ingest text and documents and model memory per user or per agent. None of them start from domain events, and none model the tenant your product already has: the end-customer of a B2B SaaS, the household of a consumer app, the team of an internal tool.

docs.title: How Keel is different
docs.text:
1. Cartridges. A vertical is declared in YAML plus a few ten-line handlers. The core stays generic. Write a cartridge for fleets, clinics, logistics, or your own product.
  2. Events in, not documents. Keel ingests structured facts with time: your Postgres tables through CDC, an outbox, a typed SDK, webhooks, Kafka, SQS. Ingestion is deterministic and cheap. The graph is exact because it is born from events, not inferred from text.
  3. Every fact carries its provenance. Source, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, and who corrected it. Audit-ready by construction.
  4. One graph per tenant. One subgraph per end-customer, household or team, with its own permissions and expiry.

Keel is not an agent framework (your agents stay where they are), not a document memory (no LLM reads your events) and not a copy of your database (the graph holds pointers to your rows).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Events are the truth and the graph is derived, so one tenant's subgraph can be rebuilt by replaying its log. Agents never see a pipeline: they see five tools (six, with the optional read-only query). Architecture walks through every box, with the options for each and when to pick which.

docs.title: Five tools, any agent (and an optional sixth)
docs.text:
Tool The question it answers context What do I know about this subject now, or at a past moment? Open facts, relations and rule verdicts. history How did it change over time, and when did we learn it? search Which subjects match? By text, kind, rule, attribute value or meaning. related What is it connected to, up to three hops? annotate Remember what an agent or a person concluded, with evidence and a scope. query (optional) Off unless enabled (keel serve --query): read-only SQL over views generated from the cartridge, to filter, join, count or aggregate. The store binds it to one tenant.

The names and signatures are part of the public standard; every parameter is in the specification.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/angelkurten/keel && cd keel
uv sync --extra dev
uv run keel validate examples/fleet --events examples/fleet/events.jsonl
uv run keel ingest examples/fleet examples/fleet/events.jsonl
uv run keel context examples/fleet examples/fleet/events.jsonl unit:MXK-4821

Then:

  • Architecture: the whole map, and your first day with Keel.
  • Your first cartridge in 20 minutes: declare your own vertical.
  • Send your events: Postgres CDC, the typed SDK, an outbox table, a webhook, Kafka, SQS or a .jsonl file.
  • Serve the tools: MCP, the HTTP JSON API, semantic search.
  • SDKs: a typed client generated from your cartridge (TypeScript, Python, Go, PHP), the way protoc does.
  • Operate: configuration, the container, and the jobs to schedule.
  • Specification: the normative contract for the envelope, the graph model, cartridges, tools and scopes.

docs.title: Keel specification
docs.text:
Version 0.35 · 2026-10-29 · Status: normative for the 0.35.x line; anything marked planned is not implemented yet.

This document is the contract. CLAUDE.md says how to work on the code; README.md says why Keel exists. If the code and this document disagree, one of them is wrong; open an issue.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.

docs.title: 1. Scope and terms
docs.text:
Keel is a context layer for the AI agents inside a product: a vertical SaaS, a consumer app, an internal tool. It turns domain events into a bitemporal context graph per tenant, declared by a cartridge, and exposes it to agents through five tools.

Term Meaning Product What runs Keel: a SaaS, a consumer app, an internal tool. Has its own database and its own tenants. Tenant The product's unit of data: one end-customer of a SaaS, a household, a team. Every graph is partitioned by tenant. Event A fact that happened in the product, with world time and source, in the standard envelope (§2). Subject The entity an event or fact is about, as <kind>:<id>. Entity A node in the graph: a kind, an id, a pointer (ref) to the system of record, and a few label attributes. Relation A typed, time-bounded edge between two entities. Fact A time-bounded (predicate, value) about a subject, with provenance. Cartridge The declaration of a domain: ontology, event catalog, handlers, rules, memory policy (§5). Handler Cartridge code that maps one event type's payload to store primitives (§4). Scope The sharing level of a fact: global, tenant, task, agent (§6). Tool One of the five operations agents use to read and write the graph (§7).

docs.title: 2. Event envelope
docs.text:
Every event, from any adapter, MUST be an envelope with these fields.

Field Type Req. Meaning id string no The source's own id when it has one. Otherwise a content hash of tenant, type, subject, occurred_at, source and payload, so the same stream yields the same ids on replay and a duplicate is recognizable. Used as evidence on derived facts. tenant string yes Tenant key. Opaque to Keel. type string yes Dotted lowercase event type from the cartridge catalog, e.g. inspection.created. subject string yes <kind>:<id>. kind MUST be an entity kind declared in the cartridge. occurred_at datetime (tz-aware) yes When it happened in the world. Valid time. recorded_at datetime (tz-aware) no When the source recorded it: transaction time. When the event declares it, what its handler writes carries it (a replay rebuilds the same history, a late event keeps its own time); when it does not, it defaults to now (UTC) and the facts carry the time they are ingested. source string yes System of record or adapter, e.g. fleet.vehicles, webhook:telematics. payload object no Event-specific data. The core MUST NOT read it. Only handlers do.

Rules:

  • A naive datetime is UTC, wherever a time enters: the envelope (a naive datetime never reaches a handler), the store primitives and every time argument of the tools.
  • occurred_at MAY be in the past relative to earlier events (late-arriving data). Handlers MUST use occurred_at as valid_from, never recorded_at.
  • Envelopes are immutable. An error in an event is corrected by a later event or by an annotate with corrected_by, never by editing the log.
  • Serialized form is JSON, one object per event. The reference development adapter reads one envelope per line (.jsonl), ignoring blank lines and lines starting with #.

docs.title: 3. Graph model
docs.text: The store holds three kinds of records, each partitioned by tenant. There is no record that spans tenants.

docs.title: 3.1 Entity
docs.text:
Field Type Meaning tenant string Partition key. kind string Entity kind from the cartridge ontology. id string Id within the kind. key = <kind>:<id>. ref string? Pointer to the row in the system of record (<source>#<id> by convention). attrs object Label attributes a tool needs to show the entity (plate, name). Never a copy of the row.

upsert_entity creates or updates in place. Entities are not bitemporal; their history is carried by facts and relations.

docs.title: 3.2 Relation
docs.text:
Field Type Meaning tenant, src, rel, dst string Edge from entity key src to entity key dst of type rel. valid_from datetime World time the relation started. valid_to datetime? World time it ended. null = open. recorded_at datetime When Keel learned it: the event's declared recorded_at, else when it was ingested. source string? Provenance. changed_at datetime? Bookkeeping: the ingest clock of the link or unlink, the cursor of relation_changes. closed_at datetime? Transaction time of the unlink: when Keel learned valid_to (the event's declared recorded_at, else when it was ingested). as_known_at counts the unlink only from then.

link is idempotent on an open edge with the same (src, rel, dst). unlink closes the open edge by setting valid_to and closed_at. Edges are never deleted.

docs.title: 3.3 Fact
docs.text:
Field Type Meaning tenant, subject string Partition and entity key. predicate string What is asserted, e.g. depth_mm, status, damage:D2. value any JSON The asserted value. valid_from datetime World time the fact became true. valid_to datetime? World time it stopped being true. null = open. recorded_at datetime When Keel learned it: the event's declared recorded_at, else when it was ingested (or when annotate wrote it). source string? Adapter or annotate:<by>. scope enum global, tenant, task, agent (§6). Default tenant. evidence string? Event id, row ref, photo URL or other pointer that justifies the fact. corrected_by string? A person or agent id when the fact is a correction or an annotation. expires_at datetime? Memory lifetime (not world time). Set from the scope's TTL, or to the close time when its task closes. closed_at datetime? Transaction time of the close: when Keel learned valid_to. With recorded_at it makes "as known at" queries possible. changed_at datetime? Bookkeeping, never a query time: the ingest clock of the fact's last write (open or close), the cursor of changes and the watermark. An event declaring an old recorded_at is still a new change. Not in tool answers. task string? The job a task-scope annotation belongs to (annotate(task=)). idempotency_key string? annotate(key=): a retried write with the same key returns this fact. A key is its author's: annotate stores it as annotate:<author>/<key>, so another author's key never finds or returns this fact. status string? null = accepted (the truth rules and context.facts read); proposed = waiting for a decision; rejected = a decision, closed at once. trace string? The caller's W3C traceparent and tool call id at write time (HTTP traceparent / X-Keel-Tool-Call headers, MCP _meta), so a Langfuse or LangSmith trace joins the audit export. cartridge string? Annotations and consolidations: the cartridge they were made under, name@version#rules (Cartridge.ident; the hash covers the rules and the calendar, so a rule edited without bumping version still shows). To replay a decision under its rules, check out that cartridge and replay the log. Facts from events leave it empty: the event log is their record.

Bitemporal rule. open_fact(subject, predicate, value, valid_from) MUST place the new fact in the predicate's history by valid_from: it closes the fact current at that instant (valid_to = valid_from) and, when a later fact already exists, closes itself at that fact's start. Arrival order does not change the result (§4). Facts that start at the same instant follow one another by recorded_at, then by evidence and value. recorded_at is the event's own when its source declares one, so the history is then the same in any arrival order; when the source declares none it is the ingest clock, which is when Keel did learn it, and two such facts at one instant follow the order they were ingested in. A source that can deliver out of order and has same-instant changes should declare recorded_at. A predicate's history is one slot per memory scope: a fact never closes one of another scope, so a private note does not end a shared diagnosis and a promotion leaves the narrower fact to its own lifetime. Task memory has one slot per task, agent memory one per writing agent, and with per_source=True (multi-valued predicates and proposals) one per author. Facts are never mutated or deleted by handlers.

Explicit closes. close_fact(subject, predicate, valid_to) is part of the predicate's history too: the store keeps it as a close mark (a row with source keel:close that no read returns) and it ends every fact of its predicate, status and scope (any author) that started before valid_to and still runs through it, including a fact that arrives later. With value=v it ends only facts whose value is v, so the end of one term never ends an overlapping later one. At one instant the close goes first: a close never ends a fact that starts at its own valid_to (closing a term and opening the next at one instant leaves the next open, even with the same value), so it never leaves an empty fact. As with open_fact, arrival order does not change the result. scope=None (every scope, how a decision settles proposals) closes only what is open at the call and takes no value. The store MAY physically drop facts whose expires_at has passed (consolidation, §8).

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Handler
    participant S as Store
    participant Q as Tool
    H->>S: open_fact(tire:T-9001, depth_mm, 5.2, valid_from=Sep 10)
    Note over S: depth_mm=5.2 valid [Sep 10, open)
    H->>S: open_fact(tire:T-9001, depth_mm, 2.6, valid_from=Oct 3)
    Note over S: close 5.2 with valid_to=Oct 3, append 2.6 valid [Oct 3, open)
    Q->>S: facts(at=Sep 20)
    S-->>Q: depth_mm=5.2
    Q->>S: facts(at=now)
    S-->>Q: depth_mm=2.6

Queries the store MUST answer:

  • facts true at a world time t: valid_from <= t < valid_to (or open).
  • facts between since and until (overlap).
  • facts as known at a transaction time t (facts(known_at=t)): recorded by t, with closes counted only when closed_at <= t (§7.6).

Values are for what a tool compares or shows. A long text (a comment body, a description, a document) belongs in the system of record: store a short label or a classification as the value and the pointer as evidence or in the entity's ref, not the text itself. The graph holds pointers and semantics (design rule 2).

docs.title: 3.4 Store protocol
docs.text:
Writes (the only write path; handlers call these and nothing else):

upsert_entity(tenant, kind, id, ref=None, **attrs) -> Entity
link(tenant, src, rel, dst, valid_from, source=None, recorded_at=None) -> Relation
unlink(tenant, src, rel, dst, valid_to, recorded_at=None) -> None
open_fact(tenant, subject, predicate, value, valid_from, **provenance) -> Fact
close_fact(tenant, subject, predicate, valid_to, status=None, scope="tenant", recorded_at=None, value=ANY) -> None
    # status: only proposals, or only rejections; scope: only that scope's facts (None: every scope).
    # The tenant default is what a handler means: it never closes agent or task memory.
    # value: only facts with that value (§3.3, explicit closes).

recorded_at (on link, close_fact, and open_fact's provenance) is the transaction time to write, closed_at for a close; None is now. Handlers do not pass it: for an event that declares recorded_at, the Ingestor hands its handler a store that fills it in, so the whole event is learned at the source's time. Every write also stamps changed_at from the ingest clock (§3.2, §3.3).

open_fact provenance keywords: source, scope, evidence, corrected_by, expires_at, recorded_at, task, idempotency_key, status, trace, cartridge, and per_source (one history per author, §3.3). A store MUST reject a second fact with the same idempotency_key on a subject by raising DuplicateKey (carrying the fact already written), atomically, so two writers racing on one key write once; the SQL stores do it with a unique index.

Reads:

entity(tenant, key) -> Entity | None
facts(tenant, subject, at=None, since=None, until=None, known_at=None) -> [Fact]
entities(tenant, kind=None) -> [Entity]
relations(tenant, key, rel=None, at=None) -> [Relation]
search(tenant, text) -> [Entity | Fact]
changes(tenant, after) -> [Fact]               # written (changed_at) after a watermark, oldest change first
watermark(tenant) -> datetime | None           # optional: latest changed_at of facts and relations
relation_changes(tenant, after) -> [Relation]  # optional: links and unlinks after a watermark (keel index)
facts_of(tenant, subjects, **filters) -> {subject: [Fact]}   # optional: facts() for many subjects at once
entities_of(tenant, keys) -> {key: Entity | None}           # optional: entity() for many keys at once
relations_of(tenant, keys, at=None) -> {key: [Relation]}    # optional: relations() for many keys at once

Tools calls entities and changes on every store. known_at is passed only when a caller asks for transaction time, so a store without it still serves every other read. Global-scope memory is stored under the reserved tenant __global__, or <account>/__global__ for a tenant <account>/<t> (§6); a store needs nothing special for it. API keys (optional, for the HTTP transport): put_key(ApiKey), api_key(sha256) -> ApiKey | None, api_keys(account=None) -> [ApiKey] and revoke_key(id, at) -> bool; they are not tenant data, so forget and reset leave them. Accounts (optional, for the HTTP transport's quotas): put_account(Account) (insert or replace), account(id) -> Account | None and accounts() -> [Account], with rps, events_month, store and retention. Metering (optional): meter([(tenant, day, item, n)]) adds to daily counters and usage(since, until) -> [(tenant, day, item, n)] reads them; the Ingestor meters events applied for the first time after each commit (never on replay), and Tools(meter=) counts each tool call. Tools(clock=) sets what "now" is for reads without as_of and for the valid_from of what annotate writes: running_from(instant) starts a clock there and lets it run, for a demo or a test pinned to a day (keel serve --clock, KEEL_CLOCK). Retention (expires_at) and ingest keep real time.

Ingest bookkeeping (called by the Ingestor, never by handlers): seen(tenant, event_id) and remember(tenant, event_id), the dedupe behind at-least-once delivery; reset forgets them too. A store MAY offer transaction(), a context manager the Ingestor wraps each event or batch in. Maintenance (jobs and operators): expire(tenant, now), close_task(tenant, task, now) (expires a task's task-scope memory at once), reset(tenant), dump(tenant) (everything about one tenant, closed facts included; keel export writes it as JSONL), and, optionally, tenants() (every tenant with something stored, never a global partition; --all-tenants on the jobs) and backup(tenant) / restore(tenant, backup): everything a restore needs (rows as stored, close marks included, applied event ids, the retention cutoff) and writing it as it was into an empty tenant, behind keel export, keel import and keel replay --check. Erasure, optional but required by the Ingestor when the cartridge declares an event that forgets: tenant: forget(tenant) -> {entities, relations, facts, annotations, ingested} deletes, in one transaction, everything stored for the tenant (facts of every scope, annotations, dedupe marks) and leaves a tombstone (the tenant and the time); it is idempotent, keeps the first tombstone's time and refuses a global partition. forgotten(tenant) -> datetime | None reads the tombstone and forgotten_tenants() -> {tenant: datetime} lists them. Retention, optional but required by the Ingestor when the cartridge declares an event that forgets: before: forget_before(tenant, before) -> {facts, annotations, relations} deletes, in one transaction, the tenant's facts (annotations included) and relations with valid_to <= before, keeps open ones and entities, and keeps the cutoff (the latest wins); it is idempotent and refuses a global partition. cutoff(tenant) -> datetime | None reads it.

A store implementation MUST pass tests/test_core.py and tests/test_store.py unchanged. Run the suite against your own store with KEEL_STORE=your_pkg.module:factory uv run pytest tests/test_store.py, where factory is a zero-argument callable (or class) returning a fresh, empty store. Reference: keel/store/memory.py (in memory). Durable: keel/store/sql.py holds one plain-SQL implementation with the same filters as the reference, and keel/store/sqlite.py (one file, WAL) and keel/store/mysql.py (MySQL or MariaDB, mysql:// URL) are its dialects; all answer identically and the conformance suite runs on SQLite and MySQL in CI. A Graphiti-backed store remains planned for graph-native queries.

docs.title: 4. Ingestion
docs.text:
The ingestor reads envelopes from an adapter and dispatches each to the handlers registered for its type.

  • The event log is the source of truth. Keel's own copy of the log (Ingestor.log, opt-in with keep_log=True) is a development convenience that grows with every event; in production the bus holds it.
  • Dispatch is deterministic: no network, no LLM, no randomness in the ingest path. Replaying the same log in the same order MUST produce an identical graph.
  • An event with no handler is reported as unhandled; in strict mode it raises. A handler exception is reported with the event id and does not stop the stream, unless strict.
  • An event is atomic: when its handler raises (not strict), whatever it wrote is rolled back and the event is not remembered, so it applies when it comes again with the handler fixed; the other events of its batch still land (the chunk is rolled back and applied again one event per commit). A store without transactions cannot roll back, and there the failed event's writes stay.
  • An event whose subject is not the kind its catalog entry declares (tire.depth_measured about a unit:) is refused before it is remembered: reported as an error, or raised in strict mode; keel validate --events finds the same ahead of time.
  • replay(tenant, events=None) wipes that tenant's event-derived subgraph (entities, relations, facts from handlers, dedupe marks) and re-dispatches its events from the external log given (the bus, the outbox table, a stream) or, without one, from the in-memory log (only kept with Ingestor(..., keep_log=True); otherwise replay without events is an error). It keeps annotations (facts whose source is annotate:... or consolidate:..., closed history included): they are earned memory, not in the log, and the events land around them as they did the first time (a store's reset(tenant, keep_annotations=True)). It is the recovery path, not the update path.
  • Ordering: adapters SHOULD deliver events in occurred_at order per subject, but the result MUST NOT depend on it for facts: open_fact places a fact in its predicate's history by valid_from, closing the fact current at that instant and closing itself at the next fact's start, so a late event lands in its slot instead of closing a newer fact backwards. Relations (link/unlink) still assume order per subject.
  • Transactions: when the store has them (the SQL stores do), each event is applied in one, so the handler's primitives and the dedupe mark land together (remember runs first, in the same transaction, and is one statement); a bulk caller passes batch= to commit every n events (the CLI and the HTTP batch do), and a chunk that raises in strict mode is rolled back whole and redelivered whole. A streaming adapter is never buffered.
  • Batches: a store MAY offer bulk(events), a context manager the Ingestor uses for chunks larger than one event. The SQL stores read the state of the chunk's subjects in a few statements, serve the handlers from memory, and write back in a few multi-row statements; the result is the same as event by event (the conformance suite checks it on every store, forwards and shuffled), about a thousand times fewer round trips.
  • Batch reads: a store MAY offer facts_of, entities_of and relations_of, the same answers as facts and entity for many subjects. context(depth=1) reads its neighbours with them, search(rule=) its candidates in chunks, and a rule that follows a relation its neighbours: a few statements whatever the neighbourhood's size, where one per subject would be a round trip each on a networked database. Without them Tools reads one subject at a time.
  • Threads: a store shared by a server's threads MUST keep a transaction, its read cache and a batch in flight to the thread that opened them: another thread waits for it or reads committed state, and never writes into it (a write that joined a batch would be lost with its rollback). The MySQL store reads on one connection per thread, so reads never queue behind a writer.
  • Erasure: an event whose type the cartridge declares forgets: tenant runs no handler; the Ingestor calls store.forget(tenant) in that event's transaction (a chunk holding one is applied event by event, never through bulk) and lists what was deleted in IngestReport.forgotten. Every later event for a forgotten tenant, a late redelivery included, is skipped without being applied and counted in IngestReport.skipped, so nothing revives it, and a replay of it yields nothing. Keel deletes only what it stores: the external log (the bus, the outbox table) belongs to the product, and global memory (§6) is every tenant's and is kept.
  • Retention: an event whose type the cartridge declares forgets: before runs no handler; the Ingestor marks it applied and calls store.forget_before(tenant, event.occurred_at) in its transaction (never through bulk), listing the cutoff and what was deleted in IngestReport.retained. replay applies the tenant's kept cutoff again after rebuilding. Events are not skipped by the cutoff: one arriving later with an earlier valid time stays until the next retention run.
  • Duplicates: an event whose id the store has already applied for that tenant is skipped and counted in IngestReport.duplicates. With content-hash ids this makes at-least-once adapters and client retries safe; a source that can emit two identical events at the same instant MUST give them ids.

docs.title: 4.1 Adapters
docs.text:
An adapter is any iterable of envelopes. It MUST NOT interpret payloads.

Adapter Status Notes JSONL file shipped Development and tests. Postgres table + polling shipped PostgresTableAdapter: a seq cursor in a file, so restarts resume; it moves only after the Ingestor commits (ack()). At-least-once. Webhook (HTTP) shipped build_app: validates the envelope, ingests, returns the report; bearer token. HTTP API and typed SDKs shipped POST /v1/events on keel serve --transport http, called directly or through events() in the generated clients (§7.7); one envelope or a list, the ingest report back. Kafka shipped KafkaAdapter (keel.adapters.bus): offset committed after the Ingestor commits the batch (ack()). At-least-once; dead_letter for poison messages. SQS shipped SqsAdapter (keel.adapters.bus): message deleted after the Ingestor commits the batch (ack()). Same semantics. keel consume --queue <url> runs it, a batch per transaction (--batch, default 100), retried one message at a time when it fails; a failed message stays for the queue's dead-letter queue, and a store that stops answering ends the process (exit 2). Postgres CDC shipped PostgresCdcAdapter, keel cdc: logical replication with pgoutput read through SQL functions; each mapped row change is <kind>.created|updated|deleted, id pgcdc:<commit lsn>:<n>; the slot advances only after the store commits.

docs.title: 4.2 Handlers
docs.text:
A handler is fn(event, store) -> None, registered for one event type with @registry.on("<type>"). It:

  • MUST only call store primitives (§3.4).
  • MUST use event.occurred_at for valid_from/valid_to.
  • SHOULD pass source=event.source and evidence=event.id on every fact.
  • MUST NOT contain business definitions (what "critical" means). Those are rules (§5.4).
  • SHOULD be about ten lines.

docs.title: 5. Cartridge format
docs.text: A cartridge is a directory with cartridge.yaml and handlers.py.

docs.title: 5.1 cartridge.yaml
docs.text:
name: <slug>            # required
version: <semver>       # optional, recommended

entities:               # required: kind -> spec
  <kind>:
    description: <text>
    ref: <table.column> # optional, documents where `ref` points
    attrs: [<attr>, ...]        # optional: attributes its handlers set, columns of the generated SQL views (keel/sqlgen.py)
    facts: [<predicate>, ...]   # optional: its predicates, for the generated views; or <predicate>: <hint> | {type: <hint>, description: <text>}
                                #   (no type: the hint of the payload field of the same name in the kind's events)

relations:              # optional: rel -> {from: <kind>, to: <kind>}
  <rel>: { from: <kind>, to: <kind> }
  <rel>: { from: <kind>, to: <kind>, symmetric: true }   # recorded from either end, shown once (direction `both`)
  <rel>: { from: <kind>, to: <kind>, one: true }         # at most one target per source at a time: a column of the generated views

events:                 # required: type -> spec
  <type>:
    subject: <kind>     # required: the kind of event.subject
    owner: <team>       # recommended: who owns this event's shape
    payload: { <field>: <hint>, ... }   # the notation in §5.5; `| null` = optional
    forgets: tenant     # optional: this event erases its tenant (§4), or `before`: deletes what closed before it; it takes no handler

rules:                  # optional: name -> definition
  <rule>:
    applies_to: <kind>  # optional; absent = applies to every subject
    definition: <text>  # human-readable, versioned with the cartridge
    <param>: <value>    # machine-readable parameters agents read
    when:               # optional: a condition the core evaluates in `context` (§5.4)
      predicate: <predicate>
      <op>: <operand>   # leaf operators in §5.4; compose with all / any / not; follow relations with via

predicates:             # optional: write policy per predicate, for annotations
  <predicate>: { multi: true, description: <text> }   # multi: one open value per author (the `by`, else the agent) instead of last-writer-wins; context lists conflicts

semantic:               # optional: what `keel index` puts in each subject's document (§7.3)
  kinds: [<kind>, ...]           # absent: every kind
  predicates: [<predicate>, ...] # what to include; or exclude: [<predicate>, ...]
  attrs: true                    # entity attributes (default); false, or a list of names
  relations: [<rel>, ...]        # open relations: the other side's key and one label
  labels: [name, nombre]         # the attribute that labels the other side (first present wins); default: name, nombre, title, titulo, label, plate, model
  lexical_weight: 0.3            # hybrid search: weight of the lexical leg (0 = dense only)
  min_score: 0.4                 # optional cosine floor; model-specific, calibrate with evals/semantic
  split: { <kind>: [<predicate>, ...] }  # also one document per open fact of these predicates, and per element of a list value (each field of a visual), not only one per subject

consolidate:            # optional: episodic memory summarized into durable facts (§8)
  <name>:
    from: { predicate: <p>, scopes: [task] }   # default [task]; agent memory is read only when listed
    applies_to: <kind>             # optional
    within: 30d                    # optional window on valid_from (world time)
    min_count: 3                   # default 2
    reduce: mode                   # mode | latest | count | min | max | avg | distinct | summary
    into: { predicate: <q>, scope: tenant }

context:                # optional: how much `context` carries (§7.1), per relation and direction
  relations: 10                  # relations listed, the most recent; the rest counted in relations_more (default 10)
  neighbors: 5                   # neighbours read with depth=1, the most recent; the rest counted in neighbors_more (default 5)

calendar:               # optional: business days for `open_for_business_days` (§5.4)
  weekend: [saturday, sunday]
  holidays: [2026-12-25]

agents:                 # optional: the agent registry (§6.1). Absent = no registry, any caller
  <id>:
    description: <text>
    kind: agent                                  # or human: a person, signed human:<id> (§6.1)
    writes: [task, agent]                        # scopes it may annotate; never global; absent = [task, agent]
    reads: { kinds: [<kind>, ...], relations: [<rel>, ...] }   # optional; absent = everything
    query: true                                  # optional: may call the optional query tool (§7.8); absent = false

memory:                 # optional; defaults in §6
  ttl:
    global: never | forever | <n>d | <n>h | <n>m | <n>   # a bare number is days
    tenant: never | ...
    task: 14d
    agent: 1d
  requires_evidence: [global, tenant]
  evidence: [event, "photo:", "human:"]   # optional; what counts as evidence there. Absent: any non-empty string

docs.title: 5.2 handlers.py
docs.text: MUST define registry = HandlerRegistry() at module level with one or more @registry.on(...) functions.

docs.title: 5.3 Validation (keel validate)
docs.text:
A cartridge is valid when:

  1. every relation's from and to are declared entity kinds;
  2. every event's subject is a declared entity kind;
  3. every cataloged event type has at least one handler, except one that forgets, which has none (forgets takes tenant or before);
  4. every handler's event type is in the catalog;
  5. every rule's when names a predicate and uses only the operators in §5.4;
  6. every agent's kind is agent or human, its writes are known scopes other than global, and its reads name declared kinds and relations;
  7. every event's payload hints use the notation in §5.5;
  8. predicates, semantic, consolidate and context use only known keys, with values in range (a weight between 0 and 1, a known reducer, a known scope, a whole number of at least 1);
  9. every via names a declared relation with a valid direction, and duration operators (open_for_*, held_for_*) take a comparison mapping.

keel validate <cartridge> --events <stream.jsonl> also checks every envelope in the stream against the catalog: the type is cataloged, the subject's kind is the event's subject, and each declared payload field is present with its declared shape (§5.5; | null makes it optional). It looks at payload keys and types, never at values; it is the one place the core looks at a payload at all.

docs.title: 5.4 Rules (semantic layer)
docs.text:
Rules are authored by product, versioned with the cartridge, and returned by the context tool for the subject's kind. Agents MUST read definitions from rules rather than hard-code them. The core interprets two keys: applies_to and when. context evaluates every applicable rule that has a when at as_of and returns true, false, or null (undecidable). A rule without when (an aggregate, a count over time) is returned as a definition only and the agent applies it.

A when is a condition:

  • Leaf: { predicate: <p>, <op>: <operand>, ... }. Operators on the subject's open fact for <p>: lt, lte, gt, gte, eq, ne, in (value in a list), within_days (a date predicate on or before as_of + n days, so dates already past count), open_for_days and open_for_business_days (how long the open fact has been open: a mapping of lt/lte/gt/gte/eq, e.g. { gte: 7 }; business days skip the cartridge calendar weekend and holidays), held_for_days and held_for_business_days (how long the leaf's comparison has held across consecutive facts of the predicate: a waiting clock that survives a change from one waiting status to another; without a comparison, how long the predicate has had any value without a gap). ci: true compares strings case-insensitively. No open fact for the predicate: null.
  • Composition: { all: [...] }, { any: [...] }, { not: <condition> }. A bare list is all. null propagates unless another branch decides: a false in all, a true in any.
  • Neighbours: { via: <relation>, direction: out | in | any, any: <condition> } or all:. The condition is evaluated on each neighbour reached by that relation at as_of (direction defaults to any; symmetric relations ignore it). No neighbours: any is false, all is true. This is how an inherited state is expressed: { any: [ { predicate: status, eq: paused }, { via: relates_to, any: { predicate: status, eq: paused } } ] }.

Rules see the whole tenant's graph: they are the product's semantics, not the calling agent's view, so the agent registry's read slice does not apply inside a when.

docs.title: 5.5 Payload notation
docs.text:
The payload: mapping of an event is a schema in a short notation. Keel checks streams against it (keel validate --events) and prints it as JSON Schema draft 2020-12 (keel schema <cartridge>), which is what SDK templates read.

Written as Means JSON Schema string, int, number, bool a scalar type string / integer / number / boolean date, datetime an ISO 8601 string type: string with format any anything {} <hint> \| null optional and nullable type: [<type>, "null"], not in required string[] (any scalar) array of scalars type: array, items [pending, paid] enum of literals enum [new, done, null] optional enum (null is a literal in the list; | null is not YAML here) enum with null, not in required [ { id: string, qty: int } ] array of objects type: array, items: object { source: string, score: number } nested object type: object, properties, required

Extra fields in a payload are allowed: the catalog documents what handlers need, not everything the source sends. An unknown hint is a validation error, so a typo never passes as any; [string] is rejected in favour of string[].

docs.title: 5.6 The generality test
docs.text: Adding or changing a cartridge MUST require no change under keel/. The repository keeps four cartridges (fleet, crm, finance, clinics) and all MUST pass the test suite after any core change.

docs.title: 6. Memory scopes and policy
docs.text:
Scope Who reads Who writes Default TTL Evidence required global every tenant's agents a privileged process (a Tools bound to no registry agent; never an agent, never an event) never yes tenant that tenant's agents handlers (from events); agents/humans via annotate never yes task calls that pass the fact's task (context(task=), history(task=)); a task fact with no task id is the tenant's agents via annotate 14 days no agent the agent that wrote it (a Tools bound to no agent id reads none) that agent 1 day no 
flowchart LR
    g["global<br/>every tenant · never expires · evidence"] --> t["tenant<br/>one end-customer · never expires · evidence"] --> k["task<br/>agents on one task · 14 d"] --> a["agent<br/>one agent · 1 d"]
    w["annotate(subject, predicate, value, scope, evidence, by)"] --> p{"MemoryPolicy.check_write"}
    p -- "scope requires evidence, none given" --> e["PermissionError"]
    p -- "ok" --> f["open_fact with scope, evidence, corrected_by=by<br/>expires_at = now + ttl"]

Rules:

  • Policy is enforced in Tools.annotate via MemoryPolicy.check_write; the calling agent is not trusted to self-police.
  • A write to a scope that requires evidence without evidence MUST raise PermissionError.
  • Facts written by handlers from events are tenant scope with evidence = event.id.
  • Promotion to a wider scope is a new annotate with evidence and by; the narrower fact keeps its own lifetime.
  • expires_at = now + ttl at write time; null when TTL is never. Reads MUST exclude expired facts even before a job physically removes them.
  • Reads are enforced in Tools, on every path that returns facts (context and its neighbours, rule evaluation, history with or without a subject, text search): an agent fact is returned only to a caller bound to its author (its source is annotate:<author>); a task fact tied to a task only to calls passing that task; a task fact with no task id to the whole tenant. Rules evaluate on the same view, so another agent's or another task's memory never decides a verdict.
  • Global memory lives in the reserved partition __global__: annotate(scope="global") writes there and every tenant's reads merge it, so one fact is seen by every tenant. No event may carry that tenant and no Tools may be bound to it. Over HTTP and MCP (bound to a tenant or per request) only the operator's secret or an account's --global key may write it: Tools(writes_global=False) refuses it below every transport. It is the one deliberate exception to invariant 1, and it holds only what a privileged process wrote. A tenant whose name has an account prefix (acme/t, given by the HTTP transport's API keys) reads and writes acme/__global__ instead, which no other account sees; over HTTP only the account's global key writes it.

docs.title: 6.1 Agent registry
docs.text:
A cartridge MAY declare agents: (§5.1). Without it there is no registry: any caller, any scope with evidence, and an agent id passed to Tools is attribution only. With it:

  • A Tools instance MUST be bound to a declared agent (Tools(..., agent=<id>), keel serve --agent <id>). A missing or unknown id raises PermissionError at construction. An id never contains : (human:ana would sign as the person ana): keel validate reports it and binding to it is refused. Agents read only the kinds and relations their entry allows, and a bare-id hint ("did you mean ...?") and the MCP instructions name only those.
  • Writes. annotate to a scope outside the agent's writes raises PermissionError. global is never writable by an agent. The scope policy (evidence, TTL) applies after the registry check. source is annotate:<agent>; corrected_by is by when given (a human correcting through the agent), else the agent id.
  • People. An entry with kind: human is a person: it is enforced like any agent, and its annotations are signed annotate:human:<id> with corrected_by = human:<id>. Approvals are writes by a declared person, so the audit export shows who approved.
  • Reads. context, history, related and annotate on a subject whose kind is outside reads.kinds raise PermissionError. Relations outside reads.relations, or whose other end is a hidden kind, are left out of context and related. search drops hits on hidden kinds. query (§7.8) reads past reads, so an agent may call it only with query: true; otherwise it raises PermissionError and a server does not list it to that agent.
  • Authentication is the host's job. Keel takes the agent id as given and enforces what that id may do; it never trusts the agent to police itself (rule 5).

docs.title: 7. The tools: five core, one optional
docs.text:
A Tools instance is bound to one cartridge, one tenant and, when the cartridge declares agents, one agent (§6.1). Cross-tenant access does not exist at this layer. The five core tools (§7.1-7.5) and the optional sixth, query (§7.8), with their names and argument orders, are part of the public standard; adding another is a spec change.

A wrong name is an error, not an empty answer: a subject without a <kind>: prefix (with a suggested key when one exists), a kind, relation, rule or scope the cartridge does not declare (with the closest name and the valid ones) and a time that is not ISO 8601 (with the expected format) raise ValueError. A list a tool cuts short says so in its first element, {"more": {...}}, with how many were shown, the total and how to read the rest (next); a caller iterating the list skips the entry that has more. Without as_of or as_known_at, context answers as of the current time rounded up to the next whole second, so the same question asked twice answers in the same bytes, and a write made earlier in that second is still read.

docs.title: 7.1 context(subject, as_of=None, depth=0, as_known_at=None, task=None, detail="full", exclude=None, only=None) -> object
docs.text:
subject may be a list: the answers come back in order, one per subject, in one call. exclude (a list of predicates) leaves those predicates out of facts, proposals and the neighbours' facts, for an evaluation in which the agent must not see the answer; rules still evaluate on the whole truth, so a verdict can reveal it. only (a non-empty list of predicates) is the opposite: just those predicates, in the same places, for the evidence a reviewer checks across many subjects without the rest of their facts; exclude still hides what it names. A list of subjects is read in a few statements (facts, proposals, relations and entities in batches), not one or more per subject. A search with a list of texts shares those reads too: each subject's facts are read once for every text, so checking many names against one subject's neighbours (search(names, kind=[...], related_to=s)) is one call.

facts holds accepted facts only. proposals (present when any) holds the open proposals; conflicts (present when any) maps each predicate that has more than one open value to those values and their authors, which happens for multi predicates (§5.1) written by several agents. detail="concise" returns the same answer for a prompt in about a third of the tokens: attrs, facts as {predicate: value} (a list of {value, by} for a multi-valued one), relations as {relation, direction, subject} (direction both for a symmetric relation, as everywhere else), evaluation, as_of, watermark, proposals and conflicts, and compact neighbours, plus since, {predicate: valid_from} of each current value (when it became true, without a history call); rule definitions are left out (their names are in evaluation).

What is true about a subject now, or at as_of (world time). detail="brief" (the cheapest, for an agent; the default over MCP and HTTP, §7.7) is concise with relations grouped as {relation: [subjects]}, an incoming one written <-relation. Relations are listed up to 10 per relation and direction (the cartridge's context.relations, §5.1), the most recent ones, ordered by relation, link time and key; past that, relations_more gives each one's relation, direction, shown and total, and related or search(related_to=...) reads the rest, so an account with hundreds of tickets does not put all of them in every answer. With depth=1 the answer also carries neighbors: for up to 5 open relations per relation and direction (the cartridge's context.neighbors), the most recent, the other subject's entity, open facts and rule evaluation, so one call brings a card and the cards it is linked to; neighbors_more counts the rest per relation and direction (relation, direction, shown, total), and past 50 neighbours in all, neighbors_truncated: true. A well-formed subject Keel knows nothing about (no entity, facts, relations or proposals) returns {subject, found: false, as_of, watermark} at any detail.

{
  "subject": "unit:MXK-4821",
  "entity": { "kind": "unit", "id": "MXK-4821", "ref": "fleet.vehicles#MXK-4821", "attrs": {...} },
  "facts": [ ...open facts at now, expired excluded... ],
  "relations": [ ...open relations at now, both directions... ],
  "rules": { "<rule>": {...} },      // rules with applies_to == subject kind or absent
  "evaluation": { "<rule>": true },  // true | false | null, for the rules above that carry a `when`
  "as_of": "2026-10-14T18:41:07Z"    // now, or the `as_of` asked for
}

docs.title: 7.2 history(subject=None, since=None, until=None, predicate=None, scope=None, as_known_at=None, task=None, changed_since=None, limit=50, detail="full") -> [Fact]
docs.text: Facts over time, oldest first, including closed ones. predicate, scope and task filter (task returns only what that task wrote; without it, task memory tied to a task is not returned, §6); limit keeps the most recent n, still oldest first (0 or None: all); when it cuts, the first element is {"more": {shown, total, omitted, next}}. as_known_at returns the facts as Keel knew them then (§7.6). With no subject and since/until (and no changed_since), it returns the tenant's facts that started (valid_from) in that window, in world time, oldest first, with predicate and scope as filters: "what changed this week", "whose assignee changed"; each fact's evidence says which event set it. Every fact that replaced a value carries was, the value of the accepted fact of its predicate and scope that ended exactly when it started (null included), read from the subject's whole history even when the window leaves that fact out; a first value, a value after a gap, a proposal and a multi-valued predicate carry no was, so "changed" is the facts with was. changed_since keeps the facts written (opened or closed) after a watermark, by the ingest clock; with no subject it spans the tenant (subjects the caller may read), ordered by the time of the change: the "since my last run" read of an incremental agent. Each fact carries valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, closed_at, source, evidence, scope, corrected_by, task. detail="concise" (the default over MCP and HTTP, §7.7) returns lean facts, about a quarter of the tokens: no null fields, no tenant, no transaction-time bookkeeping (recorded_at, closed_at, idempotency_key, trace, cartridge), scope only when it is not tenant, and subject only when no subject was given; world time and provenance stay. detail is "full" or "concise".

docs.title: 7.3 search(text="", kind=None (or a list), rule=None, limit=None, after=None, mode="text", min_score=None, related_to=None, via=None, detail="entity", depth=0, per_kind=None, exclude=None, as_of=None, where=None, as_known_at=None) -> [Entity | Fact]
docs.text:
where without text returns only the entities it keeps (with no text, no fact is a hit). as_of evaluates rules, where, neighbours and the facts returned at that instant (a text search's fact hits too: given as_of, only facts that held then; without it, every match in the history); as_known_at reads them as Keel knew them then (transaction time, §7.6; as_of defaults to it). detail="count" returns [{"count": n}]: the number of results, each subject once, with no cap and nothing listed (not with depth, after or per_kind), so "how many are blocked" costs a few tokens. A deployment may set a ceiling on one listing (Tools(max_list=n), keel serve --max-list, KEEL_MAX_LIST): a request for all (limit=0) or for more than the ceiling returns the ceiling and a leading {"more": ...} that says so; search, related and history take it, a count never does. per_kind adds up under the ceiling too, a negative limit or per_kind raises, and a list of subjects or texts holds at most the ceiling (1000 without one). Unset, there is no ceiling: a report or an export may want everything. Every time argument also takes "2026-10-03 08:00 UTC", as people and agents write times.

What each entity result carries (detail="brief", for an agent: the key, attrs, score and current facts as {predicate: value}, without tenant, kind, id or ref, which the key carries): detail="key" only the keys, as strings (a fact hit gives its subject; each key once; not with depth), the cheapest listing; detail="entity" (the default) the entity; "concise" also its current facts as {predicate: value}, "full" as facts, so a result needs no context call to be understood. depth=1 adds neighbors (relation, direction, subject, and their facts when detail asks for them; up to 50, then neighbors_truncated). Facts and neighbours of a page are read in a few statements whatever its size. per_kind=n returns the best n of every kind instead of one ranking (in semantic mode one ranking per kind, rule or kind narrowing the kinds; in text mode the text ranking cut per kind; not with after): with related_to for the scope, mode="semantic" and detail="concise", the context a task needs in one call. exclude leaves predicates out of what is returned and drops fact hits on them. as_of evaluates rule, walks related_to and reads the facts and neighbours at that instant (entities are not bitemporal; the semantic index is as of its last keel index). text may be a list: one result list per text, in order. kind may be a list: the listing covers those kinds, ordered by key (after is then a full key), a semantic ranking only them, and per_kind the best n of each (in text mode, the first n of each listing; one kind with per_kind in text mode is an error, that is limit).

where={name: value} keeps the entities whose attribute name, or current accepted fact name (at as_of), is value, or a list holding it; a list of values against a single value means any of them (where={"status": ["In Progress", "In Review"]}: "a status among" in one call), while a list-valued attribute or fact still matches the same list or one holding the wanted value; strings compare without case, and the whole value, not a part of it: search(kind="visual", where={"title": "Detalhe Ociosidade"}) finds a visual by its exact title, which a semantic search blurs. It applies in every mode, after the other filters; a name that exclude hides is an error. With detail brief or concise, each hit carries since: {predicate: valid_from} for the facts the filter matched (attributes have no time), so "in this status for 30 days or more" needs no history per hit. A name that is a relation or a kind also matches as a neighbour: where={"in_project": "project:P"} keeps the subjects linked to project:P through in_project, where={"project": "P"} those linked to that subject of kind project (by key or id; a list: any of them), with the other entries, in one call; an attribute or fact of that name still matches. facts.<name>, as the compact tables name a column, is <name>. Each ranked entity says why it is a result: matched is the attribute or predicate whose value matched (or "key"), and snippet the part of that value around the match (up to 160 characters; of a list, the element). In text mode that is the substring; in semantic mode, the split document that ranked it (below) or else the field sharing most words with the query; nothing when no field does, and never a hidden predicate. A listing without text carries neither.

related_to (a subject key the caller may read) keeps only that subject's current neighbours, through relation via when given, in every mode: search(kind="card", rule="en_pausa", related_to="cliente:BAT", via="de_cliente") is the paused cards of one client in one call, walking the client's neighbours rather than the whole kind. after has one format, the key of the last entity received (tire:T-9002); an id alone is accepted when the listing has one kind. It pages the kind/rule listing only: with mode="semantic" or a plain text search it is an error, since those rank and page with limit.

With detail="brief" or "concise" a fact hit is a lean fact (§7.2), with its subject; with "entity" and "full" it is the whole fact (over MCP, "entity" returns lean fact hits too, §7.7). Without limit (and without per_kind), a text search returns its first 20 results and a kind/rule listing its first 50; when more exist, the first element is {"more": {shown, total, next}}, next saying how to continue (the after key for a listing). A given limit is honoured without a marker (0: the whole listing); semantic ranking keeps its default of 10. Every kind must be declared, and rule must exist with a when (§7). A plain text search (no kind, no rule) of more than one word that nothing contains whole, and mode="semantic" with text on a server without an embedder and index, rank subjects instead by how many of the query's words (three letters or more, common stop words left out) their key, attributes or current facts contain, then by key; related_to, via, kind and rule still filter, and the list leads with {"note": ...} saying the ranking changed.

Every entity the tools return (here, in context.entity, in neighbors, and in keel export) carries key, the <kind>:<id> that every other call takes and that after expects.

Without kind and rule: case-insensitive substring match over entity keys and attrs, and fact predicates and values. With kind, or rule (whose applies_to gives the kind, and which must carry a when): the entities of that kind whose key, attrs or current facts' values match text (since 0.20; before, key and attrs only), and with rule only those where the rule evaluates true now, ordered by key; limit caps the page and after (the last key received) continues it. This is the work list of a sweep, a router or an orchestrator.

mode="semantic" ranks subjects by meaning: subjects whose id appears verbatim in the query come first (match: "key", score 1); then a dense leg (the embedded query against the vector index) and, when the index offers text_query, a lexical leg (BM25 over the same documents) are fused by a convex combination of min-max normalized scores, weighted by the cartridge's semantic.lexical_weight (default 0.3; 0 is dense only); then the optional reranker reorders the top candidates. The tenant, the agent's read slice, kind and rule always apply, inside the index when its query takes where; with related_to, where also carries subject (the neighbours' keys; a split document belongs to its subject), which an index MAY apply and Keel checks after retrieval either way. Each entity carries score and similarity (the cosine); min_score (or the cartridge's semantic.min_score) drops results below that cosine, and is model-specific. Default limit 10. Three adapter contracts make it pluggable (keel.semantic): VectorIndex (upsert, delete, query, clear, always by tenant, an index never returns another tenant's keys; optional where on query and an optional text_query), Embedder (embed(texts), optionally role="query"|"document" for asymmetric models) and Reranker (rerank(query, docs); bundled: the Cohere/Jina/Voyage /rerank shape and an LLM reranker over any /chat/completions). Keel ships MemoryIndex, ChromaIndex (extra chroma), WeaviateIndex (extra weaviate), OpenAIEmbedder (any /v1/embeddings API) and HashEmbedder (tests); any other is a pkg.module:factory?param=value spec, checked by tests/test_semantic.py with KEEL_VECTOR_INDEX / KEEL_EMBEDDER. The index is built by keel index, outside ingest (rule 10): one document per subject with its key, attributes, open accepted facts of tenant and global scope and the open relations the cartridge names, as chosen by the cartridge's semantic: section (§5.1); task and agent memory and proposals are never indexed; with semantic.split, each open fact of the listed predicates is also a document of its own (a list value, one per element), a hit on it ranks its subject (which keeps its best document, and says which predicate in matched and which value or element in snippet), and a changed value replaces its document; incremental from a watermark (subjects whose facts changed, and both ends of new links), --full rebuilds. A rule or kind filter never cuts the page: candidates are fetched in widening windows until limit results pass or the index runs out.

docs.title: 7.4 annotate(subject, predicate, value, scope="task", evidence=None, by=None, task=None, key=None, status=None, detail="full") -> Fact
docs.text: Writes earned memory. Applies the agent registry (§6.1) and the scope policy (§6); refused for a forgotten tenant (§4). source is annotate:<agent, or by, or 'agent'> (annotate:human:<id> for a person); corrected_by is by, else the caller. task ties the fact to one job: history(task=) and context(task=) read it, and closing the task (store.close_task, keel expire --task) expires its task-scope memory at once (task on a tenant or agent fact is provenance: the fact keeps its scope's lifetime). key makes the write idempotent, for durable-execution engines that replay steps: the same key on the same subject returns the fact it wrote; the same key with a different predicate, value, task, status or scope raises. status="proposed" writes a proposal: it never touches accepted facts, waits in context.proposals, and needs only some write right (not the right on scope), so an agent can propose a tenant fact a person accepts; the evidence policy of scope still applies. An accepted write (no status) or status="rejected" is a decision: it needs the right on scope and closes the predicate's open proposals of that scope (a private or task note settles no tenant proposal); a rejection is recorded closed at once, in history only. Proposals are kept one open per author per predicate, in their own history beside the accepted facts; the author is the writer and the by it named together, so an agent naming a person with by= never takes that person's slot (the same holds for multi-valued predicates). A value is at most 64 KB serialized: a label and a pointer, never the document. Store close_fact takes status so handlers never close proposals. Returns the stored fact including expires_at, status, trace and cartridge (the cartridge's ident). detail="ack" (the default over MCP and HTTP, §7.7) returns only what was written where: subject, predicate, scope, valid_from, and valid_to, expires_at, task, status when set. detail is "full" or "ack"; an unknown scope raises with the valid ones.

docs.title: 7.5 related(subject, relation=None, as_of=None, depth=1, limit=50) -> [{relation, direction, subject, since}]
docs.text: Open relations at now or at as_of, optionally filtered by type (one, or a list; each must be declared), with direction relative to the subject (out, in, or both for a symmetric relation, which is reported once even when the source recorded it from both ends). depth 2 or 3 keeps walking through the same relations, nearest first and each subject once: every entry then carries hops and via, the subject it was reached from, to which its direction is relative. Entries are ordered by hop, relation, link time (since, oldest first) and key, whatever the store's order. At most limit entries (0 or None: all), keeping the nearest hops and within them the most recent links; when more exist, the first element is {"more": {shown, total, omitted, by_relation, next}}, by_relation counting every entry per relation and next pointing at relation= or a search(related_to=, via=, limit=, after=) page.

docs.title: 7.6 Two time axes
docs.text: as_of is world time: what was true then. as_known_at is transaction time: what Keel knew then, which is what an agent saw when it decided. A fact counts as known at t when recorded_at <= t. It ends where the next fact of its slot (same predicate, status and scope; per author for a multi-valued predicate or a proposal) known by t starts, or at a close learned by t (closed_at <= t, or an explicit close recorded by t), whichever is earlier: closes are rebuilt from what was known then, so a late fact that later moved a close never reopens the fact before it. Memory counts when it had not expired by t. context(as_known_at=t) defaults as_of to t, and also evaluates the rules on that view; relations count when recorded_at <= t, and an unlink only once closed_at <= t. Every context carries watermark, the tenant's latest write (by the ingest clock, so a late event with an old recorded_at is still past it), which is the cursor an agent stores for its next history(changed_since=), passed back exactly as received. Every time argument of the five tools takes a datetime or ISO 8601 text, in every transport. Entities are not bitemporal and are shown as they are now. Facts written before 0.9 have no closed_at; their closes count as always known.

docs.title: 7.7 Transport
docs.text:
The tools are plain functions first. keel serve exposes the same five over MCP (stdio, or streamable HTTP at /mcp with --transport http --tenant) and as a JSON API (POST /v1/<tool>, one process for many tenants, tenant and agent from X-Keel-Tenant and X-Keel-Agent behind a shared bearer secret or per-account API keys that prefix the tenant with the account). The names and semantics MUST NOT change per transport: annotate's value is any JSON over MCP, HTTP and in Python alike.

Defaults differ by caller. Over MCP and HTTP the caller is usually an agent, so context defaults to detail="brief", history to "concise" and annotate to "ack"; Python Tools and the SDK clients keep "full". Over MCP, search with detail="entity" (its default) also returns fact hits lean. The list caps of §7.2, §7.3 and §7.5 apply in every transport; the TypeScript, Go and PHP runtimes ask for every entry (limit 0) unless the caller sets one, and drop a leading {"more"} or {"note"} element so a list keeps its declared type.

Over MCP, a result is one text block of compact JSON (no indentation, a list in one block, not one per element), and structuredContent carries the same data (a list under result) for programmatic clients. Tools publish no outputSchema (it would only say "an object" or "a list", in tokens a client may hand the model on every call). Parameters with a closed set of values (detail, mode, scope, status) are declared as enums. Tool descriptions are shared with Tools.spec() (keel.tools.DESCRIPTIONS) and fixed, so a prompt cache holds them. A server may be read-only (build_server(read_only=True), keel serve --read-only): it lists context, history, search and related and refuses annotate with the reason; a server bound to an agent whose registry entry writes no scope (writes: []) is read-only without the flag. The default lists all five; query=True adds the optional query (§7.8), read-only too, and puts the schema it reads in the instructions. A server bound to one tenant states once per session, in its instructions, what every call would otherwise repeat: the kinds, the relations (from->to) and each rule's applies_to and definition, and that search(rule=) lists where a rule holds. A kind with at most three subjects (a project, a site, an account) is named with its subjects, as the server starts (Kinds: issue, project (project:INDY)): an agent filters by it without looking its key up first. Experimental, MCP only: detail="text" on context and history renders the brief context or the concise history as lines for the model (one fact per line with its time and provenance), with the JSON in structuredContent.

A server writes that text compact by default (build_server(compact=False), keel serve --plain or KEEL_COMPACT=0 send the JSON text instead): the same data, lossless (keel.mcp_server.unpack restores it), in about a third fewer tokens on the Jira benchmark's calls, with the same accuracy (evals/jira/results/ab-compact-*.jsonl). A client that parses the text block as JSON should read structuredContent, or unpack the text. UTC times drop +00:00 for Z and zero seconds (2026-10-03T08:00Z; fractions kept, so a watermark is still exact); a list of two or more records becomes one table, {"all": {fields every record shares}, "cols": [...], "rows": [[...]]}, each row a record's values in the order of cols, followed by an object of its other fields when it has some (a field absent from a record stays absent: a first value still has no was), a map every record has written as map.key fields, and the list's leading more, note or initial as keys of the table. An object of data with both cols and rows travels as {"~": object}. The session instructions then say how to read a table; structuredContent and /v1 keep the JSON.

docs.title: 7.8 query(sql, limit=None) -> [row] (optional)
docs.text:
Read-only SQL over the schema generated from the cartridge (keel/sqlgen.py): the per-kind views (<kind>_state_at, <kind>_state_known_at, <kind>_changes), state_at/state_known_at, keel_facts, relations_at/relations_known_at, <rule>_at/<rule>_verdicts, and the tables facts, entities, relations. One SELECT (or WITH ... SELECT). Off unless the host enables it (keel serve --query, KEEL_QUERY, build_server(query=True), build_http_app(query=True), Tools(query=True)); it is served by SqliteStore, DuckdbStore, PostgresStore.from_url; not MemoryStore or MysqlStore, which raise a clear error and are never listed). Rows are objects keyed by column, instants as ISO 8601 text in UTC; at most limit rows (default 200; 0 or more than the deployment's max_list: that ceiling, else 1000), a cut list leading with {"more": {"shown", "next"}}. A query runs at most query_timeout seconds (default 5, --query-timeout). An answer carries at most 8 MB of values (cut, led by {"more"}); a row over 1 MB is refused.

Tenant isolation is the store's, never a check of the agent's SQL: the query runs where only the bound tenant's readable rows exist (SQLite and DuckDB: a per-tenant sandbox copy; Postgres: a login role per tenant reading views bound to it), so another tenant's id in a macro argument, a base table, a catalog, a file or network function, a second statement or a write reads or changes nothing (tests/test_query_security.py). What it reads: the tenant's accepted (no status) tenant-scope facts, unexpired, the global partition's global facts (as §6 lets every tenant read them), its entities and relations. Never agent or task memory, never proposals: a store cannot apply a caller's per-agent and per-task visibility to arbitrary SQL, so it leaves them out. With an agent registry (§6.1), an agent may call query only if its entry says query: true: SQL reads past reads.kinds and reads.relations.

Over MCP its description is fixed text (prompt caches hold) and the schema it reads, generated for the tenant and the store's dialect, rides in the server's instructions; Tools.spec() appends it to the description. Over HTTP it is POST /v1/query {sql, limit?} (404 when not enabled; a read, so a --read-only server may still offer it).

docs.title: 8. Jobs
docs.text:
• Expiry: drop facts past expires_at, per tenant. Shipped: store.expire(tenant) on both stores and keel expire <tenant> --db; the schedule is the operator's cron. Reads exclude expired facts regardless.
  • Consolidation: keel consolidate (or keel expire --consolidate, which consolidates before dropping, so nothing is lost unsummarized) runs the cartridge's consolidate: entries for a tenant: per subject, the matching episodic facts (predicate, scopes, kind, a window on valid_from; expired-but-not-dropped ones count; agent memory only when from.scopes lists it, since consolidating it promotes private memory) are reduced into one durable fact when there are at least min_count. Reducers are deterministic (mode with ties to the latest, latest, count, min, max, avg, distinct); summary asks a Summarizer adapter (LLMSummarizer over any /chat/completions, or yours) for one sentence. The fact carries source=consolidate:<name>, evidence naming the count, the span of their valid_from and the originals' evidence, and an idempotency key over its inputs: the same inputs never write twice, new inputs write a new value that closes the old. Proposals are never consolidated, and the written fact carries corrected_by=job:consolidate:<name>. The summarizer is chosen with --summarizer llm|join|pkg.module:factory; llm reads KEEL_SUMMARIZER_BASE_URL, KEEL_SUMMARIZER_MODEL and KEEL_SUMMARIZER_API_KEY. The originals are kept until their TTL. A job, never part of ingest.
  • Every tenant: keel index, keel consolidate and keel expire take --all-tenants instead of one tenant and run over store.tenants() one after another.
  • Erasure: keel forget <tenant> --db --yes [--index] erases one tenant (§3.4) and prints what it deleted as JSON; with --index its semantic documents go too. index_tenant clears a forgotten tenant's documents, and keel index --all-tenants does so for every tenant forgotten since its last run (its cursor file marks it as not yet cleared). annotate on a forgotten tenant raises. keel forget <tenant> --before <date> --db --yes (or --all-tenants) runs retention instead and prints one JSON line per tenant.
  • Replay: rebuild a tenant from the external log. Shipped: Ingestor.replay(tenant, events=adapter) and keel replay <cartridge> <stream> <tenant> --db.

docs.title: 9. Invariants (what a conformance test checks)
docs.text:
1. No record spans tenants; every read is partitioned by tenant (global memory is read from its own partition, §6).
  2. open_fact never overwrites: after two writes to the same predicate, both facts exist and the first is closed at the second's valid_from.
  3. A fact query at=t returns exactly the facts valid at t.
  4. Replay produces a graph equal to the one built incrementally.
  5. annotate to a scope in requires_evidence without evidence raises; when evidence is declared, so does evidence that is neither an event id the tenant's log applied (event) nor a declared ref prefix; an event must have set a fact on the subject written about.
  6. task/agent annotations carry expires_at; tenant/global with never TTL do not.
  7. The core imports nothing from cartridges/ or examples/; every example cartridge validates and passes after any core change.
  8. Ingest performs no I/O other than reading the adapter and writing the store.
  9. Ingesting the same event twice changes nothing, and ingesting the same events in any order yields the same facts.
  10. Scope reads hold (§6): agent memory reaches only its author, task memory only its task, global memory every tenant.

docs.title: 10. Non-goals
docs.text:
• Document or conversation ingestion (RAG memory). Keel can hold a pointer to such a store's output as a fact.
  • Agent orchestration, planning or tool routing.
  • A query language exposed to agents beyond the five tools and the optional, read-only, tenant-bound query (§7.8): no writes, no cross-tenant reads.
  • Cross-tenant analytics (do that on the product's warehouse).

docs.title: 11. Versioning
docs.text:
• The envelope, the cartridge format and the tool signatures (five core, one optional) are versioned together as the Keel standard; breaking changes bump the minor version while pre-1.0.
  • The public contract is what a caller builds on: the exports of keel/__init__.py, the envelope, the cartridge schema (docs/cartridge.schema.json), the five tools and the optional query in Python, over MCP and over HTTP (names, parameters, defaults, enums, read-only annotations), the store protocol (keel/store/base.py) and the Python client. tests/contract.json freezes it and tests/test_contract.py fails on any difference, telling an addition from a break.
  • Additions (a new optional parameter, a new enum value, a new field in an answer) ship in any minor version.
  • Breaks (a removed or renamed parameter or tool, a changed default, a new required parameter, a removed enum value) need a deprecation first: the old form keeps working for at least one minor version, warns (DeprecationWarning in Python; a {"note": ...} element or field over MCP and HTTP) and is named in the release notes with its replacement; only then may a release remove it, with --allow-breaking when refreshing the snapshot. Pieces marked experimental (MCP detail="text") may change without a deprecation, still named in the release notes.
  • A cartridge declares its own version; the core records which cartridge version built a tenant's graph (planned).
  • Store implementations are versioned independently; all MUST pass the conformance invariants (§9).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Everything Keel is made of, on one page: where events come from, what happens to them, where they are kept, how agents read and write them, and what runs on a schedule. Read this first; every other page goes deeper into one box of this map.

docs.title: What Keel is, and what it is not
docs.text:
Keel is the context layer for the AI agents inside a product. Domain events from your product go in. A bitemporal context graph per tenant comes out. Every agent reads and writes it through the same five tools. Your domain is declared once, in a cartridge.

Keel is not Because An agent framework Your agents live in LangGraph, the Claude Agent SDK, ADK or your backend. Keel is what they consult. A document or RAG memory It ingests structured events with time, not text. Ingestion is deterministic: no LLM reads your events. A copy of your database The graph holds pointers to your rows (ref), their semantics and what agents learned, never whole rows. One flat global memory Memory has scopes (global, tenant, task, agent), and nothing is promoted to a wider one by accident.

docs.title: What happens to one event
docs.text:
1. Your product emits a domain fact. For example tire.depth_measured with depth_mm: 2.4. It can leave through an outbox table, CDC, the SDK, a webhook, a queue or a file.
  2. An adapter turns it into an envelope. It checks the fields and that times are timezone-aware UTC. It never interprets the payload.
  3. The Ingestor dedupes and dispatches it. An id already applied is skipped. Otherwise the handler registered for its type runs.
  4. The cartridge's handler writes primitives. upsert_entity, link, open_fact. A new fact closes the one that was current at that instant, so arrival order does not change the result.
  5. An agent asks. context("tire:T-9001") returns the open facts, the relations and every rule's verdict (tire_critical: true) next to its definition.
  6. The agent writes what it concluded. annotate(..., scope="task", evidence="inspection:4821"). Keel enforces the memory policy; the agent cannot skip it.

docs.title: 1–2. Getting events in
docs.text:
Every source produces the same envelope, and you can combine several for one tenant: the event id dedupes. Details and options for each are in Send your events.

Source Use it when Start it with Guarantee Postgres CDC You would rather not touch the product's code. Each row change becomes <kind>.created\|updated\|deleted. keel cdc <cartridge> --dsn ... --map cdc.yaml --setup, or keel serve --cdc cdc.yaml The slot moves only after the store commits. Needs wal_level = logical. Typed SDK Your backend (TypeScript, Python, Go, PHP) emits events from business code, with payload types generated from the cartridge. keel sdk typescript <cartridge> -o src/keel.ts, then keel.events([emit.tireDepthMeasured({...})]) POST /v1/events. Ids are a content hash when you send none, so a retry is a duplicate, not a second event. Outbox table You already write domain events to a table in the same transaction as the business change. PostgresTableAdapter(connect, cursor_path=".keel/cursor") At-least-once, a seq cursor; restarts resume. Webhook Something else pushes JSON envelopes over HTTP. POST /v1/events on keel serve --transport http, or build_app(ingestor, token=...) One envelope or a list per request; the sender retries. SQS You have a queue, or want producer and Keel decoupled. keel consume <cartridge> --queue <url> --db ... At-least-once; a failing message goes to the queue's dead-letter queue. Kafka Your platform already publishes to a topic. KafkaAdapter.connect(...) from Python At-least-once. No CLI command yet. JSONL file Development, history backfill, tests, rebuilding the graph. keel ingest <cartridge> events.jsonl --db ..., keel replay Deterministic: the same log gives the same graph. Your own adapter Any other source. Any iterable that yields Events (example) What you implement; follow() and ack() are optional.

docs.title: 3. The ingest path and the cartridge
docs.text:
The ingest path is deterministic: no network calls, no LLM, no randomness. Replaying a tenant's log rebuilds the same graph, which is why the event log, not the graph, is the truth.
