The cartridge is the only domain code you write: a folder with cartridge.yaml and handlers.py. Keel's core knows no entity kind, relation, predicate or event type; all of them come from here.

Section What it declares entities The kinds of things, each with ref to the table it points to. relations Typed edges between kinds (mounted_on: {from: tire, to: unit}). events The event catalog: each type, its subject kind and its payload shape. keel validate --events checks a stream against it. handlers.py One small function per event type: payload in, store primitives out. rules What "critical", "overdue" or "at risk" means, as a definition and an optional when the tools evaluate. memory TTL per scope and which scopes need evidence. agents The agent registry: who may write which scope and see which kinds and relations. consolidate How episodic memory is summarized into durable facts.

Business logic lives in rules, not in handlers and not in agents. Rules compose (all, any, not), follow relations (via) and measure durations; counts and aggregates over time stay a definition the agent applies. Build one in Your first cartridge.

docs.title: 4. The bitemporal store
docs.text:
Every fact has two time axes. World time (valid_from, valid_to): when it was true. Knowledge time (recorded_at, closed_at): when Keel learned it began and ended. So Keel answers both "is the tire critical?" and "was it critical on October 3, as far as we knew that day?" (as_of, as_known_at). Facts are closed, never overwritten or deleted by a handler, and each carries source, evidence and, when someone corrected it, corrected_by.

The graph is partitioned one subgraph per tenant. No read crosses tenants; the only shared partition is __global__, which every tenant reads and only a privileged annotate(scope="global") writes.

Backend For How MemoryStore Tests, demos, a process that rebuilds from JSONL at start. MemoryStore(), keel serve --events events.jsonl SqliteStore The default durable store. One file, nothing to run. --db keel.db or KEEL_DB=keel.db MysqlStore Several processes, production. --db mysql://user:pass@host:3306/keel Your own Postgres, a graph database, anything else. Implement the protocol in keel/store/base.py and pass the conformance suite: KEEL_STORE=pkg.module:factory uv run pytest tests/test_store.py

docs.title: 5. The five tools, and an optional sixth
docs.text:
The public standard. Every agent, through any surface, uses these five and, where the host enables it, the read-only query; no other. A Tools instance is bound to one tenant (and, with a registry, one agent). Full signatures are in the specification.

Tool The question it answers context What do I know about this subject now, or at as_of? Open facts, relations and rule verdicts. history How did it change over time? Without a subject: what changed since a watermark. search Which subjects match? By text, kind, rule, attribute value or meaning (semantic). related What is it connected to, up to three hops? annotate Remember what the agent concluded: earned memory, with evidence and a scope. query (optional) Off unless enabled (keel serve --query): read-only SQL over views generated from the cartridge, to filter, join, count or aggregate. The store binds it to one tenant.

docs.title: Memory scopes and the agent registry
docs.text:
Scope Who reads it Who writes it Typical life global Every tenant A privileged caller only, with evidence Permanent tenant That tenant's agents Any agent allowed to, with evidence Permanent task Calls that pass that task id Agents working on the task A TTL, say 14 days agent Only its author The agent itself A short TTL, say 1 day

The policy is enforced in the tools, never trusted to the agent. With agents: in the cartridge, every call names a declared agent; a missing or unknown id is refused, and each agent sees only the kinds and relations it declares. Authenticating the agent is your host's job: Keel takes the id as given.

docs.title: 6. How agents reach the tools
docs.text:
Details in Serve the tools and SDKs.

Surface For Start it with Python, in process An agent that is already Python; no network. Tools(cartridge, store, tenant="acme", agent="tires-bot") HTTP JSON API A backend in any language, many tenants from one process. keel serve --transport http --db ...: POST /v1/{context,history,search,related,annotate}, POST /v1/events, GET /health; headers Authorization: Bearer, X-Keel-Tenant, X-Keel-Agent MCP Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, any MCP client. keel serve --tenant acme (stdio), or /mcp on the HTTP server Typed SDKs TypeScript, Python, Go and PHP backends: the five tools and events() with types from your cartridge. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> -o <file> Console People: browse the graph, try the tools, watch events, download SDKs. keel serve --transport http --ui, at /ui Semantic search Finding subjects by meaning; optional. keel index fills a vector index (Chroma, Weaviate or yours); keel serve --index ... --embedder ...

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
They run outside ingest, from the CLI or cron, so they may call the network or an LLM. Details in Operate.

Command What it does How often keel expire --consolidate Consolidates episodic memory into durable facts, then drops expired task and agent memory. Daily keel index Incremental indexing for semantic search. Every few minutes keel replay Rebuilds a tenant's graph from its log, keeping annotations. After changing handlers keel export One tenant's audit trail as JSONL, closed facts and provenance included. On demand keel forget Erases a tenant for good, or with --before, what closed before a date (retention). On demand, or scheduled keel usage Events ingested and calls per tool, read from the log. For metering

docs.title: Three ways to run it
docs.text: Mode What it looks like Pick it when Embedded pip install keel-context; the Ingestor and the Tools inside your Python service, on SQLite or MySQL. Your agents are Python and you want the fewest moving parts. Self-hosted service The ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel container: keel serve --transport http --db mysql://... --cdc cdc.yaml --ui, plus keel consume if you use SQS, plus cron for the jobs. Agents in several languages, or several products sharing one deployment (run it in a container). Hosted One Keel container and one database per account, with a console to upload or generate the cartridge, set up CDC, issue keys per tenant and try an agent. You would rather not run it. During the pilots, by invitation: pilot request.

docs.title: Rules that do not bend
docs.text:
• Events are the truth. The graph is derived and can be rebuilt with replay. Only annotations live outside the log, and a replay keeps them.
  • Pointers, not copies. An entity carries ref to its row and the few attributes a tool needs to label it.
  • Deterministic ingest. No network, no LLM, no randomness in handlers. LLMs belong in jobs or in the agent.
  • Facts close. Handlers never delete or mutate a fact.
  • One tenant per Tools instance. Cross-tenant reads do not exist.
  • Five core tools, plus an optional sixth. A new capability goes into the semantics of these five before anyone adds another. The sixth, query, is read-only SQL generated from the cartridge, off unless enabled, bound to one tenant by the store.
  • Provenance on every fact. source, evidence, and corrected_by when someone corrected it.

docs.title: Your first day
docs.text:
1. Run the example. uv sync --extra dev, then uv run python examples/fleet/agent_minimal.py. Read examples/fleet/: a complete cartridge with its events and its test.
  2. Pick the tenant and five to ten events. The facts your agents need today, not your whole database. Write twenty real ones to an events.jsonl.
  3. Write the cartridge. keel init cartridges/mine, entities with ref, the event catalog and one handler per type. Check it: keel validate cartridges/mine --events events.jsonl.
  4. Move business logic into rules. If an agent computes "overdue", "critical" or "at risk", that rule belongs in the cartridge.
  5. Connect the real source. CDC if you would rather not touch the product; the SDK, an outbox or a webhook for explicit domain events.
  6. Connect an agent. MCP to try it with Claude; HTTP or the generated SDK for production. Declare it under agents: with the least it needs.
  7. Schedule the jobs. keel expire --consolidate daily and, with semantic search, keel index.

The same path with a time budget per step, and our help: your first pilot in a day.

docs.title: Connect your events
docs.text:
This page was split in three:

  • Send your events: the envelope, Postgres CDC, the typed SDK, an outbox table, a webhook, Kafka, SQS and .jsonl files.
  • Serve the tools: MCP, the HTTP JSON API, accounts and API keys, semantic search.
  • Operate: configuration, the container, consolidation, export, erasure and retention.

The map of how they fit together is in Architecture.

docs.title: Contributing to Keel
docs.text: Keel is built in the open, part-time. Small, focused pull requests land fastest.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
uv sync --extra dev
uv run pytest -n auto   # parallel (pytest-xdist); each worker gets its own Postgres database when KEEL_POSTGRES_URL is set
uv run keel validate examples/fleet --events examples/fleet/events.jsonl && uv run keel validate examples/crm --events examples/crm/events.jsonl && uv run keel validate examples/finance --events examples/finance/events.jsonl && uv run keel validate examples/clinics --events examples/clinics/events.jsonl

docs.title: What we are looking for
docs.text:
• Cartridges. The best contribution. A new vertical (clinics, logistics, property management, ...) in examples/<name>/ with cartridge.yaml, handlers.py, a sample stream in events.jsonl and a test in test_<name>.py, like the four already there. It must pass keel validate and require zero changes under keel/. If it does need a core change, open an issue first: that is a bug in the core, and we want to fix it generically.
  • Adapters. Sources that yield Events (see keel/adapters/). An adapter never reads a payload.
  • Bug reports with a failing test. The fastest way to get something fixed.

docs.title: Rules the review enforces
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md is the spec and docs/SPEC.md is the normative contract. The short version:

  1. No domain names under keel/: no entity kind, relation, predicate, rule or event type.
  2. Pointers, not copies. Never copy a row or a table into the graph.
  3. Facts close. Handlers never mutate or delete them.
  4. Five tools. New capability goes into the semantics of the existing five.
  5. Deterministic ingest: no network, no LLM, no randomness.
  6. Every core change comes with a test. Every cartridge change comes with events and assertions.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
• Open an issue before a large change. For a cartridge or a small fix, a pull request is fine.
  • Run uv run ruff check . and uv run pytest before pushing.
  • Commit messages and all user-facing text in English.
  • If examples/fleet/agent_minimal.py output changes, say why in the pull request.

docs.title: Against a real Postgres
docs.text:
The table adapter's tests run on sqlite3. To run the same test on Postgres, start one and point KEEL_PG_DSN at it:

docker run -d --rm --name keel-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=keel -p 127.0.0.1:5435:5432 postgres:16-alpine
KEEL_PG_DSN=postgresql://postgres:keel@127.0.0.1:5435/postgres uv run --extra postgres pytest -k real_postgres
docker rm -f keel-pg

docs.title: Against MySQL
docs.text:
The store conformance suite runs on MySQL too (CI does it with a service container). Locally:

docker run -d --rm --name keel-mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=keel -e MYSQL_DATABASE=keel -p 127.0.0.1:3307:3306 mysql:8.4
KEEL_MYSQL_URL=mysql://root:keel@127.0.0.1:3307/keel uv run --extra mysql pytest -q tests/test_store.py
docker rm -f keel-mysql

docs.title: Your own store
docs.text:
The core talks to a Store protocol (keel/store/base.py); MemoryStore is the reference and SqliteStore the default durable one. A third store (Postgres, Graphiti, anything) is a separate package, never a core change. Run the conformance suite against it:

KEEL_STORE=your_pkg.module:factory uv run pytest tests/test_store.py

factory is a zero-argument callable or class that returns a fresh, empty store.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Bump version in pyproject.toml and __version__ in keel/__init__.py, update the roadmap, then:

git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "keel-context X.Y.Z" && git push origin vX.Y.Z
gh release create vX.Y.Z --title "X.Y.Z" --notes-file notes.md

The tag triggers .github/workflows/release.yml, which runs the tests, builds and publishes keel-context to PyPI through trusted publishing (one-time setup on PyPI: pending publisher for project keel-context, owner angelkurten, repository keel, workflow release.yml, environment pypi).

The SDK runtimes release separately, when they change, each by pushing its tag; the workflow tests the runtime end to end against keel serve before it publishes:

git tag sdk/typescript/vX.Y.Z && git push origin sdk/typescript/vX.Y.Z   # npm (sdk-typescript-release.yml, trusted publishing); bump sdk/typescript/package.json first
git tag sdk/go/vX.Y.Z && git push origin sdk/go/vX.Y.Z                   # the Go module in this repo (sdk-go-release.yml asks the module proxy for it)
git tag sdk/php/vX.Y.Z && git push origin sdk/php/vX.Y.Z                 # Composer (sdk-php-release.yml pushes sdk/php to keel-sdk-php and tags it vX.Y.Z there)

One-time setup: npm trusted publisher for @keel-context/sdk (workflow sdk-typescript-release.yml); a deploy key with write access on keel-sdk-php whose private key is the secret KEEL_SDK_PHP_DEPLOY_KEY here; Packagist registers keel-sdk-php once (Submit, with the repo URL) and follows its tags.

docs.title: Your first cartridge in 20 minutes
docs.text:
A cartridge teaches Keel your vertical. It is a folder with two files. The core never changes.

cartridges/clinics/
  cartridge.yaml
  handlers.py

Build yours in cartridges/clinics, the folder for your own cartridges. The finished version is in the repo as examples/clinics, with its events in examples/clinics/events.jsonl: point any command below at examples/clinics to run it without writing a line.

docs.title: 1. Scaffold it (1 min)
docs.text: uv run keel init cartridges/clinics

docs.title: Completion and validation in your editor
docs.text:
The cartridge format has a JSON Schema at cartridge.schema.json. Put this line at the top of cartridge.yaml:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://angelkurten.github.io/keel/cartridge.schema.json

VS Code with the Red Hat YAML extension (and any editor that speaks the YAML language server) then completes keys, shows what each one means, and flags the shapes keel validate rejects: an event without subject, forgets: always, an unknown rule operator, a payload hint typo. It checks shape only; keel validate still checks names against each other and that every event has a handler.

docs.title: 2. Declare the ontology (5 min)
docs.text:
List the kinds of things your product is about and how they relate. Use your product's own names.

entities:
  patient:     { description: A person treated at the clinic., ref: patients.id }
  appointment: { description: A scheduled visit., ref: appointments.id }
  treatment:   { description: A procedure performed., ref: treatments.id }

relations:
  booked_by:   { from: appointment, to: patient }
  performed_in:{ from: treatment,   to: appointment }

ref is a pointer to your table. Keel stores pointers and meaning, never copies of your rows.

docs.title: 3. Catalog the events (5 min)
docs.text:
Write down the 10 to 20 things that happen in your product. Each has a subject kind, an owner team, and a payload shape. This list is the least technical part and the one that saves the most arguments later.

events:
  appointment.booked:
    subject: patient
    owner: scheduling
    payload: { id: string, starts_at: datetime, treatment: string }
  appointment.no_show:
    subject: appointment
    owner: scheduling
    payload: {}

The shipped cartridge adds a third one, treatment.performed, so the treatment kind gets used. Payload hints can be richer than scalars: status: [booked, done] is an enum, tags: string[] an array, items: [ { code: string, qty: int } ] an array of objects, { ... } a nested object (see the specification).

docs.title: 4. Write one handler per event (5 min)
docs.text:
A handler maps a payload to five primitives: upsert_entity, link, unlink, open_fact, close_fact. Ten lines each. close_fact ends the tenant's fact on a predicate (with value=, only that value, so the end of one term never ends an overlapping one); what agents remembered about it (task and agent memory) keeps its own lifetime.

from keel.handlers import HandlerRegistry
registry = HandlerRegistry()

@registry.on("appointment.booked")
def booked(event, store):
    p = event.payload
    appt = f"appointment:{p['id']}"
    store.upsert_entity(event.tenant, "patient", event.subject_id)
    store.upsert_entity(event.tenant, "appointment", p["id"], starts_at=p["starts_at"])
    store.link(event.tenant, appt, "booked_by", event.subject, event.occurred_at, source=event.source)
    store.open_fact(event.tenant, appt, "status", "booked", valid_from=event.occurred_at, source=event.source, evidence=event.id)

@registry.on("appointment.no_show")
def no_show(event, store):
    store.open_fact(event.tenant, event.subject, "status", "no_show", valid_from=event.occurred_at, source=event.source, evidence=event.id)

open_fact closes the previous value of the same predicate instead of overwriting it, and a late event takes its place in the history rather than closing a newer value backwards. That is what makes the graph bitemporal: you can ask what was true on any date. Events are deduplicated by id, so retrying a batch is safe.

docs.title: 5. Add your semantics (2 min)
docs.text:
Definitions your agents should never invent for themselves:

rules:
  at_risk_patient:
    applies_to: patient
    definition: "A patient is at risk of churn after two no-shows in 90 days."
    no_shows: 2
    days: 90
  appointment_missed:
    applies_to: appointment
    definition: "An appointment is missed when its status is no_show."
    when: { predicate: status, eq: no_show }

The context tool returns the rules that apply to a subject's kind, so every agent reads the same definition. A rule with a when is also evaluated for you: context returns evaluation: {appointment_missed: true} next to the rule, so the agent neither defines nor computes it. at_risk_patient needs a count over 90 days, so it has no when and the agent applies the definition. Conditions compose with all, any and not, follow a relation with via (a patient is at risk if any of their appointments is missed: { via: booked_by, direction: in, any: { predicate: status, eq: no_show } }), compare strings with ci: true, and measure how long a fact has been open with open_for_days or open_for_business_days (or how long it has held one of several values, surviving a change between them, with held_for_days or held_for_business_days). The full grammar is in the specification.

docs.title: 6. Validate and run (2 min)
docs.text:
uv run keel validate cartridges/clinics
uv run keel validate cartridges/clinics --events examples/clinics/events.jsonl
uv run keel ingest cartridges/clinics examples/clinics/events.jsonl
uv run keel context cartridges/clinics examples/clinics/events.jsonl patient:P-1

validate fails if an event has no handler, a handler has no event, a relation uses an undeclared kind, a payload hint does not parse, a rule's when uses an unknown operator or an undeclared relation, or the agents, semantic, consolidate or predicates sections are malformed. With --events it also checks a stream against the catalog: unknown types, wrong subject kinds, missing or mistyped payload fields.

docs.title: 7. Point an agent at it
docs.text:
uv sync --extra mcp
uv run keel serve cartridges/clinics --tenant clinic-centro --events examples/clinics/events.jsonl

Any MCP client now sees context, history, search, annotate, related. Your second agent uses the same five tools; there is no second pipeline.

docs.title: 8. Declare your agents (optional)
docs.text:
When more than one agent shares the graph, say who they are and what each may do. The layer enforces it; the agent never polices itself.

agents:
  reception-bot:
    description: Confirms appointments. Writes task memory only.
    writes: [task, agent]
    reads: { kinds: [patient, appointment], relations: [booked_by] }
  clinic-copilot:
    writes: [task, agent, tenant]   # no reads: sees everything

An agent with no writes: may write [task, agent]; one with kind: human is a person and signs as human:<id>. Once agents: exists, every Tools(...) and every keel serve needs --agent <id>, and an id that is not declared is refused. annotate is signed with the agent id, so keel export shows who wrote what. Agent-scope memory is read only by the agent that wrote it; task-scope memory tied to a task id only by calls that pass that task.

docs.title: 9. Search by meaning (optional)
docs.text:
search(text, mode="semantic") finds subjects by meaning instead of by substring. Say what goes into each subject's searchable document:

semantic:
  kinds: [patient, appointment]
  relations: [booked_by]          # an appointment's document names its patient
  split: {patient: [allergy]}     # optional: each allergy (each element, when the value is a list) is also a document of its own, so one long list does not dilute it

Index outside ingest, from a durable store, and serve with the same index and embedder:

uv run keel ingest cartridges/clinics examples/clinics/events.jsonl --db clinic.db
export KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY=...    # any OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint (KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL, _MODEL)
uv run keel index cartridges/clinics --tenant clinic-centro --db clinic.db --index "examples.custom_adapters:make_index?path=vectors.db"
uv run keel serve cartridges/clinics --tenant clinic-centro --db clinic.db --index "examples.custom_adapters:make_index?path=vectors.db"

--embedder hash runs it offline for a try. The index here is the SQLite example adapter; chroma:///path is the bundled one, and your own vector database is an adapter you write (Connect, semantic search). Run keel index from cron: it only re-indexes what changed.

docs.title: The test that it worked
docs.text: Did you edit anything under keel/? If yes, some domain leaked into the core. Open an issue; that is exactly the kind of thing we want to fix.

docs.title: Send your events
docs.text:
Keel ingests envelopes, never raw rows. Every source produces the same shape, and the cartridge's handlers are the only code that reads a payload. Pick the source that matches where your events already are; you can combine several for one tenant, because the event id dedupes.

Source Use it when Guarantee Postgres CDC You would rather not touch the product's code: Keel follows your own tables. The replication slot moves only after the store commits. The typed SDK Your backend emits events from business code, with types generated from the cartridge. Ids are a content hash when you send none: a retry is a duplicate. An outbox table You write domain events to a table in the same transaction as the change. At-least-once, with a cursor; restarts resume. A webhook Something else pushes JSON envelopes over HTTP. The response is the ingest report; the sender retries. SQS or Kafka You already have a queue or a topic. At-least-once, acknowledged after each commit. A .jsonl file Development, history backfill, tests, replay. Deterministic: the same log gives the same graph.

Where this fits in the whole: Architecture.

docs.title: The envelope
docs.text:
One event, as the development adapter reads it from examples/fleet/events.jsonl:

{"tenant": "acme-logistics", "type": "unit.registered", "subject": "unit:MXK-4821",
 "occurred_at": "2026-09-01T09:00:00Z", "source": "fleet.vehicles",
 "payload": {"id": "MXK-4821", "plate": "MXK-4821", "model": "Freightliner Cascadia"}}
Field Required Meaning tenant yes The end-customer this fact belongs to. Opaque to Keel. type yes Dotted lowercase type from the cartridge catalog. subject yes <kind>:<id> of the entity the fact is about. occurred_at yes When it happened in the world. Timezone-aware. source yes System of record or adapter name. id no Generated when absent. Becomes the evidence of derived facts. recorded_at no When Keel learned it. Defaults to now. payload no Event data. Only handlers read it.

The full rules are in the specification.

docs.title: A .jsonl file
docs.text:
For development and tests. One envelope per line; blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored.

uv run keel ingest examples/fleet examples/fleet/events.jsonl

The command prints processed, duplicates, unhandled, errors and skipped (events for a forgotten tenant, see Erase a tenant) and carries on past a bad event. --strict stops at the first unhandled type or handler error instead; on a SQL store the batch in flight (5000 events) is rolled back.

docs.title: A Postgres outbox table
docs.text:
Your SaaS inserts envelopes into a table. Keel polls it in order and remembers the last row it took in a cursor file, so a restart resumes instead of re-ingesting.

CREATE TABLE keel_events (
    seq          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    id           text NOT NULL,
    tenant       text NOT NULL,
    type         text NOT NULL,
    subject      text NOT NULL,
    occurred_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
    recorded_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    source       text NOT NULL,
    payload      jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

uv sync --extra postgres

import psycopg

from keel import Ingestor, MemoryStore, SqliteStore, load_cartridge
from keel.adapters.postgres import PostgresTableAdapter

ingestor = Ingestor(load_cartridge("examples/fleet"), SqliteStore("keel.db"))  # durable; MemoryStore() for a throwaway graph
adapter = PostgresTableAdapter(lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), table="keel_events", cursor_path=".keel/cursor")

ingestor.ingest(adapter)                      # one pass over everything after the cursor
ingestor.ingest(adapter.follow(interval=5))   # or poll forever

Delivery is at-least-once: Ingestor.ingest moves the cursor only after each commit (it calls the adapter's ack()), so with batch=N a batch that rolls back, or a crash mid-batch, is read again whole; the store skips what it already applied as duplicates. Iterating the adapter by hand, the cursor moves when you ask for the next event; call adapter.ack() after storing instead if you batch your own writes. The table name, the cursor column and the batch size are parameters (table=, cursor_column="seq", batch_size=500). Any DB-API 2.0 connection works; pass placeholder="?" for sqlite3.

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Your SaaS
    participant T as keel_events
    participant A as PostgresTableAdapter
    participant C as cursor file
    participant I as Ingestor
    S->>T: INSERT envelope (seq 41)
    A->>C: read position
    C-->>A: 40
    A->>T: SELECT * WHERE seq > 40 ORDER BY seq LIMIT 500
    T-->>A: row 41
    A->>I: Event 41
    I->>I: dispatch to the handler
    I->>A: next event?
    A->>C: write 41
    Note over A,I: a crash before "write 41" re-delivers event 41 on restart

Concurrent writers

A serial cursor can skip a row that commits late while a later row was already read. Use one writer per table, or a recorded_at cursor with a lag, if that bites.

docs.title: Postgres CDC: your own tables, no outbox
docs.text:
If you would rather not write an outbox, Keel can follow row changes in the tables you already have, through logical replication. It uses the built-in pgoutput plugin (Postgres 10 or later, also RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure and Supabase), read through SQL functions, so there is no extension to install. The database needs wal_level = logical.

Map each table to a kind in a small YAML file:

# cdc.yaml
inspections: {kind: inspection, id: id, tenant: tenant_id}
tires:       {kind: tire, id: serial, tenant: fleet_id, columns: [depth_mm, unit_id]}

Each inserted, updated or deleted row becomes an event <kind>.created, <kind>.updated or <kind>.deleted, with the subject <kind>:<id column>, the transaction's commit time as occurred_at, and the row (only columns, plus the id, when you list them: pointers, not copies) as payload. Declare those event types in your cartridge; keel cdc refuses to start while one is missing, because a read would stop at it.

uv sync --extra postgres
uv run keel cdc cartridges/mine --dsn postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/app --map cdc.yaml --db keel.db --setup

--setup creates the publication and the replication slot (keel by default) and sets REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on tables with a tenant column, since by default a delete carries only the primary key. The slot moves only after Keel has stored what it read, so a crash reads it again and dedupe skips what was already stored (event ids are pgcdc:<commit lsn>:<n>). --once reads what is there and stops; without it, keel cdc follows. A slot nobody reads keeps WAL on the database server's disk: drop it with SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('keel') when you stop for good.

keel serve --transport http --cdc cdc.yaml (with KEEL_PG_DSN set) follows the same tables in a thread of the server instead of a second process: it creates what is missing, retries after a failure with a growing pause, and /health shows cdc with ok, events, last_read and the last error. --account (or KEEL_ACCOUNT, as a hosted container has) puts every tenant under that account, account/<tenant>, for both commands.

docs.title: From your code: the typed SDK
docs.text:
When your product's backend is the one that knows an event happened, emit it from there. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> generates a typed client from your cartridge: an emit constructor per cataloged event, whose payload type comes from the catalog, so a wrong key or type fails in your editor or compiler instead of in a handler. The same client calls the five tools.

import { client, emit, subjects } from "./keel-fleet";   // keel sdk typescript examples/fleet -o src/keel-fleet.ts

const keel = client({ baseUrl: "http://keel.internal:8000", tenant: "acme-logistics", secret: process.env.KEEL_SECRET });

const report = await keel.events([
  emit.tireDepthMeasured({ tenant: "acme-logistics", subject: subjects.tire("T-9001"), occurredAt: new Date(), source: "tires.measurements", payload: { unit_id: "MXK-4821", position: "P3", depth_mm: 2.6 } }),
]);
report.processed;   // 1

events() posts one envelope or a list to POST /v1/events on keel serve --transport http and returns the ingest report (processed, duplicates, unhandled, errors). When an envelope has no id, the server derives one from its content, so retrying after a network error stores it once. Python, Go and PHP work the same way: see SDKs.

Where you call it matters: right after the business transaction commits, an event can be lost if the process dies in between. When that is unacceptable, write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, or let CDC follow the table.

docs.title: A webhook
docs.text:
Keel receives envelopes over HTTP, validates them and ingests them in the request.

uv sync --extra webhook

# app.py
from keel import Ingestor, MemoryStore, SqliteStore, load_cartridge
from keel.adapters.webhook import build_app

ingestor = Ingestor(load_cartridge("examples/fleet"), SqliteStore("keel.db"))  # durable; MemoryStore() for a throwaway graph
app = build_app(ingestor, token="shared-secret")

uv run uvicorn app:app --port 8000
curl -X POST localhost:8000/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer shared-secret" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '[{"tenant": "acme-logistics", "type": "unit.registered", "subject": "unit:MXK-4821", "occurred_at": "2026-09-01T09:00:00Z", "source": "fleet.vehicles", "payload": {"id": "MXK-4821", "plate": "MXK-4821", "model": "Freightliner Cascadia"}}]'

The body is one envelope or a list. The response is the ingest report: processed, duplicates (ids the store had already applied), unhandled types, errors, forgotten (the tenants this batch erased, with what was deleted) and skipped (events for a forgotten tenant). build_app(ingestor, token=..., strict=True) fails the request at the first unhandled type or handler error instead of reporting it; on a SQL store the request's batch is rolled back, so the sender can retry it whole. A malformed envelope is a 422; a wrong token is a 401. Without a token the endpoint accepts any caller, so use that only on localhost.

docs.title: Consume a Kafka topic or an SQS queue
docs.text:
Your SaaS publishes envelopes as JSON messages; Keel consumes them. uv sync --extra kafka (confluent-kafka) or --extra sqs (boto3).

For SQS there is a command; run it as a long-lived service:

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... AWS_REGION=us-east-1 \
  uv run keel consume cartridges/mine --queue https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/keel-events --db keel.db
uv run keel consume cartridges/mine --queue http://elasticmq:9324/000000000000/keel-events --db keel.db   # SQS-compatible: the queue's host is the endpoint

Messages are stored a batch per transaction (--batch, default 100: one long poll, topped up with what is already queued) and deleted, ten per call, only once stored. When a batch fails it is retried one message at a time, and a message that still fails (not an envelope, a type with no handler, a handler error) is logged and left on the queue, so SQS redelivers it after the visibility timeout and, after the queue's maxReceiveCount, moves it to its dead-letter queue: give the queue one. If the store itself stops answering (MySQL down), the command exits with code 2 instead of dead-lettering every message: run it under a supervisor that restarts it. A connection the server dropped while idle (wait_timeout) is reopened. --once drains what is queued and stops (exit code 1 if anything failed). An erasure prints one JSON line ({"forgot": <tenant>, "event": ..., "entities": ...}) on stdout for your audit log; everything else goes to stderr. KEEL_QUEUE and KEEL_DB stand in for the flags. Kafka has no per-message redelivery (committing a later offset skips a failed one), so it has no command yet; use KafkaAdapter from Python:

from keel.adapters.bus import KafkaAdapter, SqsAdapter

adapter = KafkaAdapter.connect("broker:9092", topic="keel-events", group_id="keel")
adapter = SqsAdapter.connect("https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/keel-events")
ingestor.ingest(adapter)            # drain what is there now, then stop
ingestor.ingest(adapter.follow())   # consume forever

Delivery is at-least-once: the offset is committed, or the SQS message deleted, only after the batch that holds it is committed (Ingestor.ingest calls the adapter's ack()), so a crash mid-batch redelivers the whole batch. With batch=N on SQS, keep the visibility timeout above the time a batch takes. A message that is not a valid envelope raises and stays on the bus; pass dead_letter=lambda body, error: ... to log it somewhere and move on. KafkaAdapter.connect(..., **config) merges extra keys into the confluent-kafka consumer config (dotted keys go through a dict: **{"security.protocol": "SSL"}); SqsAdapter.connect(queue_url, **kwargs) passes them to boto3.client("sqs", ...). connect also takes the adapter's own options as keywords: KafkaAdapter.connect(..., poll_timeout=1.0, dead_letter=...), SqsAdapter.connect(queue_url, batch_size=10, wait_seconds=10, dead_letter=...); or build the adapter from your own client with the same keywords: KafkaAdapter(consumer, ...), SqsAdapter(client, queue_url, ...). Both adapters only need two calls from their client (poll/commit, receive_message/delete_message), which is how the tests run them on fakes and how you would wrap another client.

docs.title: Operate
docs.text:
Configuration, the container, and the jobs that run next to the server. Jobs run outside ingest, from the CLI or your scheduler, so unlike handlers they may call the network or an LLM.

Command What it does How often keel expire --consolidate Consolidates episodic memory into durable facts, then drops expired task and agent memory. Daily keel index Incremental indexing for semantic search. Every few minutes keel replay Rebuilds a tenant's graph from its log, keeping annotations; --check changes nothing and says whether a rebuild would give the same graph. After changing handlers; --check on a schedule keel export One tenant's audit trail as JSONL, complete enough to restore. On demand, or as a backup keel import Restores a tenant from keel export into an empty tenant of any store. To move or restore a tenant keel forget Erases a tenant, or with --before, what closed before a date. On demand, or scheduled for retention keel usage Events ingested and calls per tool, read from the log. For metering

keel index, keel consolidate and keel expire take --all-tenants to run over every tenant in the store.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Every setting the CLI reads from the environment can live in a .env file: keel loads ./.env when it exists, or the file named by --env-file (or KEEL_ENV_FILE). Variables already set in the environment win, so a deployment can override the file. KEY=VALUE lines, # comments, optional export and quotes; no interpolation. Copy .env.example and fill in what you use; keep .env out of git (it holds secrets).

Variable Used by What KEEL_DB every command with --db the durable graph: a SQLite file or mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db KEEL_TENANT every command that takes a tenant; serve (--tenant) the default tenant; with serve --transport http it is used when X-Keel-Tenant is absent KEEL_AGENT serve, context... (--agent) the declared agent acting here KEEL_CERTFILE, KEEL_KEYFILE serve --transport http TLS certificate and key (PEM) to serve https (--certfile, --keyfile) KEEL_SECRET serve --transport http the shared bearer secret, the operator's credential (--secret-env names another variable); per-account API keys: keel keys KEEL_INDEX, KEEL_EMBEDDER index, serve the vector index and embedder specs (--index, --embedder) KEEL_INDEX_CURSOR, KEEL_INDEX_WORKERS index where the cursor of the last run is kept (on a volume) and how many embedding batches go out at once (--cursor, --workers) KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL, _MODEL, _API_KEY, _QUERY_PREFIX, _DOCUMENT_PREFIX --embedder openai any OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint KEEL_RERANK_BASE_URL, _MODEL, _API_KEY serve --reranker http\|llm the reranker endpoint KEEL_SUMMARIZER_BASE_URL, _MODEL, _API_KEY consolidate --summarizer llm the chat model that writes summaries

A flag on the command line beats both.

No end-customers? Keel keys everything on a tenant, but nothing forces you to have many. Pick one fixed value, put it in every envelope's tenant and in KEEL_TENANT=default, and stop passing --tenant: every command, keel serve and the HTTP API (no X-Keel-Tenant needed) use it. The tenant scope then simply means "shared by every agent".

The Python API reads nothing from .env: a program that embeds Keel passes its settings itself.

docs.title: Run it in a container
docs.text:
ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel serves the tools over HTTP (/v1 and /mcp; KEEL_TENANT binds /mcp to one tenant) on port 8000, for amd64 and arm64. Tags follow the releases: 0.35.0, 0.35, latest, and -slim variants without the Chroma client (a third of the size, no semantic search on Chroma). The cartridge is not in the image: mount it at /cartridge. Both variants include the Postgres driver, so KEEL_CDC_MAP and KEEL_PG_DSN make the container follow Postgres too.

docker run -p 8000:8000 -e KEEL_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \
  -e KEEL_DB=mysql://keel:secret@db.internal:3306/keel \
  -v ./examples/fleet:/cartridge:ro -v keel-data:/data ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel:0.35.0
  • It refuses to start without KEEL_SECRET (or --allow-open behind your own auth proxy), since it listens on every interface.
  • /data is the working directory and a volume: a SQLite graph (KEEL_DB=/data/keel.db), the keel index cursor (/data/.keel/) and a .env live there.
  • It runs as an unprivileged user and checks its own /health (no curl needed in the image). Configuration is the environment (Configuration); every command reads KEEL_DB, KEEL_TENANT and KEEL_INDEX.
  • Any other command runs the same way: docker run ... ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel:0.35.0 index /cartridge (the entrypoint is keel).
  • To ship your cartridge inside, two lines: FROM ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel:0.35.0 and COPY cartridges/mine /cartridge.

Single sign-on for your team in front of /ui, with Caddy and oauth2-proxy and no code in Keel: deploy/sso.

deploy/docker-compose.yml runs Keel with its own MySQL, a Chroma server and keel index every 15 minutes: KEEL_SECRET=... docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d. docker build -t keel . builds this checkout; --build-arg KEEL_VERSION=0.35.0 builds a release from PyPI. deploy/smoke.sh <image> checks an image end to end.

docs.title: Consolidate episodic memory
docs.text:
Agents write task and agent memory that expires. A cartridge's consolidate: section declares which of it becomes a durable fact: the source predicate and scopes (task memory by default; agent memory is private and is read only when from.scopes lists it), an optional within: window on world time (valid_from, so a reingested history keeps its dates), how many observations make a pattern, a reducer (mode, latest, count, min, max, avg, distinct or summary) and the predicate and scope to write. It runs as a job, never in ingest:

uv run keel consolidate examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --db keel.db
uv run keel expire acme-logistics --db keel.db --consolidate examples/fleet   # consolidate, then drop expired memory
uv run keel expire --all-tenants --db keel.db --consolidate examples/fleet     # every tenant in the store, one after another

Each run prints written and unchanged per consolidation and is idempotent: the same inputs never write twice. The originals stay until their TTL. reduce: summary needs --summarizer: llm (any OpenAI-compatible chat model, from KEEL_SUMMARIZER_BASE_URL, KEEL_SUMMARIZER_MODEL and KEEL_SUMMARIZER_API_KEY), join (the distinct values joined, deterministic) or your own pkg.module:factory. The other reducers are deterministic and need none.

docs.title: Export the audit trail
docs.text:
One tenant, everything Keel knows about it, as JSONL: entities, relations and facts, closed ones included, each with source, evidence, scope, recorded_at and corrected_by. Hand it to the customer, an auditor, or a diff.

uv run keel export acme-logistics --db keel.db --out acme-logistics.jsonl

Each line is one record: {"record": "fact", "subject": "tire:T-9001", "predicate": "depth_mm", "value": 5.2, "valid_from": ..., "valid_to": ..., "source": "tires.measurements", "evidence": "<event id>", ...}. Another tenant's export never contains this one's rows. Besides entity, relation and fact, an export carries what a restore needs: close (an explicit close kept in a predicate's history, so a late event still meets it), ingested (an applied event id, so a redelivered event stays a duplicate) and cutoff (the retention cutoff). An audit reader can skip those.

docs.title: Move or restore a tenant
docs.text:
keel import writes an export back as it was, transaction times included, into a tenant that has no data (it refuses one that has), in any store: a SQLite file moves to MySQL this way.

uv run keel export acme-logistics --db keel.db --out acme-logistics.jsonl
uv run keel import acme-logistics.jsonl acme-logistics --db mysql://user:pass@host:3306/keel

docs.title: Check that a rebuild gives the same graph
docs.text:
keel replay --check rebuilds the tenant in memory from its log, around the annotations the db holds, and compares world time and provenance with the db, without writing. It prints identical, or what only the db has and what only a replay would have, and exits 1: state that no event explains (a hand edit, a handler that changed since) shows up before a real replay would drop it.

uv run keel replay cartridges/fleet events.jsonl acme-logistics --db keel.db --check

docs.title: Erase a tenant
docs.text:
When an end-customer leaves and the law (Colombia's Ley 1581, GDPR's right to erasure) or your privacy notice says their data goes, Keel deletes everything it stores for that tenant: entities, relations, facts of every scope, what agents and people annotated, the ids of the events it applied and, through the index, its semantic documents. Declare the event your SaaS sends when the customer is deleted:

events:
  household.deleted:
    subject: household
    forgets: tenant      # no handler: Keel erases the event's tenant
    payload: { id: string }

It arrives through the same stream, in order. The erasure is one transaction, and a tombstone (the tenant and the time) stays: any later event for that tenant, an old redelivery included, is skipped (skipped in the report) and annotate is refused, so nothing revives it. The ingest report lists what was deleted (forgotten), and keel consume prints it as a JSON line for your audit log. A second erasure deletes nothing and keeps the first time. The semantic documents go on the next keel index --all-tenants (or keel index --tenant <t>).

From the command line, for one tenant:

uv run keel forget household-42 --db keel.db --index chroma://chroma:8000 --yes
# {"tenant": "household-42", "forgotten_at": "...", "entities": 31, "relations": 40, "facts": 212, "annotations": 3, "ingested": 120, "index": true}

Keel erases only what it stores. The external log is yours: delete or expire the tenant's rows in your outbox table, and remember that consumed queue messages are already gone. Global memory is every tenant's and is kept, so never promote a customer's personal data to it. The tombstone holds the tenant id and the time; pick tenant ids that are not personal data on their own.

docs.title: Retention: forget what closed before a date
docs.text:
A contract or a privacy policy may ask for history older than N years to go while the customer stays. Retention deletes facts and relations that closed at or before a cutoff (valid_to <= cutoff), annotations included; open facts, current relations and entities stay. Declare the event your SaaS sends, or run it from the command line:

events:
  retention.applied:
    subject: household
    forgets: before      # no handler: Keel deletes what closed before the event's occurred_at
    payload: {}

uv run keel forget household-42 --before 2024-01-01 --db keel.db --yes
uv run keel forget --all-tenants --before 2024-01-01 --db keel.db --yes      # a retention policy, one JSON line per tenant
# {"tenant": "household-42", "before": "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00", "facts": 180, "annotations": 4, "relations": 12}

The ingest report lists each run (retained) and keel consume prints it for your audit log. The cutoff is kept per tenant (the latest wins), and replay applies it again after rebuilding, so what the log brings back goes again. An event that arrives later with a valid time before the cutoff is kept until the next run: schedule the policy (cron, a Kubernetes CronJob) rather than running it once. Semantic documents follow on the next full keel index.

docs.title: Your first pilot in a day
docs.text:
A pilot answers one question: does your second agent connect in under a day, because there is no second pipeline to write? This page is the path, with a time budget for each step. Write down how long each one really took; that number is what the pilot measures.

You need: a product with domain events (rows in Postgres, webhooks, a Kafka topic or an SQS queue), one agent you already run or plan to, and Docker or Python 3.10+.

docs.title: 1. Pick one slice (30 min)
docs.text: Choose one tenant and the three to five event types an agent actually needs: for a fleet, units, tires and inspections; for a clinic, patients, appointments and results. Leave everything else for later. Keel holds pointers to your rows, not copies, so the slice is small.

docs.title: 2. Write the cartridge (2 h)
docs.text:
uv tool install keel-context
keel init cartridges/mine        # cartridge.yaml + handlers.py

Declare the entities, relations and events, then one handler per event, about ten lines each. Put what your team means by "critical", "overdue" or "at risk" in rules, so every agent gets the same verdict. Your first cartridge walks through it in 20 minutes; examples/ has four finished ones.

Check it against a sample of real events before going further:

keel validate cartridges/mine --events sample.jsonl

docs.title: 3. Send your events (1–2 h)
docs.text:
Pick the path you already have; Send your events covers each one:

  • Postgres CDC: no code in your product. keel cdc follows your own tables through logical replication, each row change an event.
  • The typed SDK: your backend calls keel.events([emit.<event>(...)]), with payload types generated from your cartridge.
  • A Postgres outbox table: your product inserts envelopes into it, and Keel polls it in order with a cursor, so a restart resumes.
  • Webhooks: POST /v1/events with the envelope.
  • SQS: keel consume --queue <url> --db <graph>, which acknowledges only after the graph has stored the batch. Kafka: KafkaAdapter from Python, with the same guarantee.
  • A file, to start: keel ingest cartridges/mine events.jsonl --db keel.db.

Load your history first (keel ingest does a million events in under two minutes on MySQL), then leave the live stream running.

docs.title: 4. Serve the tools (30 min)
docs.text:
docker run -p 8000:8000 -e KEEL_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \
  -v ./cartridges/mine:/cartridge:ro -v keel-data:/data ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel

Or run it next to your agent over stdio: keel serve cartridges/mine --tenant <t> --db keel.db. If several products or teams share one deployment, give each its own key (keel keys create <account>); the server confines each key to its account's tenants.

docs.title: 5. Connect the first agent (1 h)
docs.text: Over MCP, any client: Claude Code (claude mcp add keel -- keel serve ...), Codex, LangGraph (examples/fleet/agent_langgraph.py), or the HTTP API and SDKs for TypeScript, Python, Go and PHP. Ask it something it used to answer from its own pipeline, and compare.

docs.title: 6. Connect the second agent (the measured part)
docs.text: Start the clock. Connect a second agent, with a different job, to the same server: no new extraction, no new rules, no new memory store. If the cartridge declares agents:, give it its own id, the scopes it may write and the kinds it may see. Stop the clock when it answers from the shared graph and what the first agent wrote is visible to it.

docs.title: What you get from us
docs.text: During a pilot we help you through these steps and fix what blocks you in the core, while keeping it generic: what your domain needs goes in your cartridge, never under keel/. The first design customer's requests have shipped as releases, most of them within days.

docs.text:

  • or write to angel@angelkurten.com.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Keel is built in the open at 10–20 hours a week. The order below is deliberate: the public story ships alongside the code, and the proof of the thesis (a second cartridge, a second agent, no second pipeline) comes before polish.

Continue/stop criterion at 90 days: open source traction. Before that, at 30 days: one issue, PR or question from someone we do not know.

Paths changed: cartridges/fleet is examples/fleet, examples/events/fleet.jsonl is examples/fleet/events.jsonl, examples/agent_minimal.py is examples/fleet/agent_minimal.py (0.23.0)

  • [x] From Toche (a tenant per household, Ley 1581): erase a tenant for good. An event declared forgets: tenant in the catalog (no handler) makes the Ingestor call store.forget(tenant) in its transaction: entities, relations, facts of every scope, annotations and applied ids go, a tombstone stays, later events for it are skipped and annotate refused; the report says what was deleted. keel forget <tenant> --db --yes [--index] for operators; the index drops a forgotten tenant's documents (0.24.0)

Tables took the server's collation (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci), so two .pbix pages RENDIMIENTO and Rendimiento were one entity and reading it was a 500; tables are now utf8mb4_bin, older ones are converted on start, and MysqlStore.collided() (and a warning) names the subjects that had collided, to publish again (0.24.2)

  • [x] From the kagent pilot's second round (semantic search had become the slow call: 17 to 20 s for per_kind with related_to): kind takes a list (listing, semantic ranking and per_kind over just those kinds); per_kind embeds the query once, not once per kind; the lexical leg's BM25 is built once per tenant and kinds and reads only the query's tokens (cached until the index changes; in ChromaIndex also for at most bm25_ttl seconds, since another process may re-index); related_to filters inside the index (where={"subject": [...]}; Chroma collections built before this need keel index --full), so its fused score is now normalized among the neighbours. On a synthetic tenant of 14,000 subjects in embedded Chroma, per_kind=5, related_to= went from 1.76 s to 0.09 s (0.21.0)

In the Python client, HTTP, MCP and the TypeScript, Go and PHP runtimes (0.20.0)

Every parameter reaches the Python client, HTTP and MCP (a test checks it) (0.19.0)
  • [x] An official image, ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel (amd64, arm64; -slim without Chroma), published on every release: non-root, /data volume, its own health check, refuses to listen without KEEL_SECRET; deploy/docker-compose.yml with MySQL, a Chroma server and the indexer. Every command with --db now reads KEEL_DB (index, expire, consolidate and export required the flag, so a container configured by its environment failed) (0.18.1)
  • [x] keel index for a production deploy (from kagent: 11,192 entities took 21 minutes): embedding batches go out four at a time with retries on 429/5xx; the cursor defaults to the index's own folder for chroma:///path (KEEL_INDEX_CURSOR otherwise) and a run without one says it is rebuilding; one run per tenant at a time, a second skips (two at once corrupted Chroma); documented that chroma:///path does not work across keel serve and keel index processes (0.18.0)

On the 14M-event MySQL graph context(depth=1) issued about 100 statements, 130 ms over Docker; now a fixed handful (0.18.0; from the stress test)
  • [x] A store shared by the HTTP server's threads keeps a transaction and a batch in flight to the thread that opened them: an annotate arriving during an ingest batch wrote into that batch and was lost if it rolled back, and other threads read its uncommitted state. MySQL reads on a connection per thread: 32 clients went from 41 to 254 requests/s on the 14M-event graph. Reads of the state now fetch only open facts (facts_open), and rule sweeps that follow a relation read relations in batches (relations_of): search(rule=unit_grounded) 1.0 s to 0.22 s (0.18.0)

SDK runtimes: TypeScript and Go 0.16.0, PHP 0.13.0
  • [x] Tool answers in fewer tokens, inside the five tools (0.31.0, 2026-10-20; measured by evals/efficiency). Breaking: over MCP and HTTP, context defaults to detail="brief", history to "concise" (lean facts) and annotate to "ack" (a receipt), and MCP search returns lean fact hits under its default "entity"; Python Tools and the SDK clients keep "full". history and related default to limit=50 (0: all) and a search without limit returns 20 matches or 50 of a listing; a cut list leads with {"more": ...}. A well-formed subject nothing is known about is {subject, found: false, as_of, watermark}, no longer an empty context. An unknown kind, relation, rule or scope, a key without <kind>: and a malformed time raise with the valid values; a semantic search on a server without an embedder ranks by the query's words (with a leading {"note": ...}) instead of raising. MCP results are one block of compact JSON with structuredContent, not indented and not one block per list element. Also: since in brief and concise contexts; a cartridge context: {relations, neighbors} block, and depth=1 reads 5 neighbours per relation and direction (neighbors_more); related ordered by hop, relation, link time and key; the default as_of to the whole second; tool enums, shared descriptions and the ontology in the MCP server's instructions; MCP-only detail="text" (experimental); no MCP outputSchema; Tools(clock=running_from(t)) and keel serve --clock for a demo pinned to a day

docs.text:
From exploring the hosted product (design note). These pieces are pulled forward because they are small and serve self-hosted deployments with several customers too. The hosted launch still waits for its gate.

  • [x] Accounts as a tenant prefix (the account is a slug, at most 32 characters, never renamed): an API key resolves to an account and the server turns X-Keel-Tenant: t into account/t; a client cannot choose the prefix; the global partition becomes account/__global__ (0.27.0)

docs.title: Exit to beta (set 2026-10-22)
docs.text:
Beta is not a feature list: it is a contract that stops moving, no known wrong answers, and real use outside our own products. It can stay 0.x; the classifier moves to Development Status :: 4 - Beta. Not required for beta: 1.0, a Postgres or Graphiti store, multi-cartridge tenants; experimental pieces (MCP detail="text") stay marked experimental.

  • [ ] A frozen contract: the envelope, the cartridge format, the five tool signatures and defaults, and the store protocol change only through a deprecation that lasts at least one minor version; four weeks in a row without a breaking change
  • [x] The contract written down and checked (SPEC §11): tests/contract.json snapshots it and tests/test_contract.py fails on any change, refusing a break unless --allow-breaking (0.33.0, 2026-10-22). The four weeks count from the last snapshot refreshed with --allow-breaking
  • [x] No known correctness bug: the open SPEC questions decided and tested (naive datetimes coerced or rejected; an undeclared subject kind at ingest; whether close_task expires tenant-scope facts written with that task; unlink without transaction time; partial handler failure without strict; reusing an annotate key with another scope; text search with as_known_at), and the SPEC battery and the store conformance suite green on memory, SQLite and MySQL in CI
  • [x] The seven decided and tested (tests/test_spec_decisions.py): naive datetimes are UTC everywhere; an event about the wrong kind is refused; close_task expires task-scope memory only; unlink records closed_at; an event is atomic (a failing handler leaves nothing and the event comes again); a reused key with another scope raises; text search reads facts at as_of. The conformance suite and the whole SPEC battery run on MySQL in CI (0.33.0, 2026-10-22). Same-instant facts without a declared recorded_at follow ingest order, documented in SPEC §3.3 as intended
  • [x] Data that survives upgrades: a test opens databases written by 0.8, 0.20 and 0.32, migrates them and answers as before; a check that replay rebuilds a graph identical to the live one; an import for keel export so a tenant can be restored or moved between stores
  • [x] tests/test_upgrade.py opens SQLite databases written by the released 0.8.0, 0.20.0 and 0.32.0 (tests/upgrade/make.py regenerates them) and checks they answer as a fresh one, before and after new writes; it found that old databases kept explicit closes without a close mark, so a migration from <= 0.32 now writes the marks (also checked by hand on a MySQL database written by 0.32.0). keel replay --check compares a rebuild with the db without writing. store.backup/restore behind keel export and the new keel import move or restore a tenant as it was (0.33.0, 2026-10-22)
  • [ ] Real use: two pilots outside our own products (the 0.1 goal) on real traffic for at least four weeks, with no lost or wrong data
  • [x] Multi-tenant security: a review of tenant isolation and the agent registry over HTTP, MCP and hosted, with adversarial tests like the SPEC battery's
  • [x] Four adversarial suites (tests/test_security_{http,mcp,hosted,tools}.py, 152 tests) found 25 weaknesses, all fixed test-first (0.33.0, 2026-10-22). High: any API key wrote the account's global memory over /mcp (now refused below every transport, Tools(writes_global=)). Medium: a private or task note settled tenant proposals; by= took over another author's proposal or multi value; a negative limit or per_kind passed the ceiling; unbounded lists; single-use invitations; login throttling; unauthenticated cartridge checks. Low: hints and MCP instructions naming hidden kinds, agent ids shaped like a person, a garbled Authorization header (500), /health echoing the CDC error, trace swaps on a bound server, value size, slugs that are not DNS labels or are reserved, Origin checks, sessions surviving a password reset, login timing, credentials in provisioning errors, the SDK proxy path. Accepted by design and pinned: rules see the whole tenant, consolidation may promote task memory, task ids are capabilities
