docs.title: SDKs generated from the cartridge
docs.text:
The cartridge is the interface definition. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> writes one typed file for your product's repo, the way protoc does; a small published runtime per language holds the HTTP client and the envelope. Decisions and milestones: the design note.

Language Generator Runtime Status TypeScript keel sdk typescript @keel-context/sdk (npm) shipped; tested end to end from Bun against keel serve --transport http Python keel sdk python keel.client inside keel-context (stdlib only) shipped; tested end to end in pytest Go keel sdk go --package <pkg> github.com/angelkurten/keel/sdk/go shipped; tested end to end with go test PHP keel sdk php --package '<Namespace>' keel-context/sdk (Composer, on Packagist) shipped; tested end to end on PHP 8.3

Every generator reads the same keel schema document and writes the same things: a type per event payload, an emit constructor per cataloged event, subject helpers, the rules and constants, and a client factory. --check on any of them exits 1 when the cartridge moved on, for CI.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
keel sdk python examples/fleet -o app/keel_fleet.py

from app import keel_fleet as kf

keel = kf.client("http://keel.internal:8000", "acme-logistics", secret=os.environ["KEEL_SECRET"])
keel.events([kf.emit.tire_depth_measured("acme-logistics", kf.subjects.tire("T-9001"), datetime.now(timezone.utc), "tires", {"unit_id": "MXK-4821", "position": "P3", "depth_mm": 2.6})])
keel.context(kf.subjects.tire("T-9001"))["evaluation"]["tire_critical"]   # True

Payloads are TypedDicts, so your editor checks the keys; a refusal raises keel.client.KeelError with status and detail. A Python product that already imports keel can skip HTTP and call Tools directly; the generated module is for the ones that want the server boundary.

docs.title: Go
docs.text:
go get github.com/angelkurten/keel/sdk/go
keel sdk go examples/fleet -o internal/keelfleet/keel_fleet.go --package keelfleet

Payloads are structs with JSON tags, enums are typed string constants, nullable fields are pointers, and Emit<Event>(tenant, subject, occurredAt, source, payload) returns a keel.Envelope. Errors are *keel.Error with Status and Detail. The output is gofmt and go vet clean.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
composer require keel-context/sdk
keel sdk php examples/fleet -o src/Keel/Fleet.php --package 'App\Keel\Fleet'

Payloads are readonly value objects with toArray(), enums become PHP 8.1 enums, Emit::<event>(...) returns the envelope as an array and Keel::client(...) the client. Errors are Keel\Sdk\KeelError.

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text:
uv run keel sdk typescript examples/fleet -o src/keel-fleet.ts     # in your product's repo
npm install @keel-context/sdk                                         # or bun add

The generated file has a type per event payload, an emit constructor per cataloged event (typed by subject kind and payload), subjects.<kind>(id) helpers, the rules, relations, agents and scopes as constants, and client(options) bound to one tenant and agent.

import { client, emit, subjects } from "./keel-fleet";

const keel = client({ baseUrl: "http://keel.internal:8000", tenant: "acme-logistics", secret: process.env.KEEL_SECRET, agent: "tires-bot" });

await keel.events([
  emit.tireDepthMeasured({ tenant: "acme-logistics", subject: subjects.tire("T-9001"), occurredAt: new Date(), source: "tires.measurements", payload: { unit_id: "MXK-4821", position: "P3", depth_mm: 2.6 } }),
]);

const ctx = await keel.context(subjects.tire("T-9001"));
ctx.evaluation.tire_critical;                                          // true
const depths = await keel.history(subjects.tire("T-9001"), { predicate: "depth_mm" });
await keel.annotate({ subject: subjects.tire("T-9001"), predicate: "assessment", value: "replace", scope: "task" });

A refusal from the server (scope policy, agent registry) is a KeelError with the status and the reason. Keep the generated file fresh with keel sdk typescript <cartridge> -o <file> --check in CI: it exits 1 when the cartridge moved on.

docs.title: The context for a task, in every runtime
docs.text:
The parameters of 0.19 (§7.1, §7.3, §7.5 of the spec) are in all four runtimes. The same calls in each:

Python TypeScript Go PHP Facts on each result search(text, detail="concise") search(text, { detail: "concise" }) SearchWith(ctx, SearchOptions{Text: t, Detail: "concise"}) search($t, ['detail' => 'concise']) Best of each kind, in scope search(t, mode="semantic", related_to=s, per_kind=3, depth=1) search(t, { mode: "semantic", relatedTo: s, perKind: 3, depth: 1 }) SearchOptions{..., RelatedTo: s, PerKind: 3, Depth: 1} ['related_to' => $s, 'per_kind' => 3, 'depth' => 1] Many subjects, one call context([a, b]) contexts([a, b]), contextsConcise Contexts(ctx, []string{a, b}, o) context([$a, $b]) Many texts, one call search([t1, t2]) searches([t1, t2]) Searches(ctx, []string{t1, t2}, o) search([$t1, $t2]) Several kinds at once search(t, kind=[k1, k2]) search(t, { kind: [k1, k2] }) SearchOptions{Text: t, Kinds: []string{k1, k2}} ['kind' => [$k1, $k2]] By a fact's value (0.20) search(kind=k, where={"title": t}) search("", { kind: k, where: { title: t } }) SearchOptions{Kind: k, Where: map[string]any{"title": t}} ['kind' => $k, 'where' => ['title' => $t]] Two hops through some relations related(s, ["r1", "r2"], depth=2) related(s, ["r1", "r2"], undefined, 2) RelatedWith(ctx, s, RelatedOptions{Relations: ..., Depth: 2}) related($s, ['r1', 'r2'], null, 2) Just some predicates (0.22) context([a, b], only=[...]) contexts([a, b], undefined, 0, { only: [...] }) ContextOptions{Only: ...} context([$a, $b], only: [...]) Hide predicates, past instant exclude=[...], as_of= exclude, asOf Exclude, AsOf 'exclude', 'as_of' Read-only SQL (server with --query) query(sql, limit=None) (keel.client.Client) query(sql, limit?) not yet not yet

docs.title: Runtime options
docs.text:
Every runtime takes the same connection options besides the base URL, tenant, secret and agent: a traceparent sent as the W3C header on every call (Keel stores it with every write) and a request timeout.

Runtime Traceparent Timeout Python keel.client.Client traceparent= timeout= seconds (30) TypeScript client({...}) traceparent none built in; pass your own fetch (one that sets an AbortSignal, or any wrapper) Go keel.Options Traceparent HTTPClient (default &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}), plus the context.Context of each call PHP Keel\Sdk\Client traceparent: timeout: seconds (30)

The generated Python client() and PHP Keel::client() take timeout and traceparent too (m.client(url, tenant, secret=..., timeout=10, traceparent=tp), Keel::client($url, $tenant, $secret, $agent, 10, $tp)). The runtime client works the same, and the generated emit and subjects work with it unchanged:

from keel.client import Client

keel = Client("http://keel.internal:8000", "acme-logistics", secret=os.environ["KEEL_SECRET"], agent="tires-bot", timeout=10, traceparent=traceparent)

$keel = new \Keel\Sdk\Client('http://keel.internal:8000', 'acme-logistics', getenv('KEEL_SECRET'), 'tires-bot', timeout: 10, traceparent: $traceparent);

The Python client keeps one keep-alive connection per thread and reuses it, so only the first call pays the TCP and TLS handshake; close() drops it. It identifies itself as User-Agent: keel-context/<version>, since some proxies (Cloudflare's browser integrity check, error 1010) block urllib's default. headers={...} adds headers to every request or overrides the defaults, User-Agent included; the generated client() takes it too.

For HTTP/2, a proxy, retries or mTLS, pass your own client: anything with httpx's post(url, content=, headers=) carries the requests, with its own timeout and pool. Keel stays stdlib-only; the dependency is yours.

import httpx  # pip install "httpx[http2]"

keel = Client("https://keel.example.com", "acme-logistics", secret=os.environ["KEEL_SECRET"], http_client=httpx.Client(http2=True, timeout=10))

keel serve --transport http --http2 speaks HTTP/2 end to end (h2 over TLS, or h2c; see connect); it pays off mostly for many concurrent calls from one process.

Reads follow the memory scopes: agent-scope memory comes back only to the agent that wrote it, so set agent to read your own, and task memory tied to a task id only to calls that pass that task (details).

docs.title: Server side
docs.text:
The SDK talks to keel serve --transport http (see connect): one process for many tenants, X-Keel-Tenant and X-Keel-Agent per request behind a shared secret. The server derives event ids (a content hash) when the product sends none, so retries are safe to reason about.

The HTTP API's defaults are for an agent calling it directly: context answers detail="brief", history "concise" and annotate "ack", and history, related and search cap their lists, leading a cut list with {"more": ...} (and a search ranked by the query's words with {"note": ...}). The clients ask for the shapes their types declare instead: detail "full"; the TypeScript, Go and PHP runtimes also ask for every entry unless you set a limit and drop a leading {"more"} or {"note"}, while keel.client.Client keeps the server's caps (history and related default to limit=50) and returns the lists as they come, marker included. A subject nothing is known about comes back as {subject, found: false, as_of, watermark}; an unknown kind, relation, rule or scope, a key without <kind>: and a malformed time are a 400 whose detail names the valid values.

docs.title: Serve the tools
docs.text:
Agents reach the five tools (and, when enabled, the optional sixth, query) through one of these surfaces. All of them enforce the same scopes, memory policy and agent registry, because the enforcement lives in the tools, not in the transport.

Surface For Start it with Python, in process An agent that is already Python; no network. Tools(cartridge, store, tenant="acme", agent="tires-bot") MCP Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, any MCP client. keel serve <cartridge> --tenant acme (stdio), or /mcp on the HTTP server HTTP JSON API A backend in any language; many tenants from one process. keel serve <cartridge> --transport http --db ... Typed SDKs TypeScript, Python, Go and PHP backends, over the HTTP API. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> -o <file> Console People: browse the graph, try the tools, watch events. keel serve --transport http --ui, at /ui Semantic search Finding subjects by meaning; optional, on any of the above. keel index, then keel serve --index ... --embedder ...

Running the server in production (configuration, the container, jobs) is in Operate. Where this fits in the whole: Architecture.

docs.title: Serve the tools over MCP
docs.text:
uv sync --extra mcp
uv run keel serve examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --events examples/fleet/events.jsonl

With Claude Code, one command registers the server. The agent sees exactly five tools and nothing else:

claude mcp add keel -- uv run --directory $PWD keel serve examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --events examples/fleet/events.jsonl

With Codex CLI (OpenAI), declare the server in ~/.codex/config.toml. Keel annotates context, history, search and related as read-only, so Codex runs them without asking even under approval_policy = "never"; annotate writes, so it prompts unless you set default_tools_approval_mode = "auto" on the server:

[mcp_servers.keel]
command = "uv"
args = ["run", "--directory", "/path/to/keel", "keel", "serve", "examples/fleet", "--tenant", "acme-logistics", "--events", "examples/fleet/events.jsonl"]
startup_timeout_sec = 60

A headless run, for a smoke test or CI:

codex exec --json "Which tires on unit:MXK-4821 are critical according to the cartridge's own rules? Use only the keel tools." < /dev/null

Checked on 2026-10-14 with Codex CLI 0.162 and openai/gpt-5.2-codex behind an OpenAI-compatible gateway: seven calls (search, related, context, history with predicate=depth_mm), the right tire, the right depth on 2026-09-20, and the threshold quoted from the cartridge rather than assumed. Any other MCP client works the same way: a stdio server, five tools, one tenant per server instance. If the cartridge declares agents:, add --agent <id>: the server then reads and writes only what that agent may, and signs its annotations. Agent-scope memory is read only by the agent that wrote it, so a server started without --agent reads none.

What the model reads is kept small. Each result is one text block of compact JSON, with the same data in structuredContent for programmatic clients. context defaults to detail="brief", history to "concise" and annotate to "ack" (ask for "full" when you need the transaction-time bookkeeping), search returns fact hits without that bookkeeping, and long lists are capped with a leading {"more": ...} that says how to read the rest. A server bound to one tenant (stdio, or /mcp with --tenant) states in its instructions, once per session, the cartridge's kinds (naming the subjects of a kind that has at most three, as the server starts), relations and rule definitions, so answers carry rule verdicts without repeating their definitions. detail="text" on context and history (experimental) renders lines instead of JSON for models that read prose better. A demo or a test pinned to a day runs with --clock 2026-10-15T12:00:00Z (or KEEL_CLOCK): reads without as_of and what agents write land on that day, so a note written during the demo is read back on the same day; ingest and retention keep real time. A deployment that serves agents may cap one listing with --max-list 200 (or KEEL_MAX_LIST): a request for everything returns 200 (a search in detail="full", an audit about 8x a brief entry, a tenth of it) and says how to page, and search(detail="count") answers "how many" without listing; unset, nothing is capped. What the model reads is written compact by default, in fewer tokens with nothing left out: lists of records as tables whose shared fields are said once, and UTC times as 2026-10-03T08:00Z (SPEC §7.7); structuredContent and /v1 keep the JSON. --plain (or KEEL_COMPACT=0) sends the JSON text instead, for a client that parses it. An agent that never writes can be served the four read tools only with --read-only (or KEEL_READ_ONLY=1): annotate's definition is not sent with every request, and a call to it (over /v1 too) is refused with the reason. An agent declared with writes: [] in the cartridge's registry is served that way without the flag; the default lists all five. --query adds the optional sixth, read-only SQL (below).

From LangGraph (LangChain's create_agent), through langchain-mcp-adapters: examples/fleet/agent_langgraph.py starts the same stdio server, hands the five tools to the agent and asks about unit MXK-4821. Its dependencies are declared inline, so uv run installs them and nothing is added to Keel:

OPENAI_API_KEY=... uv run examples/fleet/agent_langgraph.py
# any OpenAI-compatible model: OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://your-gateway/v1 KEEL_DEMO_MODEL=some/model

Checked on 2026-10-18 with openai/gpt-4.1-mini behind an OpenAI-compatible gateway: context with depth=1 on the unit, history of the tire's depth, then annotate with the depth fact's evidence; critical since 2026-10-03, 5.2 mm on 2026-09-20, the 3 mm threshold quoted from the rule. Without the system prompt's hint (keys are <kind>:<id>, find them with search) that small model guessed a key and found nothing.

Where is the graph stored?

In memory with --events: the server ingests the stream at start and serves it, which is enough for a demo. For a deployment, pass --db keel.db instead: a SQLite file (stdlib, WAL mode) that an ingest process fills while keel serve reads it. Or point --db at a MySQL or MariaDB you already run: --db mysql://user:password@host:3306/keel (mariadb:// is accepted too; uv sync --extra mysql); the tables are created on first use (with utf8mb4_bin, so keys compare exactly) and the same conformance suite runs against it in CI. Tables created before 0.24.2 took the server's collation, under which page:RENDIMIENTO and page:Rendimiento (or Numero and Número) were one entity; the first start of 0.24.2 or later converts them, which rewrites each table once, and warns with the subjects that had already collided (MysqlStore.collided() lists them): publish those entities again. Sharing the database with your application: ?prefix=keel_ names the tables keel_entities, keel_facts, and so on. In code, the same option is a constructor argument: SqliteStore("keel.db", prefix="keel_"), MysqlStore.from_url(url, prefix="keel_") or MysqlStore(connect, prefix="keel_").

uv run keel ingest examples/fleet examples/fleet/events.jsonl --db keel.db   # or adapter.follow() in your own process
uv run keel serve examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --db keel.db
uv run keel replay examples/fleet examples/fleet/events.jsonl acme-logistics --db keel.db   # wipe one tenant, rebuild it from the log

The log is the truth and the file is derived: replay rebuilds one tenant from the external log (your outbox table, your bus, a .jsonl) and never from the file itself. What agents and people wrote through annotate, and consolidations of it, is not in the log, so replay keeps it and the events land around it. The store is pluggable: SqliteStore is the default, and any store that passes tests/test_store.py (see contributing) can take its place.

docs.title: Serve the tools over HTTP
docs.text:
For a backend, or for many tenants from one process, serve the same five operations as a JSON API (uv sync --extra http):

KEEL_SECRET=change-me uv run keel serve examples/fleet --transport http --db keel.db --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

The secret is read from KEEL_SECRET; --secret-env OTHER_VAR reads it from another variable. If the variable is unset and the store holds no API key (below), the server starts open only on a loopback host (127.0.0.1, the default, ::1 or localhost), with a warning. On any other --host it refuses to start unless you pass --allow-open, for when your own proxy authenticates every request.

The console. --ui also serves the console at /ui, the same one hosted Keel runs, in its self-hosted mode: the graph (search, a subject's context as of any instant with its rules, a predicate's history, neighbours as a force graph), the five tools by hand with the same call as curl and Python, an agent's prompt exported to Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK, per-client MCP snippets, the webhook with a live log of recent events, an events.jsonl upload checked against the catalog, and the SDK generated from your cartridge. It holds no data: it asks for the secret (or a key) and the tenant once, keeps them for the browser tab, and reads through the same /v1 API, so every scope and registry rule applies. Off by default.

TLS and HTTP/2. --certfile and --keyfile (PEM; or KEEL_CERTFILE, KEEL_KEYFILE) serve https. --http2 runs the server on Hypercorn instead of uvicorn (uv sync --extra http2) and speaks HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 on the same port: h2 negotiated by ALPN over TLS, or cleartext h2c (prior knowledge or Upgrade) without it, which is what a proxy in front that talks h2c to its origin uses. HTTP/1.1 clients keep working. On the client side, keel.client.Client(..., http_client=httpx.Client(http2=True)) (SDKs).

KEEL_SECRET=change-me uv run keel serve examples/fleet --transport http --http2 --db keel.db \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --certfile cert.pem --keyfile key.pem
Call Body (? optional, default in parentheses) Returns POST /v1/events one envelope or a list the ingest report: processed, duplicates, unhandled, errors, forgotten, skipped GET /v1/events/recent the tenant's last 200 events received by this server, newest first, each with status (applied, duplicate, unhandled, skipped, error) and the reason; kept in memory, so a restart empties it POST /v1/events/check a list of envelopes what the catalog would refuse in each (index, problems), the same checks as keel validate --events; nothing is ingested GET /v1/sdk/{language} the typed client for this cartridge, as keel sdk generates it: filename, code, sha256 POST /v1/context {"subject", "as_of"?, "depth"? (0), "as_known_at"?, "task"?, "detail"? ("brief"; "concise" or "full"), "exclude"?, "only"?} what context returns; {subject, found: false, as_of, watermark} for a subject nothing is known about POST /v1/history {"subject"?, "since"?, "until"?, "predicate"?, "scope"?, "as_known_at"?, "task"?, "changed_since"?, "limit"? (50; 0 for all), "detail"? ("concise" or "full")} facts, the most recent limit; when cut, led by {"more": ...} POST /v1/search {"text"? (""), "kind"?, "rule"?, "limit"?, "after"?, "mode"? ("text" or "semantic"), "min_score"?, "related_to"?, "via"?, "detail"? ("entity"), "depth"?, "per_kind"?, "exclude"?, "as_of"?, "where"?} entities and facts; without limit, the first 20 matches or 50 of a listing, led by {"more": ...} when cut, or by {"note": ...} when ranked by the query's words POST /v1/annotate {"subject", "predicate", "value", "scope"? ("task"), "evidence"?, "by"?, "task"?, "key"?, "status"?, "detail"? ("ack" or "full")} a receipt (subject, predicate, scope, valid_from, and valid_to, expires_at, task, status when set), or the fact with "full" POST /v1/related {"subject", "relation"?, "as_of"?, "depth"? (1), "limit"? (50; 0 for all)} neighbours; when cut, led by {"more": ...} POST /v1/query {"sql", "limit"? (200; 0: the ceiling)} rows keyed by column; only with --query (else 404); see query GET /health {"ok", "cartridge", "mcp"} GET /openapi.json the contract, for generated clients

The defaults are for an agent calling directly: context answers brief, history concise (lean facts) and annotate a short receipt; pass "detail": "full" for the whole shape, as the SDKs and keel.client do. Lists are capped, and a cut list's first element says what was left out and how to read the rest (SPEC §7). Times are ISO 8601 strings. Every request carries Authorization: Bearer $KEEL_SECRET, X-Keel-Tenant (optional when the server is bound with --tenant or KEEL_TENANT, which is then the default) and, when the cartridge declares agents, X-Keel-Agent. Your product authenticates its users and sets the two headers; Keel takes them as given and builds the tools for that tenant and agent per request. /health, /openapi.json, /docs and /redoc need no token. Two optional headers are stored with every write the request makes: traceparent (W3C trace context) and X-Keel-Tool-Call (the agent's tool call id).

On /v1/events, X-Keel-Tenant is optional: each envelope names its tenant, and when the header is present every envelope must match it. The agent registry does not apply to ingest.

Status Meaning 400 bad input: missing X-Keel-Tenant, an envelope of another tenant, a subject without <kind>:, an unknown kind, relation, rule or scope (the reason names the valid ones), a time that is not ISO 8601, an invalid mode or detail 401 bad or missing bearer token 403 a refusal (scope policy, agent registry), with its reason 422 a malformed body, such as an envelope that fails validation 503 the embeddings provider is rate limiting or down, still after Keel's retries (semantic search); retry after Retry-After seconds

The same server also exposes /mcp (MCP over streamable HTTP), for agents that speak MCP and cannot run a local process. Each call takes its tenant from X-Keel-Tenant (and its agent from X-Keel-Agent), as /v1 does, so one server answers MCP for every tenant; a key narrowed to a tenant needs no header. With --tenant, /mcp is bound to that tenant instead.

curl -s localhost:8000/v1/context -H "Authorization: Bearer change-me" -H "X-Keel-Tenant: acme-logistics" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"subject": "tire:T-9001"}'

Reads follow the memory scopes. Agent-scope memory is read only by the agent that wrote it (send X-Keel-Agent to read your own). Task-scope memory tied to a task id is read only by calls that pass that task (history's task is an exact filter); task-scope memory with no task id belongs to the tenant. Global-scope memory lives in a reserved partition, __global__, that every tenant reads and no event may write; neither a tool call nor an envelope may use that tenant name. A tenant of an account (acme/t, see below) reads acme/__global__ instead.

docs.title: Several products on one deployment: accounts and API keys
docs.text:
One server can serve several products, each confined to its own data. An account is one product (a short slug: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, at most 32 characters); its tenants are its end-customers. An API key belongs to one account, and the server puts the account in front of the tenant: X-Keel-Tenant: cliente-42 with a key of acme reads and writes the tenant acme/cliente-42, and envelopes posted to /v1/events are prefixed the same way. A tenant sent with a / is refused, so a key cannot reach another account.

uv run keel keys create acme --db keel.db                         # any tenant of acme
uv run keel keys create acme --db keel.db --tenant cliente-42     # only that tenant (the header may be left out)
uv run keel keys create acme --db keel.db --agent tires-bot       # calls are made as that agent
uv run keel keys create acme --db keel.db --global                # the only key that may annotate(scope="global")
uv run keel keys list acme --db keel.db                           # JSON lines; never prints a key again
uv run keel keys revoke kk_3f9a1c2b7d4e --db keel.db              # refused by running servers within seconds

create prints the key once; only its SHA-256 is stored, in the api_keys table of the same database. Send it as Authorization: Bearer kk_.... The first key closes a server that had no secret. KEEL_SECRET keeps working as the operator's credential and reaches every tenant by its full name (acme/cliente-42). Each account has its own global memory, acme/__global__: its tenants read it, other accounts never do, and only its --global key writes it. /mcp follows the same rules per call; bound to one tenant with --tenant acme/cliente-42, it accepts only keys of that account that reach that tenant (and that agent, with --agent). The design: docs/design/hosted.md.

An account can also have limits, its own database and a retention policy:

uv run keel accounts set acme --db keel.db --rps 20 --events-month 1000000   # 0 removes a limit
uv run keel accounts set big --db keel.db --store mysql://user:pass@host:3306/big   # "" goes back to the shared database
uv run keel accounts set acme --db keel.db --retention 3y                    # 3y, 18m or 90d
uv run keel accounts list --db keel.db
uv run keel forget --policy --db keel.db --yes                               # schedule it: each account's retention, on its tenants

Over its requests per second (a token bucket in each server process) or its events for the month (from the metering counters), a key gets 429 with Retry-After. An account with no row is not limited. With --store, the server keeps that account's graph in its own database, opened on first use, while keys, accounts and usage stay in the shared one, so keel usage still sees it; jobs for that account (keel index, keel expire) run with --db pointing at its database. --policy applies each account's retention like keel forget --before, in its own database when it has one.

When accounts bring their own cartridges, run one server per account: a cartridge carries Python, and it should never run next to another customer's data. keel serve <its cartridge> --transport http --db <shared> --account acme accepts only acme's keys (others get 403) and keeps its graph in the account's database (keel accounts set acme --store ...), while keys, limits and usage stay in the shared one. Hosted Keel runs this way, one container per account (docs/design/hosted.md).

What each tenant used, per month, one JSON line per account, tenant and month:

uv run keel usage --db keel.db --month 2027-01 --account acme
{"account": "acme", "tenant": "acme/cliente-42", "month": "2027-01", "events": 18342, "calls": {"context": 911, "search": 2380}}

events counts events applied for the first time, whatever path brought them (/v1/events, keel ingest, keel consume); duplicates, events for a forgotten tenant and keel replay are not counted, so a retry or a rebuild is never counted twice. calls counts tool calls through keel serve --transport http (/v1 and /mcp), kept in memory and written every ten seconds and at shutdown. Both live as daily counters in the metering table; a tenant with no account prefix is reported with "account": null.

docs.title: Query: read-only SQL
docs.text:
The optional sixth tool. keel serve --query (or KEEL_QUERY=1; build_server(query=True), build_http_app(query=True) in code) adds query(sql, limit=None) over MCP and POST /v1/query over HTTP. The agent writes one SELECT (or WITH ... SELECT) over the schema keel/sqlgen.py generates from the cartridge: <kind>_state_at(tenant, t), <kind>_state_known_at(tenant, t, k := k) and <kind>_changes(tenant, since, until) for each kind that declares facts:, state_at, keel_facts, relations_at, <rule>_at and <rule>_verdicts, and the tables facts, entities, relations. Over MCP the tool's description is fixed text, so prompt caches hold, and the schema, generated for the tenant and the store's dialect (sqlgen.describe, about 450 to 700 tokens for the example cartridges), rides in the server's instructions; Tools.spec() appends it to the description. Rows come back as objects keyed by column, instants as ISO 8601 in UTC, at most 200 by default (limit; 0 or more than --max-list gives that ceiling, else 1000), a cut list led by {"more": ...}. A query runs at most --query-timeout seconds (5 by default, KEEL_QUERY_TIMEOUT). A --read-only server may still offer it: it is a read.

keel serve examples/fleet --db keel.db --tenant acme-logistics --query

Isolation is the store's, not a check of the agent's SQL. Whatever the agent writes (another tenant's id in a macro, a base table, api_keys, a catalog, read_csv('/etc/passwd'), ATTACH, COPY, PRAGMA, SET, two statements, a writing CTE), it reads one tenant's rows and changes nothing; tests/test_query_security.py runs about a hundred such attacks on every store, through Tools and straight to the store.

Store How a query is bound to the tenant SqliteStore An in-memory SQLite database per tenant holding only what the tenant may read, with the cartridge's macros inlined (under a 200,000-character budget, so nested macro calls cannot grow it exponentially); an authorizer allows reading those three tables and calling functions (no extension or file functions), nothing else (no PRAGMA, ATTACH, write or schema change); no string or blob over 1 MB (Python 3.11+); a progress handler stops it at the timeout. DuckdbStore A separate DuckDB file per tenant, in a folder of its own, holding only what the tenant may read and the cartridge's macros, opened read-only with external access (files, network), extension install and load, Python replacement scans, spilling to disk (no temp directory) and further configuration locked, 256 MB of memory; functions whose output DuckDB's memory limit does not bound (repeat, lpad, rpad, printf, format, list_resize, array_resize, range, generate_series, repeat_row) are refused; every row is measured in the database; interrupted at the timeout. PostgresStore (from a URL) A login role per tenant (created on first use, in one transaction; the store's user needs CREATEROLE and to own its schema, nothing more), so sessions of different tenants can neither read each other's statements in pg_stat_activity nor cancel or terminate each other. Through a group role it may only SELECT three security-barrier views in the store's schema over facts, entities and relations, each showing the rows of the tenant bound to current_user (which a session logged in as that role cannot change: no SET ROLE or set_config moves it); the query connection makes temporary views facts, entities, relations over them, so the generated functions read through them. Its password is an HMAC of a random secret stored in a table only the store's user reads, never derived from the DSN. Every query is one server-side cursor (a SELECT only), each row measured on the server, in a transaction rolled back after it, under one deadline for the whole query (a timer cancels it; statement_timeout, and transaction_timeout on PG 17+); session advisory locks are released after it. Role names carry the whole SHA-256 of deployment and tenant, and a role is bound once, never rebound. forget drops the tenant's role and binding. A superuser store also caps each role's temp files (temp_file_limit, 1 GB). MemoryStore, MysqlStore Not served: the tool is not listed and Tools.query says so.

What it reads. The tenant's accepted (no status) tenant-scope facts, unexpired, the global partition's global facts (as every tenant's tools read them), its entities and relations. Never agent or task memory, never proposals: a store cannot apply each caller's per-agent and per-task visibility to arbitrary SQL, so they are left out. With an agent registry, an agent may call query only if its entry says query: true, since SQL reads past reads.kinds and reads.relations; otherwise the tool is not listed to it and a call is refused.

Sandboxes (SQLite, DuckDB) are copied again only when the tenant's rows changed (a change counter skips even the check while nothing was written), never under the store's main lock; the copy counts against the query's timeout; a tenant over 100,000 rows is refused there, from counts alone (serve it from Postgres); forget, forget_before, expire and reset drop the tenant's sandbox, so no copy of forgotten data stays in memory or on disk; on SQLite a forget by another process drops this one's copy at its next query. An answer carries at most 8 MB of values (it stops early, led by {"more": ...}); a row over 1 MB is refused.

Accepted risks. On Postgres 15 and earlier, CREATEROLE is close to superuser (it may alter any non-superuser role and grant itself their rights); give the store's user CREATEROLE there only on a database server dedicated to the deployment, or use 16+, where a role's creator administers only what it created. A CREATEROLE-only store user cannot set temp_file_limit (a superuser's setting), so a query's temp-file spills on such a deployment are bounded only by its timeout. Two agents of the same tenant querying at once on Postgres share the tenant's role: each can see the other's running statement and cancel it (one tenant's data either way). Every query role can read Postgres's catalog statistics (pg_stat_user_tables row counts, the number of keel_q_* roles), not their contents. An agent may take the advisory locks Keel's install waits on, for at most its query's timeout. On Postgres a huge value (repeat('x', 500000000)) is built in the server's memory before the timeout or the row check stops it; the row check runs on the server over the agent's statement, which must parse alone as one SELECT (so it cannot close the check early), and a row over 1 MB is refused there, not sent to Keel. A DuckDB sandbox's own path is visible to its query (duckdb_databases()), with no file access to use it; error texts name <sandbox> instead. Without an API key bound to an agent, the X-Keel-Agent header is the host's claim, as for every tool (Keel takes it as given): with query on, a host that lets an end user set that header to an agent with query: true lets them read past that agent's reads; bind keys to agents (keel keys create --agent) where that matters.

docs.title: Semantic search
docs.text:
search(text, mode="semantic") finds subjects by meaning ("worn-out tyre" finds a tire at 2.6 mm), filtered by tenant, the agent's read slice, kind and rule. Two adapters, both replaceable: where vectors live and where embeddings come from.

uv sync --extra chroma        # only for the bundled Chroma adapter; Python 3.11+ (chromadb needs onnxruntime)
export KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1 KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_MODEL=text-embedding-3-small KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY=...
uv run keel index examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --db keel.db --index chroma:///var/keel/vectors   # cron it: incremental
uv run keel serve examples/fleet --transport http --db keel.db --index chroma:///var/keel/vectors

keel index keeps the time of its last run in a cursor file and indexes only what changed since; --full rebuilds the tenant's index. The cursor sits next to a chroma:///path index (keel-index-<tenant>.cursor), else in .keel/index-<tenant>.cursor under the working directory; --cursor or KEEL_INDEX_CURSOR puts it elsewhere. In a container, keep it on the same volume as the index: a cursor lost on deploy makes the next run a full rebuild, and keel index says so when it starts without one. Embedding batches go out four at a time (--workers, KEEL_INDEX_WORKERS), and a rate limit or a 5xx from the embeddings API is retried with backoff. --all-tenants indexes every tenant in the store, each with its own cursor (--cursor-dir or KEEL_INDEX_CURSOR_DIR puts them all in one folder), and clears the documents of every tenant forgotten since its last run. One run per tenant at a time: a run that finds another holding the lock next to the cursor skips (two runs at once corrupt a Chroma index), so a cron that overlaps a slow run is safe. --embedder on index and serve picks where embeddings come from: openai (the default, configured by the KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_* variables), hash (deterministic, for tests) or your own pkg.module:factory?k=v. Use the same one for both.

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works for embeddings (OpenAI, OfoxAI, Azure, Ollama, vLLM).

chroma:///path opens the index inside the process. When keel serve and keel index run as separate processes (a server and a cron), the server does not see what the other process writes and searches fail with Error finding id. Either run the indexing inside the server, keel serve ... --index chroma:///path --index-every 600 (every tenant every 10 minutes, cursors in KEEL_INDEX_CURSOR_DIR or next to the index; /health shows index with its last run or error), or run Chroma as a server and point both at it with chroma://host:port.

The Chroma adapter ranks the lexical leg itself: it pulls a kind's documents once, keeps their BM25 in memory and reuses it until the collection's count changes or 300 seconds pass (ChromaIndex(bm25_ttl=...)), so a re-index by another process shows in the lexical leg within that time (the dense leg sees it at once). Each document carries its subject as metadata, so related_to filters inside Chroma; a collection built before 0.21 lacks it and filters after retrieval, slower, until one keel index --full.

Weaviate. uv sync --extra weaviate and --index weaviate://host:8080 (Weaviate 1.25 or later). Query parameters: grpc_port (default 50051), grpc_host (default the same host), secure=true for TLS on both, collection (default Keel); the API key comes from KEEL_WEAVIATE_API_KEY, never the URL. Keel uses one multi-tenant collection and makes each Keel tenant a Weaviate tenant, so the server isolates them. Vectors come from Keel's embedder (the collection has no vectorizer), and the lexical leg is Weaviate's own BM25, so nothing is pulled into Keel's memory and a re-index by another process shows at once. Its tokenizer splits cus-1974 into two words where Keel's keeps one, so lexical scores differ slightly from Chroma's. Run the conformance tests against a server with KEEL_WEAVIATE_URL=weaviate://localhost:8080 uv run pytest tests/test_semantic.py.

docs.title: Your own vector store or embedding model
docs.text:
Another vector database (pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, OpenSearch...) or your own model is an adapter you write: a plain class, nothing to inherit or register. examples/custom_adapters.py is a complete, tested one, a vector index on SQLite and an embedder wrapping any encode function. Run it with uv run python examples/custom_adapters.py.

class MyIndex:                                                     # keel.semantic.VectorIndex
    def upsert(self, tenant, items): ...                           # items: [(subject key, vector, document)]
    def delete(self, tenant, keys): ...
    def query(self, tenant, vector, k, where=None): ...            # [(key, cosine)], best first, this tenant only
    def clear(self, tenant): ...

class MyEmbedder:                                                  # keel.semantic.Embedder
    def embed(self, texts, role="document"): ...                   # one vector per text, same dimension

The rules an index must keep: every call is scoped by tenant and never returns another tenant's keys; query returns (key, score) with the score a cosine in [-1, 1], best first, at most k. Two capabilities are optional and detected from the signature: where={"kind": [...]} on query filters inside the index (without it Keel filters after retrieval, which an approximate index can miss), and a text_query(tenant, text, k, where=None) method adds the lexical leg for hybrid search. An embedder that takes role gets "query" for questions and "document" for what it indexes.

Name them by a spec, module:factory?param=value (parameters arrive as text), on index and serve alike, and check them with the same conformance suite as the bundled adapters:

uv run keel index examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --db keel.db \
  --index "examples.custom_adapters:make_index?path=vectors.db" --embedder examples.custom_adapters:make_embedder
KEEL_VECTOR_INDEX="examples.custom_adapters:make_index?path=/tmp/v.db" KEEL_EMBEDDER=examples.custom_adapters:make_embedder \
  uv run pytest tests/test_semantic.py

Vectors you already compute. Keel embeds the document it renders for each subject (key, attributes, open facts, the relations the cartridge names) and the query text, with the same embedder, so both sides live in one vector space. It does not take precomputed vectors. To use your own model, wrap it as the embedder: a function from texts to vectors is enough (ModelEmbedder in the example). Vectors you computed elsewhere, from other text, would not match the documents Keel searches.

Search is hybrid by default: ids in the query come first, then a dense and a lexical leg are fused (the lexical weight is semantic.lexical_weight, 0.3). Add --reranker llm (any OpenAI-compatible chat model, KEEL_RERANK_BASE_URL / _MODEL / _API_KEY) or --reranker http (the Cohere, Jina or Voyage /rerank API) to reorder the best candidates. For asymmetric embedders set KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_QUERY_PREFIX / _DOCUMENT_PREFIX (e5: "query: ", "passage: "). How much each piece buys, measured: docs/design/semantic-evals.md.

Indexing never runs in ingest, so ingest stays deterministic and offline. Only tenant and global knowledge is indexed: task and agent memory and pending proposals are not. The cartridge decides the rest:

semantic:
  kinds: [card, cliente]
  exclude: [comentario]      # comments full of URLs and technical noise stay out
  relations: [de_cliente]    # "de_cliente: cliente:BAT (nombre: ...)" goes into the card's document

docs.title: Design note: agent registry
docs.text: Status: implemented on 2026-10-14 as proposed, with both open questions decided the same day: read filtering is in v1, and an unknown or missing agent id is refused whenever the cartridge declares agents. The normative text is now SPEC §6.1; this note stays as the reasoning.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A Tools instance is bound to a cartridge and a tenant, and to nothing else. annotate takes a free-text by; any caller may write to any scope as long as it brings evidence; context, related, search and history return everything the tenant has. That is fine for one team's agents on one box. It is not fine when several agents from different owners share a tenant's graph, when one agent must never write tenant-scope memory, when an agent should only see part of the ontology (a billing agent has no business reading inspections), or when the audit trail must say which agent wrote what and be believed.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Identity. Every tool call is made by a known agent id. annotate records it: by defaults to the agent id, source is annotate:<agent>.
  2. Write policy per agent. Which scopes it may write. Default task and agent; tenant only when declared; global never from an agent.
  3. Read policy per agent. Which entity kinds and relations it may see. Everything else is filtered out of the four read tools.
  4. Enforced in Tools, never trusted to the agent (design rule 5). No sixth tool (rule 7).

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Authentication. The host (your SaaS, the process that launches keel serve) decides who is calling; Keel takes the agent id as given. keel serve --agent tires-bot binds one server to one agent, the way --tenant binds it to one tenant.
  • Per-user permissions. Keel's unit is the agent, not the human behind it.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
Declare agents in the cartridge, next to the ontology they use:

agents:
  tires-bot:
    description: Reads tire depth, writes task memory for the inspection audit.
    writes: [task, agent]
    reads: { kinds: [unit, tire, inspection], relations: [mounted_on, has_inspection] }
  fleet-copilot:
    description: Answers the customer's questions across the whole graph. Writes tenant memory with evidence.
    writes: [task, agent, tenant]

Absent reads means everything in the cartridge. Absent agents: means no registry: today's behaviour, any caller, any scope with evidence. Backwards compatible.

Core changes, about eighty lines:

  • Cartridge.agents: dict[str, AgentSpec]; validate() checks that kinds, relations and scopes exist.
  • Tools(cartridge, store, tenant, agent=None). With an agent: annotate raises PermissionError outside writes and defaults by to the agent id; the read tools filter by reads.
  • keel serve --agent <id>; the MCP server name becomes keel:<cartridge>:<tenant>:<agent>.
  • keel export already carries corrected_by and source, so the audit trail gains trustworthy authorship with no change.

MemoryPolicy stays as it is (evidence, TTL): the registry says who may, the policy says how. Order of checks: registry first, then policy.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A separate agents.yaml outside the cartridge keeps a vendor's agents apart from the domain, but then two files must agree on kinds and relations. The cartridge already versions the ontology, so the registry belongs with it. A customer disabling an agent for its own tenant can come later as a tenant-scope fact, not a file.
  • Enforcing in the MCP layer only leaves the plain-function path open. Rule 5 says the layer enforces, so it is Tools.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Read filtering in v1, or writes only? Writes and identity are about thirty lines and cover the audit need. Read filtering touches every tool and search. Recommendation: writes and identity first; reads when a pilot has two agents that must see different slices.
  2. Unknown agent id: refuse with PermissionError, or allow with the default policy? Recommendation: refuse when a registry exists, allow when it does not.

docs.title: Design note: what agentic workflows demand from Keel
docs.text: Status: researched and exercised on 2026-10-14; items 1 to 6 and 11 shipped in 0.9.0 and 7 to 10 in 0.10.0, both on 2026-10-15 (the flow in examples/fleet/workflow_ops.py uses them); 12 stays a documented convention. Two inputs: a survey of the 2025-2026 state of the art (frameworks, memory systems, context engineering, protocols, observability, approvals) and examples/fleet/workflow_ops.py, a deliberately complex flow on Keel (five agents with different registry slices, two in parallel threads, an evaluator-optimizer loop, a human promoting a plan to tenant memory with evidence, an audit) that runs in the test suite on both stores.

docs.title: What the flow showed
docs.text: What happened What it means Triage had to enumerate units with search("unit:") and filter by kind There is no way to list subjects by kind or by rule state; every orchestrator-workers pattern needs a work list Two specialists wrote recommendation on the same unit; history kept both with their author, the open fact is the last writer's Concurrent annotations have no declared policy: last-writer-wins by accident, contradictions are not surfaced The dispatcher approving through the planner's console was refused (planner-bot may not write scope 'tenant') People are principals too; the registry must declare them, and the audit must show who approved context(as_of=30 days ago) answered what was true then, not what the triage saw at the time Transaction time (recorded_at) is stored but not exposed; post-mortems and eval replays need "as known at" A second run the same day would read the first run's task memory Task scope has no task id and no lifecycle beyond TTL Rerunning a step after a failure would annotate twice Durable-execution frameworks replay steps; writes need idempotency keys Parallel threads on one SqliteStore, the human promotion with evidence, the registry refusal, depth=1, the export: all worked as designed The core model holds; the gaps are in enumeration, identity of runs, time axes and write policies

docs.title: What the state of the art says (sources in the research summary at the end)
docs.text:
• Workflows persist state per step and resume from it. LangGraph checkpoints per super-step with time travel; Microsoft Agent Framework checkpoints at the end of each superstep including pending human requests; Temporal, DBOS and Restate journal every LLM and tool call and never re-run a completed step; LangGraph warns that side effects before an interrupt must be idempotent. ADK changes state only by appending events with an invocation_id.
  • Memory systems are bitemporal and scoped, and they never delete. Graphiti keeps four timestamps per fact and invalidates contradicted edges with provenance to the episode; Mem0 scopes by user_id, agent_id, app_id, run_id and marks conflicting relations invalid; Letta documents which shared-memory operations are safe under concurrency (append safe, replace is compare-and-swap, rewrite is last-writer-wins and an anti-pattern).
  • Context is a budget. Anthropic's guidance: return names over ids, offer concise and detailed formats (concise is about a third of the tokens), cap tool results (Claude Code: 25k tokens), avoid list-everything tools but give filtered search; sub-agents return distilled summaries and pass references, not payloads; deterministic serialization keeps prompt caches warm (Manus, MCP 2026-07-28).
  • Protocols moved to explicit handles, subscriptions and tasks. MCP 2026-07-28 removed sessions in favour of server-minted handles passed as tool arguments, added subscriptions/listen for change notifications and ttlMs/cacheScope on results, and carries traceparent in _meta; A2A groups work by contextId/taskId with terminal states; agent identity products (Entra, Okta) give each agent a credential, a human sponsor and per-agent audit logs.
  • Observability joins traces to data. OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions name execute_tool spans with gen_ai.tool.call.id; XTDB's decision-audit pattern pins both valid time and system time to the decision timestamp; the EU AI Act Art. 12 requires automatic event logging over the system's lifetime for high-risk systems.
  • Approval is a durable pause with an id. OpenAI's RunState interruptions, Microsoft request_info ids in checkpoints, A2A INPUT_REQUIRED, MCP multi-round-trip requests; findings are promoted only after verification (Anthropic's long-running harness).

docs.title: Proposals, ranked, all inside the five tools
docs.text:
# Capability Pattern that needs it Size 1 Transaction time: context(as_known_at=) and history(as_known_at=) answer "what did the agent see"; needs the close's own recorded_at on each fact post-mortems, eval replay, Art. 12 S 2 Changes since a cursor: history(since=, subject=None) returns the tenant's facts recorded after a watermark, annotations included; context carries the current watermark incremental runs, background memory formation, blackboard polling, MCP subscriptions S 3 Task ids on task memory: annotate(task=), history(task=), keel expire --task closes a task handoffs, sub-agents on one job, trace grouping (run_id, contextId, invocation_id) M 4 Idempotency key on annotate: same key, same subject and predicate returns the existing fact durable-execution replay, interrupt re-runs S 5 Enumerate: search(kind=, rule=, limit=) lists subjects of a kind, or those where a rule fires now, with a cursor routing, orchestrator-workers, blackboards M 6 People as principals: kind: human in the registry, approvals signed by a declared person human-in-the-loop with audit S 7 Detail levels and budgets: context(detail=concise) returns {predicate: value} and neighbour summaries; limit on history and search; truncation notices name the narrower filter context rot, sub-agent summaries M 8 Conflict policy per predicate: predicates: { recommendation: { multi: true } } keeps one open fact per author instead of last-writer-wins; context lists contradictions across authors concurrent agents on one subject M 9 Proposed vs accepted: an annotation can carry status: proposed; promotion is an annotate with evidence by an authorized principal; context shows proposals apart from accepted facts evaluator-optimizer, approvals M 10 Trace propagation: accept traceparent and tool_call_id on HTTP and MCP calls, store them with each write (and with refusals) so a Langfuse or LangSmith trace joins the audit export observability, "what did the agent see" together with 1 M 11 Freshness in results: the tenant watermark and ingest lag in every context, in a stable position; deterministic key order everywhere agents deciding whether to re-query, prompt caches S 12 Progress notes: a documented convention, predicate: note at task scope with TTL, for agents that must survive a context reset long-running agents docs

Items 1 to 6 and 11 are one release (0.9.0): three new columns on facts (task, idempotency_key, closed_at) with an additive migration in the SQL stores, and extensions to the five tools that keep every existing call valid. Items 7 to 10 are the one after.

docs.title: Design note: ingesting millions of events
docs.text: Status: researched, measured and implemented on 2026-10-14 (design A, SqlStore.bulk, shipped in 0.8.0). The numbers after implementation are at the end.

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text:
Measured in this repo (Keel 0.7.1, fleet cartridge, synthetic streams):

Measure Value Round trip per SQL statement, MySQL 8.4 in Docker on macOS (PyMySQL) 0.64 ms Statements per event after 0.7.1 (remember, upsert, link, read facts, close, insert) about 4 3030 events on MySQL, batch of 500 8.9 s (30.3 s on 0.6.0) 101 000 events on SQLite, batch of 500 4.0 s (25 000 events/s) Handlers against MemoryStore (indexed by subject since daad802) 160 000 events/s Parsing and validating envelopes 157 000 events/s Multi-row INSERT of fact rows into MySQL (executemany, 1000 rows per statement) 60 000 rows/s Batched lookup of 500 (subject, predicate) pairs with a row constructor IN 20 ms

So the library's own work is a few seconds per million events; on MySQL 85 to 90 percent of the wall time is network round trips, one per statement. Extrapolated, one million events today would take about 45 minutes on MySQL and 40 seconds on SQLite. Indexes are not the issue: every query uses one and touches one to ten rows.

docs.title: What the literature says
docs.text:
Ranked by expected gain for this workload (sources in the research below):

  1. Set-based batches: one statement per table per batch instead of four per event removes the round trips. Multi-row INSERT is 10 to 30 times faster than row-by-row on MySQL (Karwin: 1M rows, 527 s row-by-row, 63 s with 100 rows per statement and 100 statements per transaction; FromDual: 881 s to 4.5 s on 100k rows). PyMySQL's executemany only rewrites INSERT ... VALUES into a multi-row statement; UPDATE stays one round trip per row, so closes need a CASE/VALUES ROW form.
  2. Group the batch by key in memory so each (subject, predicate) is read once per batch and later events in the batch resolve against memory. Batched reads use row constructors (WHERE (tenant, subject, predicate) IN (...)), which MySQL turns into range access on the composite index as long as the list stays in the hundreds to low thousands (above range_optimizer_max_mem_size it silently falls back to a scan, warning 3170).
  3. One transaction per batch of 500 to 5000 and inserts in primary-key order (done); each extra secondary index multiplies the cost (DoltHub: 4 indexes, 4.4 times slower).
  4. LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE for replays and imports: a further 1.5 to 3 times over multi-row inserts (100k+ rows/s), at the cost of enabling local_infile on both sides and temp files.
  5. Parallel workers by tenant, 4 to 8, each with its own connection, READ COMMITTED: 2 to 6 times, flattening past four. Partition by tenant, never by subject within a tenant, so no two writers share a unique key (concurrent INSERT IGNORE on the same keys deadlocks or stalls, Bug #106610).
  6. Server knobs (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, unique_checks), the C driver, multi-statement packets: 5 to 30 percent each once batching exists, some with correctness or ops risk. Not the library's business.

Event-sourcing projections do the same: Marten fetches 500 events per batch and, for rebuilds, aggregates a stream in memory and writes once; Kafka Connect's JDBC sink batches 3000 rows; EventStoreDB stores the checkpoint in the same transaction as the rows.

docs.title: Recommended design
docs.text:
A. Buffered flush per batch, both SQL stores. Ingestor.ingest(..., batch=N) already groups events; the store gains a bulk path the Ingestor uses when the batch is larger than one:

  1. Collect the batch's keys: subjects, (subject, predicate) pairs, relation triples, event ids.
  2. Three batched reads (row-constructor IN, chunks of 1000): open facts per pair, entities, open relations; plus one SELECT of already-seen event ids.
  3. Run the handlers against an in-memory overlay seeded with that state, in event order. Placement and closing (place_fact) happen in memory, exactly as today, so arrival order and provenance keep the 0.4.1 guarantees.
  4. Write back: multi-row INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for entities, multi-row INSERT for new relations and new facts, one UPDATE ... CASE seq (or VALUES ROW join on MySQL 8.0.19+) for closed facts and relations, multi-row INSERT into ingested. Commit.

About eight statements per batch of 1000 instead of 4000. Estimated for one million events: handlers and parsing about 12 s, four million rows at 60 000 rows/s about 70 s, round trips negligible; two minutes on MySQL against 45 today, and SQLite under 20 s with executemany. A failed batch rolls back whole, as now. batch=1 keeps the current per-event path for streams.

B. Replay fast path (later, MySQL). A replay starts from an empty subgraph, so no reads at all: build the tenant in memory, spill to TSV, LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE. About one minute per million events; needs local_infile on.

C. Parallel driver (later). keel ingest --workers N sharding tenants across processes. Only when backfills span many tenants.

docs.title: Caveats to carry into the implementation
docs.text:
• Keep IN lists at or under 1000 tuples; check SHOW WARNINGS in tests on MySQL.
  • executemany is per-row for UPDATE on PyMySQL: closes must be one statement with CASE or a VALUES ROW join.
  • Memory per batch is bounded by the batch, not the tenant: the overlay holds only the touched keys.
  • The audit seq order of facts is insertion order within a batch; dump and export are unaffected.
  • innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit is global: document it for operators, never set it from the library.

docs.title: Research sources
docs.text:
• MySQL insert cost model and bulk loading: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/insert-optimization.html, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/optimizing-innodb-bulk-data-loading.html
  • Row constructor range optimization and its memory limit: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/range-optimization.html, https://www.percona.com/blog/why-are-queries-with-many-in-values-more-expensive-after-upgrading-to-mysql-8-x/
  • Table value constructors for set-based updates: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/values.html
  • Measured bulk-load numbers: https://www.slideshare.net/billkarwin/load-data-fast, https://fromdual.com/node/106, https://www.dolthub.com/docs/sql-reference/benchmarks/import, https://planet.mysql.com/entry/?id=2007881
  • PyMySQL executemany rewrite: https://github.com/PyMySQL/PyMySQL/blob/main/pymysql/cursors.py
  • InnoDB locking of duplicate inserts and auto-increment modes: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-locks-set.html, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-auto-increment-handling.html, https://bugs.mysql.com/bug.php?id=106610
  • SQLite: https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html#q19, https://avi.im/blag/2021/fast-sqlite-inserts/, https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_synchronous
  • Projection practice: https://martendb.io/events/projections/rebuilding, https://martendb.io/events/optimizing, https://docs.confluent.io/kafka-connectors/jdbc/current/sink-connector/sink_config_options.html, https://developers.eventstore.com/clients/dotnet/5.0/subscriptions/

docs.title: After implementation (0.8.0)
docs.text:
SqlStore.bulk(events) is the overlay described in design A; Ingestor.ingest(batch=N) uses it for every chunk larger than one event, so the CLI (500), the HTTP batch and replay get it without changes; streams (batch=1) keep the per-event path. Prefetch reads the batch's event ids first, so a redelivered batch costs one lookup per thousand events and loads no state.

Measure (same machine, same streams) 0.7.1 0.8.0 3030 events on MySQL 8.9 s 0.5 s 101 000 events on MySQL about 300 s (extrapolated) 8.4 s 101 000 events on SQLite 4.0 s 2.9 s 101 000 events re-sent to MySQL (all duplicates) 2.1 s

About 12 000 events per second on MySQL through Docker: a million events in under a minute and a half, write-bound (four million rows at 60 000 rows per second), with round trips no longer measurable. Designs B (replay through LOAD DATA) and C (workers per tenant) stay on the shelf until someone needs more.

docs.title: Design note: the Keel console
docs.text: Status: proposed and built on 2026-10-18, shipped in 0.29.0. Replaces the hosted sign-up form and usage page (hosted/app.py) and the read-only browser at /ui (keel/ui.html) with one console. Mockup: https://claude.ai/artifact/KbwgvjBcMGJxiWMAcNyVqF.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The premise: someone who wants to try Keel does as little as possible before it works. Today:

  • Sign-up asks for five things before anything happens: account, email, invitation code, a cartridge choice and two files to upload.
  • The key is shown once with no way back: no login, no rotation, and /panel asks for the key every time.
  • Nothing says when the Keel is up. "It takes a minute or two", then silence.
  • The graph starts empty. Seeing anything means posting events by hand.
  • The MCP snippet does not work. /mcp is served only when the server starts with a tenant, and an account's container starts without one, so the configuration handed out at sign-up gets nothing.
  • Two disconnected UIs. The usage page and /ui do not know about each other, and /ui asks for the secret and the tenant by hand.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
1. Invitation link. Each pilot gets keel.angelkurten.com/?invite=<code>. The code travels in the URL; no field for it.
  2. Email, an account already filled in, a password. The account slug is proposed from the email's domain (angel@acme.com → acme, a suffix on collision) and editable on the same screen, because it is permanent. The password is stored as scrypt. Sign-up opens a session at once (a random token, its hash in the control database, an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie); later visits sign in with email and password.
  3. The account is created on sign-up, born with the fleet example and its events ingested into a tenant demo. A waiting screen shows the steps (database, container, example data, first key) by polling the control plane, which polls the container's /health.
  4. The console opens on the graph of the example, with a checklist: Keel running, example data, connect an agent, send your own events, your cartridge.

What the user typed: an email and a password. No mailbox round trip: the invitation link already vouches for them.

docs.title: The console
docs.text:
One SPA (React + Vite), served by the control plane in hosted and by keel serve --ui self-hosted, where the account tabs are hidden.

Tab What it does Graph Today's /ui: search, subject, related graph, facts, history; the tenant picked in the sidebar. A banner while it shows example data. Playground Two modes. Tools: the five tools as forms against the selected tenant, the JSON result, and the same call as curl and Python. Agent: a name, a model, the cartridge's agent identity, a system prompt started from the cartridge and the five tools; chat with it against the tenant, every tool call shown; then export it as code. Connect One tab per client (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop, LangGraph, curl) with the endpoint, a key narrowed to the tenant and the tenant already in the snippet. It waits for the first tool call and says when it arrives. SDK Pick TypeScript, Python, Go or PHP: the command that installs the runtime, the typed client generated from the deployed cartridge to download, and an example with the cartridge's own kinds and events. Says when the cartridge changed and the download is stale. Events Webhook (endpoint, envelope, snippets, a live log of recent events with their errors); upload an events.jsonl (checked against the catalog, then ingested in batches); Postgres CDC (a URL and tables). Keys List, create (shown once), revoke. Scope: account, tenant, agent, global. Usage Events against the monthly limit, requests per second, tool calls per tenant and tool. Cartridge The current one; replace it by uploading files, by picking an example, or by generating it from a few real events. Replacing it forgets demo.

Look: a sober developer tool (Linear, Vercel, Supabase), dark first, monospace for keys, endpoints, JSON and subject ids.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The console never holds a user's key. It calls the control plane, which proxies /v1/* to the account's container with that container's KEEL_SECRET (generated at sign-up, already in its environment), prefixing the tenant with the account. The secret is kept in the control database; it is a credential of a container we run, not of the customer.
  • MCP for many tenants in one server. Connect needs /mcp per tenant in an account's container. The server builds the MCP Tools per request from a key narrowed to a tenant (and agent), instead of once at start-up from --tenant. A core change in keel/http.py and keel/mcp_server.py; --tenant keeps working as today.
  • Example data. After the container answers /health, the control plane posts examples/fleet/events.jsonl under tenant demo.
  • Live event log. The container keeps the last 200 ingest results per tenant in memory (applied, duplicate, refused with the reason) behind GET /v1/events/recent. Not a sixth tool: an operator endpoint like /v1/events.
  • Upload. Cartridge.check_event per line before anything is posted; the report lists what would be refused.
  • CDC in hosted. The control plane keeps the Postgres URL and tables; the provisioner adds keel cdc as a second process in the account's container.
  • Cartridge generator. The user pastes two or three real events; the control plane asks a model through OfoxAI (the gateway already used) for cartridge.yaml and handlers.py, checks the YAML with check_cartridge, shows both for review, and deploys them to the account's own container on request. Handlers run only there, as uploaded ones do. A limit of generations per account and day. An LLM here is fine: it writes the cartridge once, it is never in the ingest path (rule 10).
  • The agent in the playground is tried in the console and exported, never hosted: Keel stays out of the agent framework business. The control plane runs the loop: the model through OfoxAI (an allowance of messages per account and day) or the user's own Anthropic or OpenAI key, the five tools as function definitions, each call sent through the proxy. The starter prompt is a template filled from the cartridge (kinds, relations, rules, "call context before answering"); no LLM writes it. Agent configurations are kept per account in the control database. Export writes one runnable file per framework, connected to the account's /mcp with the key from an environment variable: Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK.
  • SDKs. load_cartridge imports handlers.py, so the control plane never generates them itself: the account's container, which already runs that code, serves GET /v1/sdk/<language> (the operator secret only) with keel sdk's output, and the console compares its hash with the last download to say it is stale.
  • Replacing the cartridge updates the container's files and redeploys it; the control plane waits for /health to report the new cartridge's revision (a hash of its two files), puts the previous cartridge back if the new one does not start, and forgets tenant demo when the example goes. Problems are found without importing handlers.py: its @registry.on types are read with ast.
  • Self-hosted. The SPA's build ships inside the wheel (keel/console/, about 200 KB) and replaces keel/ui.html. Its calls carry the secret the operator types once, kept in the browser's session.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
All four shipped together in 0.29.0.

Phase Items 1. Entry invitation link, email and password, proposed slug, account born with the example, waiting screen, SPA shell with Graph, Playground (tools and agent, with export) and Connect, the proxy, MCP for many tenants 2. Data Events (webhook and live log, upload), Keys, Usage, SDK 3. Own cartridge replace by upload or example, the generator, CDC in hosted 4. Self-hosted the SPA in the wheel, keel/ui.html removed

docs.title: Decided on 2026-10-18
docs.text:
• One console for hosted and /ui, built as a SPA (React + Vite).
  • Sign-in by email and password (first proposed as a magic link; changed the same day). No reset by email yet: the operator sets a password with python -m hosted password <account>.
  • Sign-up asks for no cartridge: the account starts with the fleet example and its events.
  • The invitation travels in a link.
  • Connect offers both a playground and per-client snippets.
  • Own data through webhook, file upload, Postgres CDC and a generated cartridge.
  • The generator uses OfoxAI.
  • The playground also configures an agent (prompt, model, the five tools), tried in the console and exported to Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK; never hosted.
  • The playground's model runs on OfoxAI with a daily allowance per account, or on the user's own key.
  • SDKs are a console tab: install command, download of the generated client, a typed example, a stale warning.
  • Dark, sober developer-tool look.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• Teams. One email per account for now; inviting teammates comes when a pilot asks.
  • Password reset by email. Needs a mail provider (Resend was the candidate); until then the operator resets.

docs.title: Design note: hosted Keel
docs.text: Status: proposed on 2026-10-18. Decided the same day: accounts, API keys and metering go into the core now, because they also serve anyone self-hosting Keel for several customers. Retention is designed as a dated forget. A shared database is the default, with a database per account as the enterprise plan. Keys live in a table in the store. Account names are short slugs; only a key marked global writes an account's global memory; tool calls are counted, not billed. The hosted launch itself waits for the gate below. Accounts and API keys are implemented as proposed (keel/keys.py, keel keys), metering with one change (counters, not ingested.recorded_at, below) (keel/usage.py, keel usage), and retention with two simplifications (below) (forgets: before, keel forget --before), shipped in 0.27.0. Quotas, a database per account and a retention policy per account (keel/accounts.py, keel accounts, keel forget --policy) shipped in 0.28.0, and so did Postgres CDC (keel cdc), SSO in front of /ui (deploy/sso), keel serve --account and the control plane (hosted/: invite-only sign-up, a database and a Coolify container per account, the usage panel). Running on Coolify since 2026-10-18: the control plane at https://keel.angelkurten.com (sign-up by invitation), a shared MySQL with daily backups, and one container per account under *.keel.angelkurten.com; a demo account was signed up, ingested the fleet events and answered context end to end.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Today one keel serve belongs to one SaaS. Every request carries the same shared secret (_Bearer in keel/http.py). The tenant arrives in X-Keel-Tenant and is never checked against the caller: whoever holds the secret reads every tenant. That is right when the SaaS owns the box. It is wrong once Kubbo runs one deployment for several SaaS products, which is what the 2027 roadmap promises: "Kubbo operates graph, bus and jobs; billed by events ingested per month".

Two more gaps block billing:

  • Usage cannot be counted. ingested holds (tenant, id) with no time, so "events per month" cannot be read from the store. The event log lives at the source, not in Keel.
  • Nothing limits one customer. One noisy SaaS slows down every other one.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Accounts. An account is the SaaS that pays. Its tenants are its end-customers, exactly as today. A credential never reaches another account's data, whatever the request says.
  2. Keys. API keys belong to an account and can be narrowed to one tenant or one agent. They can be created, listed and revoked without a restart.
  3. Metering. Events applied per account, tenant and month, read from the store.
  4. Quotas. A rate limit and a monthly event limit per account, answered with 429 and Retry-After.
  5. Retention. An account can drop domain history older than a date, deterministically and with an audit trail.
  6. The core stays unaware of accounts. Tools, handlers and stores keep seeing one tenant string. Rules 6, 7 and 8 hold unchanged.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• SSO for the API. Agents authenticate with keys. SSO concerns the people who open /ui, and a proxy in front of it covers that (oauth2-proxy, Cloudflare Access) without code in Keel.
  • Billing. Keel exposes usage; invoices, plans and payment live outside it.
  • Cross-account reads, including a shared global partition across accounts.
  • Per-user permissions. The unit is still the agent (see the agent registry).

docs.title: Accounts are a tenant prefix
docs.text:
An account is named by a slug chosen at creation and never renamed: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, at most 32 characters (acme). It is short because it appears in every tenant key, in logs and in keel usage.

The HTTP layer resolves the key to an account and prefixes the tenant: X-Keel-Tenant: cliente-42 under account acme becomes the tenant acme/cliente-42. The prefix is added by the server and cannot be chosen by the client: a tenant header that already contains / is refused when keys are on. Everything below the HTTP layer sees an ordinary tenant, so stores, conformance tests and replay are untouched.

The global partition follows the account: annotate(scope="global") writes to acme/__global__, and reads merge acme/__global__, never another account's. This is the one change inside Tools: the global partition's name is derived from the tenant's prefix instead of being the constant __global__. Without a prefix it stays __global__, so self-hosted deployments see no difference.

Envelopes posted to /v1/ingest go through the same rule: their tenant is prefixed, and one naming another account is refused.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
A new table, api_keys (KEYS is reserved in MySQL), sits in the same store, so there is one backup and rotation needs no restart:

column meaning id public prefix shown in listings (kk_7f3a…) hash SHA-256 of the full key; the key itself is shown once, at creation account the account it belongs to tenant optional: only this tenant agent optional: binds calls to this agent id, as --agent does global true for the account's privileged key: the only one that may annotate(scope="global"), and only into account/__global__ created_at, revoked_at when it was issued and when it stopped working

keel keys create <account> [--tenant] [--agent] [--global], keel keys list <account> and keel keys revoke <id> manage the table. The middleware looks a key up by hash, refuses revoked ones, and caches lookups for a few seconds. When the table is empty, the single secret of today keeps working, so nothing changes for anyone who never creates a key. Once keys exist, the secret stays the operator's credential: it reaches every tenant by its full name.

docs.title: Metering
docs.text:
Counters per tenant, day and item in a metering table: (tenant, day, item, n), where item is events or a tool's name. keel usage [--month 2027-01] [--account acme] groups them by account (the tenant prefix), tenant and month.

  • Events are counted by the Ingestor after each commit: events applied for the first time, from any path. Duplicates and events for a forgotten tenant are not counted, and neither is replay. The first proposal, a recorded_at on ingested, would have billed a replay twice: reset deletes a tenant's applied ids so the log can be applied again. Counting after the commit means a crash in between undercounts, never bills twice.
  • Tool calls are counted but not billed: Tools(meter=) calls the meter once per tool call, and the HTTP transport passes one that keeps counts in memory and writes them every ten seconds and at shutdown (/v1 and /mcp). It feeds quotas, abuse detection and the plain question of whether agents use Keel at all.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text: They go in the same middleware as the keys: a token bucket per account for requests per second, and a check of the month's count against the account's event limit before /v1/ingest applies a batch. Both answer 429 with Retry-After, the way an exhausted embeddings provider already answers 503. Limits are columns on an accounts table that holds only the account id and its limits.

docs.title: Retention as a dated forget
docs.text:
Rule 1 says the graph must be rebuildable from events. Physical deletion of history is compatible with it if the deletion is itself recorded and applied again on every rebuild. That is what forgets: tenant already does for a whole tenant (0.24.0). Retention extends it:

  • An event declared forgets: before in the catalog makes the Ingestor call store.forget_before(tenant, event.occurred_at) in its transaction. It deletes facts (annotations included) and relations whose valid_to is at or before the cutoff. Open facts, current relations and entities stay. The report says what was deleted (retained), and the store keeps the cutoff per tenant, the latest one winning.
  • keel forget <tenant> --before 2024-01-01 --db --yes does the same for operators, and --all-tenants makes it a retention policy to schedule.
