  • replay rebuilds from the log and then applies the kept cutoff again, so what the log brought back goes again.
  • Annotations follow their own TTL (MemoryPolicy). A retention cutoff also removes closed annotations older than it, because a contract that asks for deletion means all of it.

Two simplifications against the first proposal. Applied event ids are kept, because they are what stops an old redelivery from reviving deleted history, and they are hashes, not content. Events are not skipped by the cutoff: an event that occurred before it can still open a fact that is current today, and skipping it would lose that fact. The price is that an event arriving later with a valid time before the cutoff stays until the next run, so the policy is scheduled, not run once.

docs.title: Isolation: a container per account (decided 2026-10-18)
docs.text: A cartridge carries Python (handlers.py). A shared server that loaded every account's cartridge would run one customer's code in a process that holds every other customer's data. So hosted runs one Keel container per account, with its cartridge and its own database, and a shared control plane (sign-up, keys, accounts, usage, a panel) on a shared database. keel serve --account acme --db <shared> makes a server accept only that account's keys and keep its graph in the account's database (accounts.store), while keys, limits and usage come from the shared one. The control plane creates each account's container on Coolify through its API. Declarative handlers, which would let one server load many cartridges safely, stay a later option.

docs.title: Control plane (hosted/)
docs.text: Sign-up creates the account in the control database, a MySQL database and user for it, its first key (the hash written to both databases) and its container on Coolify. The account's container gets only its own database's credentials, so the key and limits it enforces are copied into that database, and the panel reads usage back from it. A customer's handlers can therefore change their own counters; acceptable for invited pilots, to be closed by metering at the edge before billing strangers.

docs.title: Storage per account
docs.text: By default every account shares one MySQL database, isolated by the tenant prefix. An enterprise account can get its own database: the server maps the account to a store URL (accounts.store), opened lazily and kept in a small pool. The store is pluggable already, so this is configuration in the HTTP layer, not a change to any store.

docs.title: Gate before launching hosted
docs.text:
The goal of 0.1 is "used by two SaaS products that are not ours". Building the hosted shell before the demand is the main risk. Hosted launches once all of these hold:

  • [x] A design customer with evaluations in Keel's favour (kagent: +0.35 on the dev assistant, +0.80 on technical instructions).
  • [x] Production wired at that customer (22,285 entities, 79,220 facts, 36,796 events).
  • [ ] Real usage measured in production (today, a weekend of traffic).
  • [ ] A second SaaS pilot with real events.
  • [ ] A customer who asks to pay so as not to run it.

Accounts, keys, metering and dated forget do not wait for the gate. They are small, and they are useful to self-hosted deployments too.

Revised on 2026-10-18 (later the same day): the whole hosted product is built before looking for the second pilot, on the reasoning that a pilot says yes more easily to a hosted Keel it can sign up for than to a deployment it has to run. The gate still decides when hosted is announced and billed; it no longer decides when it is built. Operations run on Coolify.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phase Items Where Now accounts as tenant prefix, api_keys table and keel keys, metering counters and keel usage core Now forgets: before and keel forget --before core Next (revised 2026-10-18) quotas, a database per account, a retention policy per account, Postgres CDC core Next (revised 2026-10-18) operations on Coolify (backups, per-account jobs), self-serve sign-up, a usage panel, SSO in front of /ui through a proxy infra + product

docs.title: Decided on 2026-10-18
docs.text:
• Account names are short slugs chosen at creation and never renamed, because they appear in every tenant key.
  • The global memory of an account is written only by a key created with --global, and only into account/__global__. The SaaS manages its own semantics; no other key of the account can touch them.
  • Tool calls are counted per account, tenant, day and tool, for quotas, abuse and real usage. Billing stays on events ingested.

docs.title: Security review (2026-10-22)
docs.text: An adversarial review (tests/test_security_hosted.py) closed these: an invitation opens one account (hosted_invites, the code its primary key, so two racing sign-ups cannot share it); failed logins and failed invitations are throttled per email and address (10 in 15 minutes, then 429), and an unknown email costs the same scrypt as a known one; a session ends when the account's password changes (python -m hosted password), since it keeps a fingerprint of the password it was opened with; a state-changing request whose Origin is not the console's own is refused, because customer containers on sibling subdomains are same-site for SameSite=Lax; slugs are DNS labels and infrastructure names (www, admin, api, mcp, ...) are reserved; /api/cartridge/check needs a session and a size limit and reports a malformed section instead of failing; the SDK proxy accepts only the four languages; a provisioning error hides the database URL and secret it may echo. Accepted: per-process throttling (one control plane), counters checked before they are written (a burst can pass a daily cap by a little), and /api/slug telling which slugs are taken.

docs.title: Design note: the paper
docs.text: Status: week 1 of 16 (plan at https://claude.ai/artifact/L1ZYTBKwJqx16z8uSKfyyZ). Decided 2026-10-20: a benchmark of our own over the Public Jira Dataset (MSR 2022, Zenodo, CC BY 4.0); five systems (Keel, RAG, the product's API as tools, Graphiti, Mem0); agents openai/gpt-6-luna and anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5; no judge (answers are structured and graded by exact match; decided in week 5); a preprint on arXiv in early February 2027; about 110–140 USD of API.

docs.title: What is not ours to claim
docs.text:
Related work already has these, so the paper cites them and builds on them:

  • A bitemporal store an agent can ask "what did we believe on date X", with retract kept apart from correct: TGMS (arXiv 2607.10265, Apache-2.0), Zep/Graphiti (arXiv 2501.13956), TOKI (arXiv 2606.06240).
  • An append-only log as the truth, replayed to an identical state across backends: TGMS (Kùzu and DuckDB, byte-identical).
  • No LLM where facts become true; deterministic, bounded operators; MCP: TGMS.
  • Fewer prompt tokens because structure stays out of the context: TGMS (about 6.5k tokens per task against 32k for long-context RAG).

docs.title: The thesis
docs.text: Agents inside a product should read the product's own events, compiled deterministically, instead of facts an LLM extracted from text. Every memory system we found builds memory from conversation; none builds it from a product's structured event log, and no study compares the two on cost, fidelity and reproducibility. The evidence so far is indirect: write-time extraction misses or garbles facts (HaluMem, arXiv 2511.03506: extraction recall under 60%; Ground Truth First, arXiv 2607.21962: questions backed by badly written facts fail 24.2% of the time against 1.6%), construction is slow (MemoryAgentBench: Mem0 up to 18,483 s to build memory, BM25 0.1 s), and LLM writers drift on replay (TOKI). Agents also find the new fact and still answer from the stale one (STALE, arXiv 2605.06527: Zep 6.0%, Mem0 8.3%).

docs.title: Claims and the experiment behind each
docs.text:
C1. Deterministic ingest of product events is cheaper, more faithful and reproducible where LLM extraction is not. E1: ingest the same Jira events into Keel, Graphiti and Mem0 (extractor: GPT-6 Luna; one ablation with a stronger extractor). Per 1k events: LLM calls, tokens, dollars, wall time, failures and retries. Write fidelity: precision and recall of stored facts against the changelog, and the rate of facts no event supports. Determinism: ingest twice and once in shuffled arrival order, and diff the graphs. Keel's side needs no model; kagent's numbers (101k events in 8 s on MySQL) set the scale.

C2. That fidelity carries into answers, most of all on time. E2: about 300 questions generated from the changelog, gold computed by replay, in five types: current state, as of a valid time, as known at a recorded time (with injected late and corrected events), multi-hop over issue links, and rule verdicts (blocked, waiting, inherited pause, the rules kagent uses). Plus abstention questions and a closed-book baseline, since public Jira may be in the models' training data. Structured answers (status, assignee, dates, sets of issue keys) are graded by exact or set match; the judge grades only free text. Systems without a recorded-time axis are reported as "not supported" on as-known-at, not scored as failures.

C3. One domain-agnostic core serves different products, with the domain declared once. E3: the cartridges in examples/ (fleet 193 lines, crm 85, finance 142, clinics 77, relay 219), the Jira cartridge and kagent in production, each with zero changes under keel/. E4: TGMS's correction-probe pairs on its own data (SNAP communication networks) through a cartridge, against TGMS's published numbers. Only the probes are comparable; Keel has no motif or reachability operators.

C4. Agents can write memory into the graph under policy the server enforces. TGMS leaves agent write-back open. Keel ships scoped annotate (global, tenant, task, agent), TTL and evidence rules, a per-agent registry, isolation per tenant, and annotations that survive replay. E5: property tests and an adversarial agent that tries to read another tenant, another agent's memory, or a kind it is not registered for; leakage reported as a count (expected 0).

C5 (secondary). How tool results are shaped is a cost and accuracy lever. Already measured (evals/efficiency, 0.31.0): tool-result tokens 45.2k to 12.3k on a fixed call set; Sonnet accuracy 0.90 to 0.98; DeepSeek Flash calls 10.4 to 5.7. In the paper: the brief/full and capped/uncapped ablations inside E2, framed as complementary to TGMS.

docs.title: Evaluation protocol
docs.text:
• Gold from the log, never from a model.
  • Judge: a family neither agent belongs to. Two people label a stratified 20% per question type; report Cohen's kappa and judge-human agreement. Plant wrong answers, stale values on as-of questions among them, and report how many the judge accepts. LongMemEval's rule that a knowledge-update answer is correct while it still mentions the stale value does not apply.
  • Statistics: 3 runs per agent, system and type; bootstrap 95% intervals; paired tests.
  • Fair baselines: same extractor model for Graphiti and Mem0. Graphiti gets JSON episodes, the Jira ontology as Pydantic types, reference_time = occurred_at, one group per tenant, and we wait for its background processing before asking. Mem0 gets one user_id per tenant and timestamps as metadata. Versions pinned; configs and harness published; Zep and Mem0 get a review window before the preprint (the lesson of their LoCoMo dispute).
  • Read side: accuracy per type, tokens per answer (each model's tokenizer), tool calls and turns, p50/p95 latency from the same host for every system.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• The judge (DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813) is not confirmed.
  • E1's write-fidelity scoring for Graphiti and Mem0 means mapping their stored facts back to changelog fields; it may add a week to the harness (weeks 5–7).
  • E4 depends on TGMS's repo running as published.
  • kagent promised keel usage around 2026-11-08: real usage for C3.
  • Transaction time from the envelope (decided 2026-10-20, core change). Until now stores stamped recorded_at, closed_at and link times with the ingest clock, so replay did not rebuild when Keel learned things and late arrivals could not be simulated. Now an event that declares recorded_at writes with it (the Ingestor wraps the store its handler gets); changed_at, a new ingest-clock column, carries the change feed and the watermark so a late event is still a new change. Determinism (E1) can now compare whole graphs, transaction time included; only changed_at and row ids differ between runs.

docs.title: Week 2: the Jira cartridge and adapter
docs.text:
evals/jira/: cartridge.yaml and handlers.py (issues, projects, six link relations, three rules: blocked, stalled, urgent_unassigned; nulls are facts, so a rule can test "nobody assigned"), adapt.py (issues with changelogs in Jira's REST shape, JSON or the dataset's BSON, to events; values named by id as they are today, links recorded from their outward end, moved issues under their final key) and check.py (replay must end where Jira is today). On kagent's 359 cards: 2,341 events, no mismatch with Jira's current fields, the same file byte for byte on a second run.

The tenants, one whole project per Jira instance (whole projects keep links inside the tenant), restored from the dataset's mongodump with mongorestore --nsInclude and exported with mongoexport --jsonArray:

Tenant Project Span Issues Events Links hyperledger INDY (Hyperledger Indy) 2017-04 to 2020-11 2,323 18,036 1,590 (relates, blocks, clones, duplicates) mariadb MXS (MaxScale) 2014-01 to 2021-01 3,333 17,934 805 (relates, blocks, duplicates) spring SEC (Spring Security) 2005-06 to 2016-03 3,150 15,699 630 (relates, duplicates, depends on)

All three: no mismatch with Jira's current fields, and the same graph, transaction time included, in log order, reversed, and three shuffles (memory and SQLite in batches). Ingest takes 0.1–0.2 s per tenant in memory.

Two core bugs surfaced on the way and are fixed, each with a conformance test: a close took the arriving fact's recorded_at instead of the later of the two (so a successor arriving first gave a different closed_at), and facts starting at the same instant (INDY-1393 moved to "To Test" twice in one second) were ordered by arrival, which left two open statuses. A predicate's history is now ordered by valid_from, then recorded_at, then evidence and value.

docs.title: Week 4: questions and gold answers
docs.text:
evals/jira/questions.py fills templates with a fixed seed (7) and computes every gold answer with its own oracle, a walk over the log that imports nothing from Keel. 105 questions per tenant, 315 in all:

Type Per tenant What it asks Gold current 20 a field's value now value as_of 25 a field's value at an instant inside its history; in 80% the value is no longer current, so today's value does not pass for remembering value known_at 25 a field's value at an instant, as recorded by a later one, over the injected windows, before and after the record arrived value links 15 of the issues linked to one by a relation at an instant, which were done (or not) then sorted list of keys rule 15 blocked, stalled or urgent and unassigned at an instant, the definition in the question; yes and no balanced; Spring SEC has no blocks links, so its share goes to the other two bool abstain 5 an issue that does not exist, or a field the tracker does not keep unknown

Instants are whole minutes at least an hour from any change the question reads. None as a value means none (unassigned, unresolved). Statuses whose category no current issue shows (a migrated workflow: Spring's Open, Resolved, Reopened...) take it from a declared table of Jira's standard workflows (FALLBACK_CATEGORIES in adapt.py); without it, 61% of Spring's status events had none and its rules could not be evaluated over history.

--check answers every question with Keel's primitives directly, no agent: 315 of 315 agree. That is the ceiling an agent with Keel can reach, and the oracle and Keel checked against each other. Regenerating gives the same file.

docs.title: Human review (2026-10-20)
docs.text: Angel reviewed the 50-question sheet (review-50.md, stratified by tenant and type, drawn from the final questions) against the issues' history: all 50 ok.

docs.title: Review by independent judges (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Three agents, one per tenant, rebuilt the gold answer of 50 stratified questions (17, 17, 16) from the raw Jira export with code, never from the event log, so a bug shared by the adapter, the oracle and Keel could show. 46 ok, 3 ambiguous, 1 wrong. Fixed:

  • Wrong (an adapter bug): Jira can hold the same link twice (INDY-2293 linked INDY-2292 twice and removed it once; 58 duplicate adds in Hyperledger alone). The adapter treated links as a set, so one removal dropped a link that still existed. It now counts adds and removes, as kagent's exporter did. check.py now also compares each issue's open links with its current issuelinks (relates_to without direction, since Jira shows it outward on one end): no mismatch in the three tenants, 4 with the old adapter.
  • Ambiguous (rule wording): "stalled when it is in progress" tested the indeterminate category, which includes Confirmed (MariaDB) and Waiting for Feedback (Spring); MariaDB also has a status named Stalled. Rule and link questions now list the tenant's statuses that count as done or in progress, and the stalled rule is asked as "idle".
  • Abstentions on fields the raw tracker may hold (sprint, due date: MariaDB has 2,129 sprint changes) were unfair to systems that read raw Jira. Abstentions are now issues that never existed and issues asked about before they were created.
  • Link questions whose linked issues were all in one category made the done/not-done filter moot; now 80% have a mix.

To state in the paper: a correction window's gold answer before the correction arrives is the injected wrong value, a value that never existed in Jira, by design. Jira's "includes" / "is part of" links map to relates_to. An issue moved to another project keeps its old key in the changelog and its new one in issuelinks, so a link to it can split across two keys; links outside the tenant are not asked about.

Round two (24 new link, rule and abstain questions, same method): 24 ok; the three fixes hold. One more change from it: link questions ask only about the tenant's own issues (one asked about MDEV-20119, reached only through MXS issues' links).

docs.title: Week 5: the harness (Keel, RAG, the product's API, closed book)
docs.text:
evals/jira/bench.py. Every system reads the same source, the tenant's log as written (each event with when it happened and when it was recorded, corrections included), in its best ordinary form: Keel's five tools through a real MCP session; RAG with one text record per event, both times in it, hybrid search (dense text-embedding-3-small at 512 dimensions plus BM25, fused by RRF) and an optional issue-key filter; a Jira-like API (get_issue, get_changelog with both times, search_issues); and no tools at all, a contamination control. Same model, same prompt but for the paragraph about the tools, temperature 0. The agent ends with ANSWER: <json>, graded by exact match after normalising (case, none/unassigned, sets of keys, yes/no), so no judge model is needed: every answer in this benchmark is structured. That drops the judge's cost and its bias, and the judge-validation step shrinks to checking the normaliser.

Smoke run (Hyperledger, one question per type, 2026-10-20): Haiku 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, 48 runs, 0.17 USD, every answer parseable. Keel, RAG and the API all answered the six correctly; closed book got only the abstention, so the models do not know these trackers from training. Six questions separate nothing; the differences will be in the full run and in cost (DeepSeek on RAG read 43k input tokens per question, on Keel 15k, on the API 3k).

openai/gpt-6-luna answers 401 through OfoxAI since 2026-10-20 (the gateway's OpenAI account is deactivated; embeddings still work). Agents: to be decided.

docs.title: Graphiti and Mem0 (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
evals/jira/memories.py, pinned to releases at least two weeks old: graphiti-core 0.30.2 (0.31.x came out 2026-10-15 and 10-20) and mem0ai 2.2.1 with its extras (BM25 on). Configured as their guides say for an OpenAI-compatible provider (checked against their current docs): Graphiti with OpenAIGenericClient on Neo4j 5.26 (its Kuzu backend is deprecated and fails in 0.30.2); json_object structured output made Haiku add text after the JSON (5 failed calls in 29), the default json_schema had none. Mem0 with its openai LLM and embedder pointed at the gateway and Qdrant embedded on disk; its OSS SDK refuses a timestamp, so times travel in the text and metadata, as its guide does for dates.

Ingest cost, measured per event with Haiku 5.5 as the extractor (12 events each):

LLM calls Input tokens Output tokens Seconds Graphiti 3.3 9,984 432 11.0 Mem0 1.0 13,398 427 5.9 Keel 0 0 0 ~0.00001 (51,669 events in ~0.5 s)

The whole log through Graphiti would be ~134 hours and ~46 USD. Both ingest the subset the questions touch (asked issues and their linked ones: 2,321 + 1,122 + 938 = 4,381 events), about 12 USD and 7 hours with the three tenants in parallel. That subset is less noise than the other systems read, which favours Graphiti and Mem0; bench.py --subset gives every system the same subset for a like-for-like table. Both systems run through the harness end to end (search_memory).

Agents confirmed (2026-10-20): openai/gpt-6-luna and anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5, no judge (exact match). Luna answered again through OfoxAI the same evening; it is also the extractor for Graphiti and Mem0. Luna smoke run (Hyperledger, six questions): every answer parseable; on Keel 1.8 tool calls and 5.6k input tokens per question.

Pilot finding (2026-10-20): the blocked-rule question defined "blocked while an issue that blocks it is not done" and left out that the issue itself must not be done, which the rule and the gold require. Haiku on Keel answered MXS-1270 (closed at the time, its blocker open) by the definition as written, and said in its reply that Keel's rule evaluated false and why. The wording now states both conditions; the ten blocked questions keep their ids and gold, and their pilot runs are redone.

Pilot findings to act on before the full run (2026-10-20): - The API baseline's changelog lacked each issue's initial values (Jira's history shows them), so the API agent answered unknown to as_of questions whose answer was the initial status. Fixed (4d782cd); the API runs were redone. - Keel rejects times written as in the questions ("2016-09-14 07:38 UTC"): 3 of Haiku's 172 Keel calls failed on it, each costing a turn before the agent sent ISO 8601. Decided with Angel: accept that form in the core after the pilot and before the full run, rerun Keel there, and say so in the paper.

docs.title: A sixth type: questions over the whole tenant (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
The pilot with Haiku on MariaDB saturated: Keel, RAG and the API each answered 105 of 105 (closed book 0 of 90, all "unknown"), and the API was the cheapest (3.2k input tokens a question against Keel's 7.5k; Keel the fastest, 7 s against 17 s). Every question so far names one issue, and for that a per-issue API is enough. Agents inside a product also ask about the whole project at once ("what is blocked today?"), a category the benchmark lacked; it is added, and the one-issue questions stay and are reported as they are.

tenant, 24 per tenant, appended last so the 315 earlier questions keep their text and gold (checked): which issues had a status at an instant (6), how many were in progress (4, a count), where a rule held (6), which changed a field in a window (4), and which had a status as recorded by a later instant (4, over an injected window). Instants keep an hour from every change in the tenant; set answers hold 1 to 41 keys. Keel's primitives agree on all 72 (search(rule=, as_of=) for the rule listings).

Fairness: the API gets what Jira's JQL offers for history, <field> WAS <value> ON <instant> and <field> CHANGED DURING (<from>, <until>), as filters on search_issues; with them it answers the 42 status, count and change questions exactly (checked without an agent). What neither the API nor Keel has a primitive for is reported as found: the API has no rule evaluation and no transaction time, and Keel's search has no as_known_at and no tenant-wide listing of changes in a world-time window.

docs.title: Core changes after the pilot (2026-10-20, decided with Angel)
docs.text:
From the pilot's Keel transcripts: agents copied times as the questions write them ("2016-09-14 07:38 UTC"), which Keel refused (3 of 172 calls); on tenant-wide questions they began by listing every issue with its facts (search(kind="issue", detail="brief", limit=0), 80k to 250k tokens) to count or to orient, then made the right call (search(where=..., as_of=...), 8 to 120 tokens); and search had no as_known_at, so a set "as recorded by K" was approximated. Changes, each with a conformance test, all reruns of Keel to come in the full run:

  • Every time argument takes a trailing " UTC".
  • search(detail="count") returns [{"count": n}], no cap, nothing listed.
  • search(as_known_at=...), as context and history have it.
  • A deployment's ceiling on one listing (max_list, keel serve --max-list), off by default: a report or an export may want everything, and the operator decides; the paper measures Keel with it off.

Extraction refused (2026-10-20). OpenAI's content filter (through OfoxAI) refused Mem0's extraction prompt for harmless Jira text: the same prompt passes on Haiku and DeepSeek, no single line of it is refused alone, and Mem0 carries its last 10 messages in every prompt, so one flagged record refused the next several. A burst of refusals then tripped the gateway's circuit breaker for Luna. Not to charge Mem0 (or Graphiti) for OpenAI's filter, a refused event is retried once with Haiku 5.5 (same price) after a 30 s cool-down and recorded as fallback; refused by both, it is recorded as not stored. The counts go in the paper: an LLM extraction pipeline can decline to store a record, which a deterministic one cannot. - history() with no subject and since/until: the tenant's facts that started in that world-time window (a fifth change, decided with Angel after the pilot showed Keel had no primitive for "which issues changed X between A and B": the agent dumped every issue, 245k tokens, and got 1 of 3). The four MariaDB change questions are answered by one such call each, 450 to 1,000 tokens, all correct (checked without an agent). The pilot's runs with the earlier Keel stay as the "before".

docs.title: TGMS, on the pilot only (2026-10-20, decided with Angel: no budget for more)
docs.text: TGMS 0.8.0 (evals/jira/tgms_system.py) answered 18 of MariaDB's 24 tenant questions with Luna before the spending brake stopped it: 7 correct (39%), 1.22M input tokens a question on average (one question 4.4M), 2.22 USD for the 18 (the brake was 1.50; runs in flight finished). By subtype: status at an instant 4/6, counts 1/4, rule listings 1/6, changes 1/2. Keel with the 200 ceiling on the same questions: 22/24, 21k tokens a question. TGMS loads MariaDB in 2 s with no LLM, as Keel does; its cost is on the read side, its tools return large results. It is not run further (no Haiku, no other tenant, no full run) for lack of budget; the paper reports this pilot as a bounded comparison, says the load was ours (offered to its author for review), and that "as recorded by" questions cannot be answered natively by it.

docs.title: The full run: plan B (decided with Angel, 2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Costs per question measured in the pilot, times 3 tenants and 2 agents (Luna, Haiku). Three repetitions where the comparison is close, one where the gap is far larger than run-to-run noise; confidence intervals by bootstrap over questions. MariaDB pilot runs of systems that did not change since count as their first repetition.

System Questions Reps USD Keel with --max-list 200 one-issue and tenant 3 3.33 API (JQL) one-issue and tenant 3 4.74 RAG one-issue 3 1.06 RAG tenant 1 6.57 Keel without a ceiling (ablation, Luna only) tenant 1 0.98 Graphiti, Mem0 one-issue 1 0.70 Closed book all 1 0.10

About 18 USD, plus ~4 USD to finish the Graphiti and Mem0 ingests; ~10.5 USD spent by 2026-10-20 (TGMS 2.22 of it, not run further). Plan A (three repetitions of everything) was 39.60 USD; plan C (one of everything) 13.20.

docs.title: Claude through the Anthropic endpoint (2026-10-20)
docs.text: OfoxAI stopped serving Claude on its OpenAI-compatible endpoint on 2026-10-20 (protocol_not_supported). The harness now sends anthropic/* models to the gateway's Anthropic messages endpoint with the same system prompt, turns and tools, thinking off (evals/efficiency/run.py, to_anthropic/from_anthropic). The pilot's Haiku "before" rows went through the OpenAI endpoint; every Haiku row of the full run goes through the Anthropic one, so the paper compares Haiku runs from one route only. The gateway bills a Claude prompt above 100K input tokens at 5x, and the cost accounting does too. A 429 now waits the gateway's retry-after (at least 1 s) or 1–3 s with jitter; only an outage waits long.

docs.title: Keel runs with the 200 ceiling (decided with Angel, 2026-10-20)
docs.text: In the MariaDB pilot the ceiling kept accuracy and cut cost: on the tenant questions Haiku answered 10/12 uncapped (1.82 USD, 311k tokens a question; two runs overflowed its context) and 10/12 with --max-list 200 (0.07 USD, 53k tokens; both misses were reasoning over correct data); Luna 23/24 uncapped, 22/24 capped (24/24 in content). Uncapped, a single listing reached 257k tokens and the gateway's 5x rate for Claude prompts above 100K made three questions cost 1.80 USD. So the full run uses the ceiling (the bench's default, --keel-max-list 200); the uncapped ablation runs with Luna only (--keel-max-list 0), and Haiku uncapped is reported from the 12 pilot rows. Keel's per-question costs from the pilot: Luna 0.0005 USD one-issue and 0.0025 tenant; Haiku 0.0010 and 0.0060. Haiku's costs for the other systems were measured on the OpenAI route, without the 5x rate, so the full run sets --max-usd per invocation.

docs.title: Claude straight from Anthropic, and what the credit buys (decided with Angel, 2026-10-20)
docs.text:
Angel has 100 USD of Anthropic credit, usable only for Claude. Three uses, all approved:

  1. Every Haiku run goes to Anthropic directly, not through OfoxAI: the gateway's Claude access failed twice on 2026-10-20, its Anthropic endpoint is served from Bedrock, and its 100 requests a minute are shared with Graphiti and Luna. The Gateway takes this route whenever ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or ~/.anthropic_key is set (run with --with anthropic), through the official SDK; each result records its route. Same list prices as the gateway (Haiku 0.10/0.50 USD per million, five times above 100K prompt tokens); the conversation is cached, so each turn's resent history is billed at 0.1x. Straight from Anthropic, Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 refuse a non-default temperature, so their runs use the default; Sonnet turns thinking off with between_tools, Haiku with disabled.
  2. Haiku moves from plan B to plan A: three repetitions of every system, for narrower intervals.
  3. A frontier subset with Sonnet 5.5 (2/10 USD per million): the tenant questions, Keel with the 200 ceiling and the API, one repetition, three tenants, about 25–30 USD. RAG is left out at that price. It answers the "no frontier model" limitation.

Expected draw on the credit: about 45–55 USD. Luna stays on OfoxAI.

docs.title: Design note: SDKs generated from the cartridge
docs.text: Status: decided on 2026-10-14, in progress. The cartridge is the interface definition, the way a .proto is for gRPC; Keel generates the client code for the languages a product is written in.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. Both sides in the first version. Producer (emit events with typed payloads) and consumer (the five tools, typed with the cartridge's kinds, relations, rules and agents).
  2. Payload notation: a subset of JSON Schema. The short hints stay (id: string, amount: number | null) and grow enums, nested objects and arrays. Keel translates them to JSON Schema draft 2020-12. Every existing cartridge remains valid. See SPEC §5.5.
  3. Our own generator, with templates. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> -o <dir>. Templates are plain Python modules (f-strings), no new dependency; a template engine only if they get hairy.
  4. Languages: TypeScript, Python, Go and PHP. TypeScript first, validated against Toche, then the other three from the same intermediate model.
  5. Consumer transport: Keel's own HTTP JSON API, described by OpenAPI, next to MCP over HTTP on the same server. Same five operations, two transports; the names and semantics never change per transport (SPEC §7.6).
  6. Distribution: a published runtime per language, generated code vendored in the product. The runtime holds the HTTP client and the envelope; the generated file holds the cartridge's types, constructors and constants, and lives in the product's repo like protoc output.
  7. Tenant and agent per request from the product, with a shared secret. Authorization: Bearer <secret>, X-Keel-Tenant, X-Keel-Agent. The product authenticates its users; Keel takes the ids as given (same stance as the agent registry).

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
cartridge.yaml  ->  keel schema  ->  intermediate model (JSON)  ->  template  ->  <lang> file

keel schema <cartridge> prints one JSON document: the envelope schema, every event with its subject kind, owner and payload schema, the entity kinds, relations, rules (with their when), agents and memory policy. It is the generator's only input and a public artifact: a third party can write a template for a fifth language without reading Keel's code.

docs.title: What a generated file contains
docs.text:
• A type per event payload and per entity's attributes.
  • emit.<event>(subject, payload, occurred_at) constructors that return a valid envelope (id as content hash, when the product gives none).
  • Subject helpers per kind: subjects.tire("T-9001").
  • Constants: rule names, agent ids, relation names, scopes.
  • A Client bound to tenant and agent: context, history, search, annotate, related, plus events(batch) to ingest.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
keel serve --transport http --db keel.db --secret-env KEEL_SECRET serves one process for many tenants:

Method and path Body Returns POST /v1/events one envelope or a list ingest report POST /v1/context {subject, as_of?} the context object POST /v1/history {subject, since?, until?, predicate?, scope?} facts POST /v1/search {text} entities and facts POST /v1/annotate {subject, predicate, value, scope?, evidence?, by?} the fact POST /v1/related {subject, relation?} neighbours /mcp MCP streamable HTTP, when the server is started with --tenant the same five tools GET /openapi.json the contract

Errors: 401 wrong secret, 403 a refusal (scope policy, agent registry), 400 bad input, 422 malformed envelope. Every request carries X-Keel-Tenant; X-Keel-Agent is required when the cartridge declares agents. A Tools instance is built per request; nothing is cached across tenants.

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text:
1. Payload notation and keel schema. Shipped.
  2. HTTP transport: the API above, MCP over HTTP for one tenant, headers, OpenAPI. Shipped.
  3. TypeScript template and @keel-context/sdk runtime. Shipped: generated for fleet and finance, exercised from Bun against keel serve --transport http; Toche's own cartridge is the next real test.
  4. Python, Go and PHP templates and runtimes from the same model. Shipped: keel.client (stdlib), sdk/go (module github.com/angelkurten/keel/sdk/go), sdk/php (Composer keel-context/sdk); each exercised end to end against the server.
  5. Publishing: npm (@keel-context/sdk 0.1.0, 2026-10-14), PyPI (inside keel-context), a Go module, Packagist. Registry accounts are Angel's step.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• MCP over HTTP for many tenants from one process (a path per tenant and agent, /mcp/<tenant>/<agent>, each with its own session manager). Not needed by Toche, whose own MCP server will proxy the five tools; one process per tenant covers the rest for now.
  • Whether generated files carry a --check mode in CI (regenerate and diff) from the start.
  • Streaming or batching for POST /v1/events beyond a list per request.

docs.title: Semantic search: research and evals
docs.text: Status: 2026-10-15. Research on vector stores, RAG and hybrid retrieval, plus a labeled eval bench (evals/semantic/) run with real embeddings. Items 1 to 7 of the ranked list shipped in 0.12.0 the same day and were measured again on the bench (end of this note); item 8 waits for real queries.

docs.title: The bench
docs.text:
Three sandboxes built through the real store primitives, each with labeled queries in seven families chosen to probe known weak spots of dense retrieval (evals/semantic/sandboxes.py):

Sandbox Shape Queries fleet 40 units, 160 tires, noisy inspection comments with URLs, one policy 14 cards 125 Jira-like cards in Spanish, 4 clients, comments with URLs and commit hashes, a pause rule 12 finance a household's debts and dues, Spanish, creditors and amounts 8

Families: paraphrase (no shared word), exact, id ("CUS-1990"), crosslang (Spanish query, English document or the reverse), relation (answerable only through a related subject), negative (nothing relevant exists), rule (semantic query plus a rule filter).

KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY=... KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL=https://api.ofox.ai/v1 uv run python -m evals.semantic.run --models small,large

Embeddings are cached by model and text, so reruns are free. A full run embedded about 25 000 tokens per model (fractions of a cent with text-embedding-3-small). tests/test_evals.py keeps the harness working offline.

docs.title: Results (2026-10-15, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and -large through OfoxAI)
docs.text:
MRR@10 per family, all sandboxes:

Configuration paraphrase exact id crosslang relation rule all (small) all (large) substring (today's text mode) 0.00 0.80 1.00 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.28 0.28 dense (today's semantic mode, cartridge policy) 0.78 1.00 0.45 1.00 0.50 1.00 0.82 0.85 bm25 over the same documents 0.45 1.00 0.80 0.00 1.00 0.67 0.58 0.58 hybrid RRF(k=60) 0.59 1.00 0.88 0.80 0.67 1.00 0.79 0.81 dense + exact-key shortcut 0.78 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.50 1.00 0.89 0.95 convex (0.7 dense + 0.3 bm25, min-max normalized) 0.85 1.00 0.78 1.00 0.67 1.00 0.89 0.92 convex + exact-key shortcut 0.85 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.67 1.00 0.93 0.98

Family columns are the small model. Hit@1 over all positive queries: dense 0.72 (small) and 0.83 (large); convex + key 0.86 and 0.97. Precision@10 on relation queries (many relevant subjects): dense 0.50, convex + key 0.88 (small); 0.75 and 0.88 (large). The offline test caught one impossible label in the first run (a tire that did not exist); these numbers are after the fix.

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
1. Dense alone loses on identifiers (MRR 0.45 small, 0.28 large): a pooled vector blurs "CUS-1990" into "some card". Today's substring mode gets every id right. An exact-key shortcut fixes ids with no cost elsewhere.
  2. RRF hurts paraphrases (0.78 to 0.59): with equal weight, a weak lexical leg drags good dense results down. A convex combination weighted toward dense keeps paraphrases and still gains on ids and relations, in line with Bruch et al. (ACM TOIS), who found convex fusion beats RRF and is easy to tune with a few labels.
  3. Lexical carries relation queries (BM25 precision@10 1.00): the client's name in the rendered relation line is an exact word match. Dense spreads over similar-sounding cards.
  4. The cartridge policy is not free. Excluding noisy comments did not measurably help these embedders (noise-only equals no policy). Relation lines help relation queries (precision@10 0.50 vs 0.30) but, combined with the exclusion, cost two paraphrase queries: every tire's document now repeats its unit's model and plate, which makes tire documents look alike. Hypothesis to test next: render relations as key plus one label attribute, not every attribute.
  5. A fixed cosine threshold cannot say "nothing here". Positives' top score starts at 0.36 to 0.39 while negatives reach 0.44 to 0.45; at 0.45 the large model drops 21% of positives to silence all negatives. The literature agrees: absolute cosine is model-specific (text-embedding-3 averages about 0.43 where ada-002 averaged 0.85), so any threshold must be calibrated per model, and better signals are a reranker score or agreement between the lexical and dense legs.
  6. The large model buys little once fusion is in (0.93 to 0.98 MRR at 6.5 times the price). Small with fusion beats large without it.

Caveats: 34 positive queries and 9 negatives, written by us, so results are directional; differences of one or two queries per family are noise. Synthetic queries are known to be easier than real ones (higher lexical overlap); real agent queries from kagent and Toche should join the bench.

docs.title: What the research adds (sources in the research summary)
docs.text:
• Hybrid search is standard in production stores: Weaviate relativeScoreFusion, Elasticsearch RRF retriever, Qdrant sparse vectors, turbopuffer BM25. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval: adding BM25 to contextual embeddings cut top-20 failures from 3.7% to 2.9%, a reranker on top to 1.9%.
  • Seen in our own tests: with 121 vectors, Chroma's HNSW returned at most 90 results however large k was, and which 90 varied when many documents were identical. Keel's widening post-filter loop stops when the index returns fewer than asked, so with an approximate index a filtered match can still be missed. Filtering inside the index (item 6 below) is the real fix.
  • Filtering belongs in the store when a kind is a small slice of a tenant: pgvector 0.8 iterative scans, Qdrant filterable HNSW (99.8% recall at 1% selectivity) and is_tenant payload indexes, sqlite-vec metadata columns. Keel's widening post-filter loop is correct but costs round trips at scale.
  • Asymmetric embedders (multilingual-e5 "query:" / "passage:", Qwen3 instructions) lose 1 to 5% recall without their prefixes; Keel's Embedder.embed(texts) cannot express the role yet.
  • MySQL 9 Community has the VECTOR type but no distance function or index (HeatWave only): not a backend.
  • GraphRAG-style LLM summaries at index time conflict with deterministic ingest; what transfers is query-time fusion and one-hop expansion from top hits.

docs.title: Ranked improvements
docs.text: # Change Evidence here Size 1 Exact-key shortcut in search(mode="semantic") id MRR 0.45 to 1.00, no regression elsewhere XS 2 Hybrid with convex fusion (dense 0.7, lexical 0.3) and a lexical leg over the same documents, deterministic tokenizer overall MRR 0.82 to 0.93 (small), 0.85 to 0.98 (large); relation p@10 0.50 to 0.88 M 3 min_score option, documented as model-specific, off by default; the eval's threshold sweep as the way to choose it negatives cannot be separated by a fixed cut S 4 Compact relation lines (key plus one label attribute) hypothesis from finding 4 S 5 Embedder.embed(texts, role="query"|"document") for asymmetric models research: 1 to 5% recall S 6 Optional where={"kind": ...} in VectorIndex.query, mapped by adapters that filter natively research: recall and round trips at scale M 7 Reranker adapter over the top 30 to 50 fused candidates research: +5 to 15 nDCG points; not measured here M 8 Grow the bench with real agent queries from kagent and Toche synthetic-query bias ongoing

docs.title: After implementation (0.12.0)
docs.text:
The bench now also runs search(mode="semantic") as shipped (keel) and with an LLM reranker (gpt-4.1-mini through OfoxAI, keel+rerank). MRR@10, all sandboxes:

Configuration small large hit@1 small relation p@10 small dense (0.11 behaviour, before compact relations and the key shortcut) 0.82 0.85 0.72 0.50 dense in 0.12 (key shortcut and compact relations, lexical weight 0) 0.90 0.97 0.83 0.62 keel 0.12 (keys, convex fusion 0.7/0.3, compact relations) 0.95 0.98 0.90 0.88 keel 0.12 + LLM reranker 1.00 1.00 1.00 1.00

What shipped matches the best prototype (convex+key) exactly. Compact relation lines (the other side's key and one label instead of every attribute) lifted dense relation precision from 0.50 to 0.62 on their own. The reranker cleared the remaining paraphrase misses, at one chat-model call per search (about a second with a small model) and a few cents per thousand searches. min_score stays off by default: on this bench the best floor (0.45, large model) still drops 17% of positives.

docs.title: Design note: the support showcase
docs.text:
Status: published on 2026-10-19 at https://demo.angelkurten.com (0.30.0). A public page at https://demo.angelkurten.com where a support agent answers the same question twice, once with Keel and once without, over the same data. Decided the same day: a B2B SaaS with subscriptions as the domain; RAG over the same data as the baseline (then RAG plus the product's API, see Fairness); guided scenarios plus a free question; generated data with planted stories; an expected answer and an LLM judge per scenario; openai/gpt-6-sol through OfoxAI on both sides; the Keel side is an account of hosted Keel.

Since 2026-10-19, ahead of the Product Hunt launch, the public page shows the Keel side only (SHOWCASE_SIDES=keel, the default); SHOWCASE_SIDES=keel,rag brings back the side by side described below.

docs.title: What it must show
docs.text:
Keel's claim is that agents inside a product need context with time, rules and scope, and that a pipeline per agent rebuilds it badly. The showcase makes four of those visible, each in at least one scenario:

  1. The customer's context in one call: plan, open tickets, invoices, payments and incidents together, not stitched from search hits.
  2. Time: what was true when something happened, and what was superseded since. Text retrieval mixes current and past.
  3. Rules: SLA breached, refund eligible, account at risk are defined once and evaluated, never improvised by the model.
  4. Scope: one customer's data never answers for another, and memory written for one stays with it.

And it must show what it costs: time and money per answer, side by side, because a context layer that answers better but slower or dearer is a trade-off a buyer has to see.

And it must be fair, or it convinces no one.

docs.title: Fairness rules
docs.text:
• Same model, same base prompt, same help center. Both agents run openai/gpt-6-sol with the same system prompt except the paragraph that describes their customer-data tools, and both get the same search_help tool over the product's help articles. Keel is not a document store; the help center is not what is compared.
  • Same source data. One generator writes the SaaS's events. The Keel side ingests them into a hosted account (one tenant per customer company). The RAG side renders the same events, tickets and invoices as text chunks (one per record, with dates and the customer's name) and embeds them.
  • Each side gets its best ordinary setup. Without Keel (decided 2026-10-19, after the first runs): the product's own API as tools (get_account, list_subscription_changes, list_invoices, list_tickets, get_ticket with its activity, list_incidents, list_integrations, list_contacts), the records' current state rebuilt from the same events, plus top-k similarity search over the events as text, filtered by customer, and a save_note tool (its equivalent of annotate): the strongest agent without Keel we could build. Business rules are not computed for it; it applies the help center's policies itself, as an agent on a product's API does. Keel: the five tools with semantic search on (the same embeddings), the cartridge's rules, nothing hand-tuned per scenario.
  • One scenario RAG should win or tie: a how-to question answered from the help center. It shows both work where they should.
  • Everything is visible: each side's tool calls with arguments and results, tokens, latency and cost per answer.

docs.title: The product: Relay
docs.text:
Relay is a fictional workflow-automation SaaS for teams. Plans: Starter (SLA 72 h), Pro (24 h), Enterprise (4 h, a named CSM). Billing monthly, prorated on plan changes; refunds within 14 days of a charge.

Cartridge relay (one tenant per customer company):

Kind What it is account the customer company (plan, seats, region, CSM) contact a person at the customer (role, language) subscription the plan over time (plan, seats, status as facts with valid time) invoice a charge (amount, status, period) ticket a support ticket (priority, status, category, opened and resolved times) incident a platform incident as it affected this customer (severity, region, start, end) integration a connected app (status: connected, failing, disconnected)

Events (from the SaaS, deterministic): account.created, contact.added, subscription.started, subscription.changed, subscription.cancelled, invoice.issued, invoice.paid, payment.failed, refund.issued, ticket.opened, ticket.status_changed, ticket.commented, incident.affected, incident.resolved, integration.status_changed.

Rules: sla_breached (a ticket open longer than its plan's SLA), refund_eligible (an invoice paid less than 14 days ago with no refund), account_at_risk (a failed payment in 30 days and an open high-priority ticket), integration_failing.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: A generator (showcase/generate.py, seeded, so it is reproducible) writes about 50 customers and six months of events, and plants the stories the scenarios need in seven of them. Some names are deliberately close (Hooli and Hooli Labs) and some records deliberately superseded (a ticket reopened and resolved again, a plan changed twice), because that is where retrieval goes wrong in real products. The same output feeds both sides; a test checks the planted facts hold in both.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Each has a question, the expected answer the page shows, and the strength it exercises. "Today" is fixed at 2026-10-15 so answers do not drift.

# Question Expected Strength 1 Acme says they were overcharged in September. What happened? Pro → Enterprise on Sep 12; the Sep invoice is prorated, not a double charge context 2 Which plan did Globex have when they reported the outage on Oct 3? Pro (upgraded to Enterprise on Oct 10) time 3 Is Initech's sync problem still open? No: reopened Oct 6, resolved Oct 14 time (superseded) 4 Can we refund Umbrella's last charge? No: paid Sep 20, outside the 14 days rules 5 Does Stark have any ticket past its SLA? Yes: T-3112, high, open 31 h on Enterprise (4 h) rules 6 Show Hooli's last two payments. Hooli's, not Hooli Labs' scope 7 Is Wayne's 502 error related to an incident? Yes: INC-7 in eu-west affected them Oct 2 09:10–11:40 context + time 8 How do I set up SSO with Okta? From the help center; both should answer honesty

Two agents, one memory (replaces the first memory pair, 2026-10-19): a support agent records that Lucía Gómez, who receives Acme's invoices, wants them in Spanish; a billing agent, in a new conversation, prepares Acme's November invoice (who receives it, in which language); then Globex's, where nothing about Spanish must appear. With Keel both agents read the same graph: the support agent's annotate (scoped to the run, so a public page never keeps it) comes back in the billing agent's context. Without Keel each agent keeps its own notes, as two agents built separately do; sharing them is infrastructure the baseline would have to add.

What it took to build: a section with each side's files and their real line counts (blank lines and comments left out), and what each brings: Keel's cartridge declares rules that are evaluated, keeps every fact's history, shares memory between agents with scope and evidence, and enforces tenant isolation in the tools; the baseline's API, event-to-text pipeline and index give current state, the activity the API happens to log, per-agent notes, and isolation by a filter in code. The line counts are close; the difference is what the lines buy.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
• Header: one line on what is compared and the fairness rules, linked to this note.
  • Scenario list on the left; on the right, the question, the expected answer, and two columns (with Keel / without Keel), each with the answer, the judge's verdict (correct, partial, wrong, with its reason), the tool calls (expandable), tokens, latency and cost.
  • Guided scenarios show a cached run (date shown) with a "run it live again" button. A free question box runs both sides live, without a judge.
  • Metrics on every answer, side by side: time, cost, tokens and tool calls, as numbers. Wall time covers the whole answer (every model and tool call, end to end), cost comes from the tokens each model call reports at the gateway's prices. The summary band gives the correct answers per side, the median time and the total cost and tokens over the guided runs. No relative percentages (decided 2026-10-19): the absolute numbers are shown and the reader compares.
  • A footer with links: the cartridge, the generator, the data, the code of both agents, hosted Keel sign-up.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• App (showcase/, a FastAPI service and a small page) on Coolify at demo.angelkurten.com: runs both agent loops (reusing hosted/agent.py's loop), the RAG index, the judge, the cache and the limits.
  • Keel side: a hosted account showcase with the relay cartridge, its data ingested once; the app calls it with a key narrowed to read tools (no annotate except for the memory pair, which resets after each run).
  • RAG side: embeddings with openai/text-embedding-3-small through OfoxAI (it serves it), computed once and kept in a file in the image; no vector database to operate.
  • Limits: the free question is capped per IP per day and globally per day; guided runs live are capped the same way. The cache is a JSON file per scenario, refreshed by an operator command.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• Whether the judge is the same model or another, to avoid it favouring its own style.
  • How often to refresh the cached runs, and whether to show the history of past runs.
